Touhou Kishinjou: Double Dealing Character is a fast-paced vertical bullet hell shooter that continues the long-running Touhou Project series with another visually chaotic and mechanically demanding adventure filled with dense projectile patterns, supernatural folklore, and intense arcade-style gameplay. Developed by 上海アリス幻樂団 and published by Mediascape Co., Ltd., the game builds upon the franchise’s established formula while introducing new systems and themes centered around rebellious objects, living weapons, and supernatural imbalance within the world of Gensokyo. Although the game remains brutally difficult for newcomers unfamiliar with bullet hell shooters, it stands out as one of the more refined and creatively designed entries in the Touhou series thanks to its excellent boss encounters, memorable soundtrack, and highly polished gameplay structure.

The story revolves around strange incidents spreading across Gensokyo as ordinary objects suddenly begin rebelling against their owners. Weapons refuse to obey commands, magical tools become hostile, and supernatural artifacts awaken with dangerous intentions. Players can choose between familiar Touhou protagonists including Reimu Hakurei, Marisa Kirisame, and Sakuya Izayoi, each paired with different weapon styles and gameplay variations that significantly affect combat strategy and movement patterns. The premise embraces the series’ signature mixture of Japanese folklore, fantasy absurdity, and lighthearted supernatural conflict while providing a fitting setup for the escalating chaos that unfolds throughout the stages.

Gameplay follows the traditional Touhou structure where players navigate vertically scrolling stages while avoiding enormous waves of enemy projectiles covering nearly every part of the screen. Success depends entirely on movement precision, reflexes, memorization, and the ability to identify safe gaps inside increasingly overwhelming bullet formations. At first glance the game appears visually impossible because of the sheer amount of projectiles flying across the screen simultaneously, but over time players begin to understand the hidden structure behind each attack pattern. This gradual learning process becomes one of the game’s most rewarding aspects.

One of the strongest elements of Double Dealing Character is how smooth and carefully balanced the gameplay feels despite the chaos constantly unfolding on-screen. Every projectile pattern is designed with deliberate spacing and rhythm, allowing skilled players to weave through impossible-looking attacks using extremely precise movement. The hitbox system remains incredibly small, which creates the signature Touhou experience where survival often depends on narrowly slipping through tiny openings between hundreds of bullets. The tension created during these moments becomes deeply satisfying once players begin mastering the game’s mechanics.

The game also introduces new systems connected to the theme of rebellious weapons and aggressive playstyles. Certain mechanics encourage players to collect bonus items and maintain offensive pressure while surviving dangerous situations. These additions reward more active and risky movement rather than purely defensive dodging, giving the gameplay additional depth beyond simple survival. While the core formula remains familiar to Touhou veterans, these subtle mechanical changes help Double Dealing Character feel distinct from previous entries.

Boss encounters are easily the centerpiece of the experience. Every stage culminates in lengthy battles against unique characters who unleash increasingly elaborate spell card attacks filled with complex projectile patterns and visually spectacular formations. These encounters constantly evolve during each fight, introducing new movement challenges and attack variations that test both memory and reaction speed. Some attacks focus on slow precision weaving while others require sudden directional changes and split-second movement decisions. The creativity behind many spell card patterns is genuinely impressive, making boss fights feel both mechanically challenging and artistically expressive.

The visual presentation contributes heavily to the game’s identity. While Touhou games traditionally operate with simpler graphics compared to major commercial shooters, Double Dealing Character compensates through strong art direction and remarkable visual clarity. Projectile colors, enemy attacks, and environmental effects remain readable even during the most chaotic sequences. Backgrounds shift between fantasy landscapes, supernatural locations, and surreal environments that reinforce the game’s folklore-inspired atmosphere effectively.

The soundtrack is another major highlight and remains one of the strongest reasons Touhou games continue attracting dedicated fans. The music combines energetic melodies, rock influences, jazz-inspired compositions, and emotional stage themes that perfectly match the frantic pacing of gameplay. Every boss theme carries its own identity and atmosphere, helping major encounters feel memorable beyond the mechanics alone. The soundtrack constantly maintains momentum and intensity while also contributing emotional personality to the characters and environments.

Replay value is extremely high due to multiple playable characters, alternate shot types, scoring systems, hidden content, and higher difficulty modes. Like many arcade-inspired shooters, the game is designed around repeated playthroughs where players slowly improve through practice and memorization. Completing later difficulties becomes a genuine achievement because of how demanding the bullet patterns eventually become.

Another impressive aspect is the consistency of the pacing. Stages escalate naturally from manageable enemy waves into increasingly complex attack sequences without ever feeling random or unfair. Even during moments where the screen becomes almost completely filled with projectiles, experienced players can still identify safe routes through observation and pattern recognition. This careful balance between chaos and control is one of the reasons the Touhou series remains so respected within the bullet hell genre.

However, the game’s greatest strength is also its biggest barrier. Double Dealing Character is extremely unforgiving for newcomers unfamiliar with bullet hell design. Even on lower difficulties, the sheer volume of projectiles and reaction requirements can overwhelm inexperienced players quickly. The game expects players to improve through repetition, failure, and memorization rather than offering extensive accessibility options or simplified mechanics.

The narrative presentation may also feel underdeveloped for players unfamiliar with Touhou lore. Much of the storytelling occurs through short dialogue exchanges before and after battles, and many character interactions rely heavily on existing franchise knowledge. While longtime fans will appreciate the returning characters and references, newcomers may struggle to connect emotionally with the story without additional context.

Another minor criticism is that the game remains relatively close to the traditional Touhou formula without introducing dramatic structural innovations. While the refined mechanics and new systems help distinguish it somewhat, players seeking major experimentation may find the experience familiar compared to previous entries.

Touhou Kishinjou: Double Dealing Character stands as one of the strongest modern Touhou entries and an excellent example of bullet hell design done right. While its brutal difficulty may intimidate newcomers, players willing to dedicate time to learning its systems will discover an incredibly rewarding shooter filled with creativity, precision, and nonstop adrenaline.

(Cleared on Lunatic 1cc) DDC is one Touhou game I don't see getting much recognition despite how good it is.

This game has one of the most fun gimmicks in the series: You gain resources by collecting a bunch of items by using the point of collection. This rewards aggressive play and makes the stages far more interesting. There are also bosses and patterns with interesting gimmicks like reversing controls, changing hitbox size and in the extra stage, even screenshake. While these can be frustrating at times, they still put an interesting spin on the typical danmaku dodging and force you to approach patterns differently.

The game's difficulty is very low in the first 2 stages and the stage 2 boss is the easiest stage 2 boss of the series. The resource collection system still keeps those stages engaging. Stage 3 is very fun to play through and its boss is one of the hardest stage 3 bosses in the series, but you should have plenty of bombs at this point. The overall pattern difficulty after stage 2 is quite high but you can farm plenty of resources to compensate for it.

The music is very good as well. Stage 3 theme flows well with the aggressive gameplay and stage 5 has what I would call the best stage theme in the Touhou series, with a midboss that syncs well with the music. The final boss theme is also very good as per usual for Touhou.

Overall, Touhou DDC is one of the best games in the series with a fun resource mechanic and interesting gimmicks. (Tip for Reimu A: The first hits of the bomb deal the most damage, so plan out your bombs and use them at the start of the pattern while in range to hit the boss)

The main gimmick of the game is that autocollecting items (through either the Point of Collection or bombing) will generate life and bomb pieces. The only major complaint I have is that the hitboxes on the final boss' 'you grow bigger' attack are a bit janky, especially when playing as Marisa or Sakuya.

Really solid entry, almost as good as 6, 7 and 8.
After a couple of really uneven games this one really feels like a return to form.
Difficulty is challenging enough to not bore you but is not insanely overtuned like in UFO.
Gimmick is simple enough to grasp with *no* RNG whatsoever and depends entirely upon your skill in point collecting.
Resource collecting is tied to said point collecting gimmick and your skill in capturing spellcards which offers great risk-reward gameplay.
Music is phenomenal, there is not a single track that is bad, almost all of them are extremely memorable and final boss theme in particular might be one of the most beautiful songs in the entire franchise.
However there are some minor problems that prevent me from placing this entry next to the great 3 of the early Windows era. Some of the spellcards rely on messing with the player rather than the pure difficulty which is annoying. Sejia's screen flipping is mostly annoying not due to reversed controlls but due to the fact for a moment you won't be able to see your character which feels unfair in a game where pixel perfect precision and split-second decisions are required. Same with Raiko's "Land Percuss" which just uses screenshake to disorient you and that feels cheap. There is a reason why most video games allow player to remove screenshake, making it a gimmick is a bad idea. Shimmy's "You Grow Bigger" feels also unfair as inflated hitbox doesn't feel correctly scaled and you'll get hit by bullets that you swear you should have grazed.
And there is also a bigger problem of once again terrible shottype balancing. Out of the 6 of them 2 feels nearly unplayable. I can kinda get SakuyaB as a gimmick character meant for high-level high score runs, but MarisaA is just unusable. Big hitbox, average dps, bad spellcard, no spread, no homing, no nothing. I wish ZUN would understand that giving a character piercing laser is not a proper advantage when he also doesn't provide any bosses or enemy patters that would actually be weak to piercing attacks.
But other than that - amazing game, highly recommended.

Double Dealing Character kicks off the 3rd and most current generation of mainline Touhou games on Windows. It is at this point in the series where the series starts to feel modern, the past of no visible hitboxes and (relatively) low resolutions. ZUN started exploring the style of each game here, or at least started doing it well. What once felt like "gimmicks" in SA and UFO now feel like style, undeniable personality these games are flowing with that dominates the fell of the 3rd Windows Generation. Double Dealing Character sets the expectation of what it means to own the concept of style. This game isn't the most notable on the surface, the patterns aren't as absurd as LoLK, the difficulty isn't as looming as UFO, the gameplay mechanics aren't as in depth as UM, however, it excels at polish in gameplay feel, presentation, and having the best self-contained plot in the series. In every aspect of the game you get a unshaking feel of professional execution. This isn't to say that this game is some higher art and transcends the scope of the series, it is still a Touhou game, but through and through it is excellent.

ZUN has really honed his craft by this point in the series and I feel this is the last tried and true, pure to the Touhou formula game in the series and I believe the effort, precision and quality are shown best through the natural progression of the game. During stage one, you visit an area seen often before, the Misty Lake, but it now looks and feels modern, and the music sounding more realistic, using more natural sounding instruments. These more natural and "earthy" instruments are consistent through the game, making the feel of the soundtrack stand out in comparison to most of the series, focusing more on execution and tone more so than bombastic melodies or insane pace that other soundtracks are known for. Some of my favorite songs from Double Dealing Character are Magical Storm, Illusionary Joururi, The Shining Needle Castle Sinking in the Air and Primordial Beat ~ Pristine Beat. All of the aforementioned tracks are more low-key in production but all add to the atmosphere of their respective sections in the entry, Primordial Beat getting special mention for incorporating Raiko's main feature, drums, for the solo of the song, creating an even more thunderous atmosphere for the Extra boss. 

With Raiko being mentioned, it is hard to ignore the strength of the latter half of the cast of Double Dealing Character. Benben and Yatsuhashi being a personal favorite pair of the genre of characters that show up in pairs. Seija being one of the coolest characters in the series, so much so ZUN thought that he could make a spinoff with her (Impossible Spell Card). Personally Shinmyoumaru isn't fantastic to me but I can't deny her danmaku being interesting and her motives are fun to play with and consider for the entire hierarchy of Gensokyo. Raiko leaks swagger like a broken faucet and is a joy to fight and look at. Not to mention there's not a single design in this game that isn't interesting to look at or marvel. These characters all have that sense of individuality that looms over this entire game. I wouldn't say any of them are lacking love design wise or personality, they all fit in with the overarching theme of this game being society being flipped on its head. With that theme being considered, these designs aren't overtly glamorous or colorful (outside of Seija lol) but have the sense of quality and planning put into them, which in turn makes them all feel thoroughly fleshed out. 

Visually this game is fantastic, the Misty Lake return already being mentioned in how revitalizing it feels, but the same applies to the Bamboo Forest of the Lost. The stage, in all aspects feels like playing Imperishable Night stage 4 all over again with a modern twist. And with IN Stage 4 being one of  my favorite stages in the series, is an extremely fun call back. The storms that crash upon Stage 4 and the Extra Stage have fun elements of music syncing with lighting crashes on the stage, and a real sense of motion moving above the skies of Gensokyo. But obviously the greatest visual piece in this game is the Shining Needle Castle, the intro to Stage 5 with the castle being actively flipped and the stage enemies spawning in what seems to be an upside down pattern is one of the most memorable moments in the series and still takes my breath away sometimes. While flipping is being mentioned, obviously Seija does it too, and its fun there as well. Visual clarity in this game is fine too, no real complaints about it. The danmaku in this game looks fantastic, Banki throwing her head around, Shimmy making her bullets big and then making you big afterwards is fun, Seija flipping everything is fun too, great overall. 

Gameplay wise, DDC is in a bit of a weird spot. The patterns and raw difficulty of dodging is rather high, but the main gameplay mechanic is extremely intuitive and abuseable almost. This is where I mention how busted half of the shot types in this game are; for each character in this game you get the choice of using a cursed weapon with them or not. For Reimu this is her Gohei, Marisa it is her Hakkero, and Sakuya it is her knife. Each character has something busted. Reimu A can tap focus with her Gohei out to keep it over a boss to melt them quicker than intended. Marisa B has a bomb where you can farm life pieces with it if used correctly. Sakuya A has the second best survival bomb in the series that can refund you a bomb eventually with enough uses. Everyone has something busted, which in a way makes sense with the plot, instruments are being put on top of society so of course instruments used by the MC's would be better. This added tool of busted shot types and rather abusable way to gain lives in this game don't make it too tough to 1CC, but it does require some commitment to route. The main mechanic of this game is rewarding the player with either a spell card fragment or a life piece dependent on how many items are collected at the Point of Collection. This mechanic isn't a drastic, gameplay changing one like the mechanics in UFO or UM, but it is there and is constantly on the players mind on how to utilize it. I'd call it classy in execution and feel, it feels fantastic to chain life pieces from jiggling around the POC and rewards routing to find when the best times to go to the POC are. 

Classy is the best way to descibe this game in my opinion, everything feels classy and polished, nothing extremely foreign to the series (outside of the screen FLIPPING), but this is done well. The old stuff is polished and feels modern, and the new stuff added feels like logical continuations of standards set in the series. I don't believe ZUN was trying to go back to basics with this game, unlike he deliberately stated for HSiFS, although how I'm describing this game it may seem like it. I believe his goal was more to set the standard for the modern Windows generation. That standard being a focus on building on what the past 13 games had laid the groundwork for and making these games still feel unique, even after (at that point) 17 years of installments. And in this he succeeded. DDC is fantastic, a great starting point for those turned off by early Touhou crust. DDC set the standard for what it means to be "modern" for a very in concept and practice at times archaic series.

The 14th installment in the Touhou Project series, Double Dealing Character, offers a heap of unique gimmicks, but some falter in increasing the game's fun factor. 

Touhou Kishinjou ~ Double Dealing Character, tells the story of a social uprising in Gensokyo, where the weak gain power in an attempt to rule over the strong, but behind the scenes, not everything is as it would appear. Like the plot, this entry in general strays away a bit from the series' norm. The gameplay is similar to that of others in the series, but the shot types offer unique abilities. Thematically, this is because of the main characters' weapons of choice becoming tsukumogami, which are basically living tools, after the weak of Gensokyo are filled with an otherworldly power. All of the characters have different, more powerful bombs to use, and pulling them off correctly in a tough spot is very satisfying. Obtaining extra lives and bombs in this game is a bit different too, as you can only do so by obtaining a certain amount of point items at the collect line. Basically, to get enough items to survive in this game, you're going to need to quickly kill enough enemies and then head to the top of the screen to grab all the items that they dropped before they fall to the bottom. This mechanic is rough to get used to at first, but before too long you'll find yourself becoming a master of aggressively obtaining items. You won't make it far in this game if you don't learn this skill. While DDC isn't too difficult for an experienced player, it's tougher than a lot of other Touhou games, so it's definitely not a good one to start with if you're new to the series.

Now, let's get to my less than positive thoughts on this game. I have mixed feelings for Double Dealing Character, and that's not to say I think it's a bad game, but it's just kind of average due to a few flaws it has. Firstly, I don't find the danmaku anywhere as unique as other games. However, I think it's made up for by the unique gimmicks that a few of the bosses have, like Sekibanki's flying heads, Kagerou's wolf mode that lunges at you, and Seija's headache of a screen flipping mechanic. Whether you've played this game or not, you've definitely heard about the latter. Besides that though, the danmaku isn't remarkably original. But it's worsened by the frankly awful visibility in some of the later levels. What I mean by that is the bullets will often blend into the background due to their similar colors. This is really bad in stages 3 and 4; it's like trying to shuffle through bullets in a deadly mist. You can't really tell when a bullet is a bullet until it's too close to you, so it just ends up feeling unfair when you eventually get hit by one. I've never had this problem in any other Touhou game, and it really makes me question why ZUN chose such vibrant colors for those stages. Not only are these colors what create the problem, but they also don't even make thematic sense. Stages 3 and 4 both take place during the night, therefore, you would expect a lot darker of colors.

Moving on from the gameplay, I don't have much else overwhelmingly positive to say. The soundtrack is good like usual, but I think it marks a downward spiral with the quality of the music in the Touhou Project series. Some tracks, like Wakasagihime's theme, are just downright terrible, and quite a few are just forgettable or  blatantlyoff-sounding. There are a few hits, like the stage 4 theme, and Shinmyoumaru's theme, but both don't have as much impact when being listened by themselves. My opinion on Shinmyoumaru's theme improved after hearing it played in the game.

Similarly with the soundtrack, I don't have that many positive feelings for DDC's story and cast. I do respect how ZUN tried to do something different with the plot, since he mostly keeps the subject of social problems and politics embedded in more obscure works of his. But I think that he really should've developed the themes of the revolution-focused story much more, because otherwise, it's simply not effective. I believe that ZUN really wanted to tell a proper story of how revolutions, and salvation-seeking people in general are taken advantage of by power-seeking opportunists, but because of it's format as a game, and Touhou's general themes, his ambition could not be fully accomplished. Such a plot probably sounds a bit too serious and philosophical. 
 When it comes to the cast, I honestly don't care for the characters themselves that much; the only ones I can say I've grown a liking to are Sekibanki and Seija. It's apparent to me that ZUN tried to create characters who came across as feeling more western, with Wakasagihime being a mermaid, Sekibanki being a dullahan, Kagerou being a werewolf, and Shinmyoumaru being an inchling. The backstory of inchlings does have it's roots in Japanese culture, but fictional races of miniature people are more frequently depicted in Western works. 

In summary, Touhou Kishinjou ~ Double Dealing Character is a decent addition to the Touhou Project series, but no game is without it's flaws, and this one has too many for me to give it a mostly positive review. I recommend this game if you're a Touhou fan, but unless you're able to look past these aforementioned flaws, you won't be blown away. If you're new and looking for your first Touhou game to play, this one probably isn't for you unless you believe yourself to be above average at bullet hell games. Check out DDC if you think it's for you, but most importantly, have fun!

Why?

[h1]Game balance[/h1]
This game has, in my opinion, one of the most linear increases of difficulty of any Touhou game as a Normal/Hard mode player. This makes it really nice and easy to pick up, and very thoroughly enjoying in that you can pick it up, play a good chunk of time before getting frustrated, then continue it some other time with actual progression.

Here's why [spoiler]Kagerou's spellcard[/spoiler] difficulty increase in Stage 3 is not bullshit: it actually serves a great stepping stone into stage 4, which has always traditionally been a stage where the difficulty ramps up very heavily, making it a pretty big barrier to those who want to complete the game; instead of suddenly being hit with a very big wall to climb, you have a bigger challenge, and smaller increases of difficulty from stages 3-6.

The Extra stage is on hard difficulty, stage 5-ish level. Not impossible to beat, but it does mean you need to retry a few times before getting the hang of it. As usual, there's also a whole bunch more spellcards you have to beat as well, in comparison to a regular end-of-stage boss.

[h1]'Fun'[/h1]
As much fun as you can get from constantly dying from colliding into projectiles. There's WAY MORE FUN in later stages which have nice, intuitive gimmicks (no spoilers, but it's a lot of """fun""").
Gameplay mechanics wise, this game rewards you very generously with bomb/health shards for collecting a large number of powerups at once by moving to the top of the screen collection point. This is a very fun and risky gameplay element, and allows you to pull some very cheese strats with certain characters (the 2.0 *ding ding ding* sounds)

[h1]Music[/h1]
One of the more memorable soundtracks. Stage 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 bosses and extra stage has some nice sounding tracks. One of the first modern-era 2 games to start using synth and electric guitars to have a more gritty feel, in addition to ZUNpets.

Разработчики проделали колоссальную работу над созданием уникальной эстетики, где каждый уголок локаций наполнен деталями, рассказывающими свою историю. Исследование кажется по-настоящему захватывающим, ведь никогда не знаешь, что скрывается за следующим поворотом.

Геймплей представляет собой смесь выживания и хоррора, где каждая стычка с противниками требует тщательного планирования и использования ресурсов. Ощущение уязвимости и постоянной угрозы не покидает, заставляя играть осторожно и продумывать каждый шаг. Элементы головоломок органично вплетены в повествование, добавляя глубины и стимулируя умственную активность.

Сюжет, хоть и нелинейный, постепенно раскрывает тайны этого странного мира, оставляя пространство для интерпретаций. Атмосферное звуковое сопровождение усиливает эффект присутствия, а порой заставляет сердце биться чаще. "The Lar" — это не просто игра, это опыт, который надолго остается в памяти.

The Lar is, despite its simple appearance, a lovely game, filled with a lot of personality and charm. While the English translation is very lacking, the personality and humor still shines through, even if it took me a second gameplay to really understand the plot. The parts that made the poor translation the most problematic were those, where it was unclear whether to take a word literally or figuratively. For example [spoiler] The abyss is not simply a literal hole in the ground, but is in fact a metaphysical space that holds much power. [/spoiler] It's issues like these that made it hard to keep up with the plot. 
However, despite those issues, if you're patient enough with the game, it will be an enjoyable experience.

From a visual standpoint I can say that the sprites look absolutely delightful and add a lot of personality to the game. In a quite stark contrast the interior design appears fairly unsettling and creepy, which allows the game to still feel serious, despite its colorful characters. 

If there is one thing I'd outright criticize, it's the fact that it's unclear who is speaking at which times. Sure, the characters light up when they're talking, but the difference in color is so slim, that I often had troubles knowing who was speaking at any given moment.

Finally I can say that this game is a hidden gem that absolutely deserves to be played and supported. This holds especially true, once the game has received a proper English translation.

The way this game was built is so dangerous that not even piracy will be able to preserve it. It is entirely realistic to say that, in the future, the only way to experience The Outlast Trials will be by watching YouTube videos.

Don't get me wrong. The Outlast Trials is possibly the best game I've ever played in my life. Its gameplay, atmosphere, sound design, visuals, co-op, lore, difficulty, and replay value are simply masterpieces. It's a game I genuinely love and would like to keep playing for many years.

However, I cannot give it a positive review because of one major concern: the game is entirely dependent on Red Barrels' servers to function.

If Red Barrels eventually decides to shut down the servers, we will lose access to the entire game, regardless of how much we love it. There is currently no offline mode or alternative that would allow players to continue playing without official server support.

This is not just a hypothetical concern. Red Barrels' own End User License Agreement explicitly states that the company may suspend or cancel the game at its discretion, and also makes it clear that offline access will not be provided. In other words, the possibility of losing access to the game is already covered by the terms players agree to when purchasing and playing it.

Unfortunately, adding a peer-to-peer system and an offline mode at this stage would be a significant technical challenge for Red Barrels, considering how the game is currently built. The developers have previously explained that the game was designed around an online multiplayer infrastructure, involving dedicated servers, player progression, friend and party systems, and gameplay mechanics built around dynamic systems such as enemy AI and random events. This means that transitioning to a player-hosted or fully offline experience would likely require much more than simply changing how multiplayer sessions are hosted. If, in the future, the revenue generated by the game becomes lower than the cost of maintaining its servers, developing an update to make the game playable offline might be too expensive to justify financially. This could make the eventual disappearance of The Outlast Trials almost inevitable unless the community puts enough pressure on the developers to find a solution.

I don't expect Red Barrels to maintain its servers forever. That would be unrealistic, but I do believe players should have the opportunity to keep enjoying a game they purchased, even after official support comes to an end.

The Outlast Trials is at its best when you think you finally have a trial figured out. You know where the objective is, your Stun Rig is ready, and then you turn a corner and immediately forget the plan.

I mostly play solo, and that’s where the sound design really gets me. Hearing footsteps in the next room while I’m trying to finish an objective makes me second-guess whether I have time for one more move. And landing a last-second stun to get out of a bad spot is still one of the most satisfying things in the game. Co-op brings a different kind of chaos. Somebody says “I got this,” and suddenly everyone’s running.

My biggest gripe is that replaying familiar objectives can start to feel like a grind, especially when I’m farming event tokens. Once I know the routes, some of that first-run fear wears off. But I still catch myself trying to shave time off a solo clear, only to end up hiding under a table because I got greedy.

If you like horror games where you can get better at surviving and still get humbled by one bad decision, this one’s easy to recommend.

The Outlast Trials has become one of my favorite games over the last year. I picked it up towards the end of 2025 and play it constantly. The game follows a simple gameplay loop of solving puzzles while dodging the enemies and the traps they lay around the map. In this game there is not really much of a way to fight back. You are the pray. Your goal is to finish the puzzle before you die. Some of the funniest moments I've ever had while gaming come from this game. It's a fantastic horror game when you start but slowly as you get better and better it becomes less of a horror game and more of a fun puzzle game. It's decently customizable. Difficulty, custom mission modifiers, outfits, tools, perks, and upgrades are all at your choosing. As much as I love this game, I have also never been more pissed off at the bullshit that this game can and will throw at you. Sometimes you'll be at full health and an enemy will show up out of nowhere and mollywhop you causing you to stumble and fall onto a trap or gas mine. There's always an event going on for you to participate in. There are multiple game modes as well. There's a roguelike, a PvP, Custom Missions, and the base game. There's a continuous ongoing story that you actively participate in. I confidently say that this is a 9/10 game for me and my friends.

Wordle 3, developed by PreoNus Games and published by Gigantum Games, is a casual word puzzle game that takes inspiration from familiar wordplay concepts and reshapes them into a more expansive, replay-focused experience tailored for PC players. Instead of centering itself around a single daily challenge, the game offers a broad selection of levels, categories, and scoring systems that encourage extended play sessions and steady progression. It positions itself as a relaxed but mentally engaging title, aimed at players who enjoy testing their vocabulary without the pressure or rigidity often found in more competitive puzzle games.

At its core, Wordle 3 is about constructing valid words from a given pool of letters. The rules are easy to grasp, making the game immediately accessible: players combine letters to form words, with longer and more complex words yielding higher scores. This simplicity is one of the game’s strengths, as it allows players of varying skill levels to participate comfortably. However, beneath this straightforward premise lies a scoring and progression system that rewards creativity, pattern recognition, and linguistic flexibility, pushing players to think beyond obvious or common solutions.

One of the defining features of Wordle 3 is its extensive use of themed categories. Rather than pulling words from a single, generic dictionary, the game organizes challenges around specific topics such as food, space, textiles, hygiene, and many others. These themes subtly shape how players approach each puzzle, as familiarity with a category can influence word choice and strategy. This design choice keeps the experience fresh over time and prevents the gameplay loop from becoming stale, while also adding an educational element that expands vocabulary within specific subject areas.

The inclusion of power-ups and special mechanics further distinguishes Wordle 3 from simpler word games. These features can modify how letters behave, enhance scoring potential, or provide assistance in particularly challenging situations. While not overly complex, these additions introduce small tactical decisions that add depth to the otherwise relaxed pacing. Players must decide when to use these tools for maximum benefit, striking a balance between experimentation and efficiency.

Presentation is clean and understated, clearly designed to keep the focus on the words themselves. The interface is readable and intuitive, with letter tiles, scoring information, and category indicators laid out in a way that minimizes distraction. Visual flair is minimal, but this restraint works in the game’s favor, especially during longer sessions where clarity and comfort are more important than spectacle. Audio elements are similarly subtle, offering gentle feedback for successful word creation without becoming repetitive or intrusive.

Progression in Wordle 3 is tied closely to achievements and completion goals. With a sizable list of Steam achievements, the game provides additional objectives beyond simply earning high scores. These challenges encourage players to explore different categories, experiment with longer or less obvious words, and fully engage with the game’s systems. For completionists, this adds a layer of long-term motivation that complements the otherwise casual structure.

Replayability is one of the game’s strongest qualities. The combination of varied categories, flexible word creation, and achievement-driven goals ensures that sessions rarely feel identical. Players can dip in for a few minutes to solve a handful of puzzles or settle in for extended play as they chase higher scores or unlock remaining achievements. This adaptability makes the game well suited for both quick breaks and longer, more focused sessions.

That said, Wordle 3 does not aim to provide narrative depth or complex puzzle mechanics. Its appeal lies squarely in repetition refined through variety rather than through evolving systems or story progression. Players seeking dramatic twists, intricate logic puzzles, or competitive multiplayer elements may find the experience too gentle. However, this simplicity is intentional, positioning the game as a low-stress, mentally stimulating pastime rather than a demanding challenge.

Overall, Wordle 3 succeeds as a polished and content-rich word puzzle game that expands upon familiar ideas without overcomplicating them. Its themed categories, scoring incentives, and achievement structure give it longevity, while its accessible design ensures that it remains welcoming to a wide audience. For players who enjoy wordplay, vocabulary building, and relaxed puzzle-solving, Wordle 3 offers a satisfying and thoughtfully constructed experience that rewards curiosity and creativity over speed or pressure.

Wordlee 3 once again presents itself as a word-based puzzle game, following closely in the footsteps of the previous entries. It offers the same categories, the same core mechanic of connecting adjacent letters to form words, and the same extremely minimal interface. The presentation still feels more like a prototype or a student project than a polished, commercially released game.

However, despite the familiar setup, something has finally changed. While the first stages feel too easy, with obvious words and levels that require very little thought, I began to notice a clear increase in difficulty around the halfway point. I often found myself restarting levels after making a mistake while connecting letters, which made it impossible to complete all the words needed to finish the puzzle. This challenge was entirely missing from the previous titles and added a welcome layer of tension. I genuinely appreciated this, as games like this need a real sense of challenge in order to be satisfying. Starting from the middle of the experience, Wordlee 3 finally manages to deliver that.

Regarding the price, unfortunately it is still completely unreasonable. Seeing this game listed for as much as $29.99 continues to make it feel like an amateur product being sold at a premium price. That said, if bought on sale for just a few cents, Wordlee 3 becomes the most justifiable purchase in the series. Compared to the previous games, it offers a bit more variety and introduces a challenge that gives the experience more weight.

One last point concerns the audio. Although there is still no background music, several sound effects have been added. I must admit they make the gameplay a bit more pleasant and provide some light satisfaction as you progress. Unfortunately, there is no option to adjust or disable these sounds, which may be an issue for players who prefer to play in silence or use their own music.

In conclusion, Wordlee 3 remains a simple and minimalistic title. However, for the first time in the series, it starts to show signs of care and thought behind its design. While it is still far from being a truly good game, it can be considered a worthwhile purchase, but only if found at a heavily discounted price.

Congratulations, you're 99% done with the game already. Aside from a few obscure words that may take a moment to remember, you're just dragging your mouse across words to spell them.

Maybe, just maybe that has some minimilist puzzle value to you; but you know what it might have been worth? Less than $1. And for years on Steam, that's basically what these games cost. They were $1 and then would go on sale for even less. Under a dollar for a quick simple puzzle and easy achievements? It has its place for some people.

But these games have had their price raised to $20 each. It wouldn't be worth $20 for all of them, let alone each.

And worse than that they get more low effort with each new game. Each game has less words and even less "challenge" when there wasn't much to begin with. By Wordle 4 many of the chapters are a single puzzle and it even tells you what letter the words start with. It even breaks the value of how hints work (which would start by revealing letters from start to end) because you already knew the first letter due to the new (simpler, dumbed down) chapter headings.

As a series it went from low effort, low value puzzles at a cheap price to low effort, lazy, stupid puzzles for an even higher price.

And if you're curious why I have hours in it: 1. I play these dumb games for achievements. 2. You have to run the game for even longer to get the card drops, which gives it a few cents of meta-value in some weird twisted way.
---

Bottom line: I can't recommend this junk unless you're intentionally buying it as a super cheap bundle just for the sake of stupid achievements. Just be aware of what you're getting. Whatever you paid, it probably won't be worth it.

Disc Space is a focused multiplayer sports game that takes Ultimate Frisbee and converts its passing, movement, positioning, and teamwork into an accessible competitive experience. Developed and published by Vadim Slyusarev, it was released on November 13, 2020 as a free-to-play title. Rather than attempting to imitate the feature-heavy structure of major sports franchises, the game concentrates on a relatively unusual sport and builds its identity around quick team matches. Its modest scope is immediately apparent, but that simplicity is also one of its strongest qualities because players can understand what the game wants from them without working through complicated management systems or lengthy progression mechanics.

The main attraction is Ultimate Frisbee played with teams of different sizes. Disc Space accommodates up to ten online players and provides 3v3, 4v4, and 5v5 configurations. These formats create meaningful differences in how matches unfold. A 3v3 contest leaves more open space and places greater responsibility on each participant, while larger teams create additional passing opportunities and make coordinated positioning more important. The basic idea is easy to grasp, yet effective play requires more than simply chasing the disc. Players need to anticipate where teammates are moving, create passing lanes, recognize defensive openings, and avoid giving possession away through reckless decisions.

Teamwork is consequently at the heart of the experience. Disc Space works best when players treat themselves as components of a coordinated unit rather than attempting to dominate every possession individually. Moving into useful areas when a teammate controls the disc can be just as valuable as making the eventual throw. Defensive awareness is similarly important because disrupting passing routes and applying pressure can force mistakes. This produces a satisfying rhythm in which possession can shift quickly, and successful scoring sequences often feel like the result of several players contributing rather than a single character performing everything alone.

The game also provides computer-controlled opponents, which is an important addition for such a multiplayer-oriented concept. Players can compete with friends or face Computer AI, allowing newcomers to familiarize themselves with the mechanics without immediately entering human competition. AI matches also give Disc Space some usefulness when a full group of players is unavailable. Human opponents naturally provide more unpredictability, but the computer option makes the game less dependent on matchmaking and provides a practical environment for understanding movement and throwing before facing more experienced players.

Another notable feature is the specialization system. The Steam description lists Handler, Cutter, Cannon, Newbie, and D-Machine as selectable play styles. These choices introduce some role-based identity to the otherwise straightforward sporting structure. Instead of every participant approaching a match in exactly the same fashion, players can select a specialization that better reflects how they prefer to contribute. This encourages experimentation and helps emphasize the team-based nature of Ultimate Frisbee. Someone who enjoys controlling possession may naturally gravitate toward a different role than a player who prefers aggressive movement or defensive responsibilities.

The specialization concept is particularly effective because it adds variety without making Disc Space unnecessarily complicated. The game does not need an enormous collection of character statistics or elaborate tactical menus to establish distinct approaches to play. Its roles are enough to encourage players to consider what their team needs and where their own strengths fit. This makes the experience accessible while providing additional depth for players who spend enough time learning how different specializations complement one another.

Disc Space's presentation is similarly functional. Its 3D visuals prioritize clarity over realism, which suits a competitive game where players constantly need to identify teammates, opponents, available space, and the movement of the disc. Anyone expecting detailed stadiums, elaborate broadcast presentation, realistic athletes, or the production values associated with expensive sports simulations will find the package considerably more restrained. However, visual simplicity helps keep attention on the actual competition. The third-person perspective also provides a suitable view of the surrounding field and reinforces the importance of situational awareness.

The relatively lightweight nature of the game extends to its technical requirements. It asks for only 200 MB of available storage, although the listed minimum requirements include 8 GB of RAM, DirectX 11, an Intel Core i3 or AMD equivalent processor, and graphics hardware comparable to a GTX 660 or Radeon HD 7950. Recommended specifications move to a Core i5-class processor and GTX 960 or Radeon R9 280-class graphics card. Broadband internet is required for its online functionality, while Steam also lists partial controller support. English is the supported interface language.

Where Disc Space is most vulnerable is in its limited overall scope. Its Steam description revolves almost entirely around Ultimate Frisbee matches, AI competition, multiplayer, and specialization choices. Players looking for a substantial career mode, story campaign, extensive customization, numerous sporting disciplines, or a huge collection of alternative activities will not find that kind of package here. Enjoyment therefore depends heavily on whether the central Ultimate Frisbee gameplay remains entertaining over repeated matches. The focused design is admirable, but it inevitably narrows the game's appeal.

That narrow focus becomes less problematic because Disc Space is free to play. There is very little barrier to trying it, and friends can experiment with the game without everyone needing to purchase a copy. The combination of online PvP, online cooperative functionality, computer opponents, and several team configurations gives the relatively small concept enough flexibility to work as a casual group activity or a more competitive team game.

Overall, Disc Space is an interesting example of how a less commonly represented real-world sport can translate effectively into a multiplayer videogame. Its strongest elements are the flexible team sizes, emphasis on coordinated passing and positioning, computer AI option, and specialization system. Its principal weakness is simply that there is not an enormous amount surrounding those core mechanics. For players attracted to Ultimate Frisbee or uncomplicated team-based competition, however, that focus can be a virtue rather than a limitation. Vadim Slyusarev, serving as both developer and publisher, created a straightforward sports game that understands its niche and largely stays committed to it.

I laughed when I watched the trailer; DiscSpace looks and plays really simple at first. But when my friends and I came up against some veterans, oh boy... it all flipped. We soon realised what we thought were limited controls were actually anything but and found ourselves forced to devise plays and movements with continual communication just to clinch the tightest of points all the while clenching the tightest of cheeks. I think the trailer massively underplays some of the gameplay i've experienced.

So why isn't it so popular...?
Reading a few comments its possible people are playing it in a way it wasn't designed. For instance some complain about the path of the frisbee in that it requires almost no thought in accuracy which looks ridiculous – and this is true, the game is about a lot lot more.

I have no idea whether the devs intended to make a game that required so much thinking and strategy, but when you're up against good players this is exactly what happens – and just when you think you've nailed it, you come up against an opponent with a completely different playing style.

My only gripe is the small player-base which I can only assume is partly because many underestimate the gameplay. This is without a doubt one of my favourite games this year, and definitely up there as an all time fave.

Developed and published by David Czarnowski under the davidczar label, Clawfish is a delightful indie title that reimagines the concept of fishing through an inventive arcade-inspired premise. Instead of casting rods into rivers or lakes, players visit a quiet fishing arcade near a lonely train station where fish are captured using claw machines. This unusual blend of fishing, exploration, and crane-game mechanics gives the experience an identity that immediately separates it from traditional fishing simulators. Rather than emphasizing challenge or competition, the game focuses on providing a calm, cozy atmosphere where curiosity and relaxation take center stage.

The core gameplay revolves around mastering three distinct claw machines, each introducing its own variation on the familiar crane-game formula. Success requires patience, timing, and careful positioning instead of luck alone, making every successful catch genuinely rewarding. Collecting all 23 unique fish species provides a satisfying progression system without overwhelming the player with unnecessary complexity. The gameplay loop remains simple throughout, but the variety between the machines helps maintain engagement while encouraging players to refine their approach as they continue expanding their aquatic collection.

Exploration complements the arcade mechanics surprisingly well. Beyond the claw machines, players are free to wander around the peaceful station, stroll along the waterfront, take a relaxing boat ride, and interact with the small but charming environment. Even casual conversations, including amusing encounters with a talkative seagull, add personality to the world. The setting feels intentionally intimate, allowing every corner of the environment to contribute to the game's welcoming atmosphere. Rather than filling the map with repetitive objectives, Clawfish encourages players to appreciate its surroundings at their own pace.

One of the game's most appealing features is how collecting fish actively transforms the environment. Once rescued from the claw machines, the fish are released into the surrounding waters, gradually making the once-quiet landscape feel more alive. This progression system creates a subtle sense of accomplishment because every successful capture visibly improves the world around the player. It reinforces themes of restoration and discovery while giving players an additional reason to continue searching for every available species. This environmental feedback is simple yet remarkably effective, making each achievement feel meaningful beyond merely filling a collection log.

The presentation perfectly supports the game's relaxing tone. Its colorful low-poly graphics create a playful aesthetic that resembles a handcrafted miniature world, while soft lighting and vibrant scenery enhance the peaceful setting. The soundtrack remains gentle throughout, accompanied by calming environmental audio that encourages players to slow down and enjoy the experience. Rather than relying on graphical realism, the visual style embraces simplicity and charm, allowing the game's personality to shine through every location and interaction.

Although the adventure is relatively short and can comfortably be completed in a single sitting, its concise design works in its favor. Every activity feels purposeful, with very little unnecessary padding or repetition. Players seeking dozens of hours of content may find the experience too brief, but those who appreciate focused indie games will likely admire how efficiently Clawfish delivers its ideas. The game understands its scope and remains committed to offering a polished, relaxing journey from beginning to end without overstaying its welcome.

Replay value is naturally limited once every fish has been collected and the world has reached its fullest state, though completionists may still enjoy unlocking every achievement or revisiting the peaceful setting simply to unwind. The lack of extensive post-game content is balanced by the game's originality and consistently pleasant atmosphere. Rather than attempting to become an endless simulator, Clawfish succeeds by providing a memorable experience built around a creative concept executed with confidence and heart.

Overall, Clawfish demonstrates how an imaginative idea can elevate a modest indie project into something memorable. By combining claw-machine gameplay with exploration, environmental storytelling, and a relaxing presentation, it offers an experience that feels refreshingly different from conventional fishing games. Its short duration may leave players wanting more, but the enjoyable mechanics, charming world, and satisfying progression make excellent use of every minute. For anyone looking for a cozy, unconventional adventure that values creativity over complexity, Clawfish is an easy recommendation.

In Clawfish, you catch a water train out to a train station on a set of tiny, linked islands. There are three claw machines on said station where you can use tokens to catch a variety of fish. Each of the claw machines has a different gameplay mechanic as far as the controls are concerned. As you catch the fish, they are released back into the water. And you get a little description for each type of fish as well.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3507972949

Additionally, there are buckets of water with fish trapped in them. You will dump them back into the sea as well. Beyond all that, there are a few interactable objects and a bird you can speak with. And finally, there is a boat to travel between the three islands that make up the station.

The graphics are pretty much all soft tones and definitely carry a peaceful vibe; while the music is completely chill and just adds to the overall cozy setting. It's nicely done.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3507972914

After you've wrapped everything up, the train comes back, you jump on, the train departs with a final musing on the station's peaceful nature; and that is the game. This was 89 cents recently on Steam, which is fine for the content IMO. Which ultimately is just a peaceful and pleasant little half hour distraction. Enjoyable for what it is, easy enough to one and done. I see no reason not to give it a look.

The atmosphere and the world is just, beautiful. It's almost exactly how I wanted my perfect getaway to be. Abandoned docks, empty japanese-style train station, leftover posters and pamphlets for a days gone by, and somehow, a still working vending machine. It really captures the atmosphere it's going for, and I am totally in love with it. The crane game can be there or not, and I'd still enjoy the game.

The main game though, hit or miss. Love crane games, love how it's implemented here, though it feels a bit, off. It's either 'too easy' to catch a fish, or it's baffling how it didn't catch, which I guess is how real life crane game would also be if it's trying to catch a moving fish. The coins felt redundant, because it cost nothing to get coins, and nothing resets when you leave the machine. The physics too feels wonky, as you may get fish stuck sometimes, and that's not mentioning the player's movement (or lord forbid, the boat).

For the price, especially on discount, I'd say go for it if you love the vibe of the screenshots. Otherwise, only if you REALLY love the vibe. It's been released for a while and doesn't feel like the dev's going to add much more. Oh and yeah, 100% it within my playtime.

Clawfish is an admittedly charming amateur game, a Japanese themed slice of life where you visit a dockside train station (where, weirdly, the tracks are underwater because, um, amateur developer), look around and play a facsimile of a claw vending machine.

And, while this is a bit off-topic, I should point out those machines are rigged, they calculate a certain profit ratio (far, far above the value of the items you could "win") and only grasp properly after a certain number of failures.  Yeah, it's gambling, so don't waste your money.  Cheaper just to buy whatever thing you want that's in the machine.  Anyway.   I'm sure the machines in Clawfish are not rigged.

One important note is that even though this is an amateur project, it does seem to be sincerely and genuinely made.  I couldn't find any flipped assets, plagiarism or any other kind of insincere actions from the developer, but unfortunately genuine intentions alone are not enough to produce a brilliant PC gaming experience.

The game is very very short and can be finished in 30 minutes.  Developers have at least some responsibility to provide enough content to make a game last more than 2 hours if they're serious about providing something of value to gamers.  There's less content here than some free game demos.

The game is very simplistic, small and limited in scope and ambition.  This feels more like a tech demo, proof of concept or student homework assignment rather than a fully fledged product designed for PC gamers.  As such it doesn't offer any real value as a serious PC game.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

The game features lazy minimalist/untextured low-polygon "retro" assets and visuals, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the early 1990s.  The lack of textures is a method that lazy devs often use to disguise their lack of talent/interest in doing the graphics properly and trying to disguise it under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It looks bad as a result of their decisions, and that's just another reason to avoid it.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, left handed gamers or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The game never really caught on with the millions of gamers on Steam, with a very low peak player count close to launch, and then just a handful of players launching this game every couple of days.  This is undoubtedly caused by factors such as those raised in this review.  It's always helpful with buying decisions to consider how popular and successful the product is, and unfortunately while this did accumulate a few participation trophy reviews, overall, people just aren't using it.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Clawfish is relatively cheap at $3 USD, but it's not worth it. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  This is also competing with over 11,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.

But, again, this is one of those ones where I might give it a "maybe" option [i]if I had one[/i].   I know Valve doesn't give us a "maybe" because then the store would be full of millions of meaningless maybe reviews.    My advice as always is to read only the negative reviews and if you don't mind the problems, then go ahead and buy the game.

[i]Clawfish[/i] is not a long or complex game, and its price tag doesn't suggest it. It's as short as a dream, bittersweet and filled with beauty. It feels nostalgic like a personal story retold dearly by its creator. For a game about fishing within a claw machine, it's pretty sweet. And for the price of a bag of Doritos (or less), it's an easy recommendation.

There are some really basic things that are just expected to exist in a game now a days. A save system is one of them. Especially when a game is as buggy as this. The first time I was playing the game I had a fish get stuck on the side of the machine. It COULD NOT be picked up and it would not move. It was impossible to grab it. So I turned off the game thinking maybe when I came back later the fish would be unstuck. That was last night.

Then just now I got on the game again... and realized it did not save. Is this a glitch? I don't know. So I shrug my shoulders and just replay. I hadn't gotten far before anyways. So I finished one machine. Took me a second to figure out I had to ride a little boat to another area to get to the next unlocked machine... finished that machine. Got on the boat again and started to go back to another spot. Only to get out of the boat and be teleported back to the previous machine. This wouldn't be a problem, but walking in the knee deep water in this game is so painfully slow that it's a real issue that this happened. Then I get to the third claw machine. I managed to pick up some fish, but mostly. Over and over and over again I'd have a fish highlighted with the claw only for the claw to go through the fish and come no where near grabbing it. Other times I'd grab a fish. It would be fully held by the claw and then just phase through the claw.

If it was kinda this funny frustrating thing of like when you play an actual claw machine and the claw every so slightly grabs something and then drops it... I'd be fine. But no. The fish will fall through the claw.

This game.... is SO glitchy. I don't return games often either. Especially when they are this cheap. In fact I'm keeping that other game I briefly mentioned because it was only $4 and I'm hopeful that the dev will add a tutorial and make it playable. This game though..... this game isn't even worth the 89 cents I paid for it. That might sound harsh, but that's how FRUSTRATING this was to play. And I plan on returning it.

Especially when, as the fish kept glitching through the hook, I assumed something was up again and closed the game to restart... only to find out that my game not saving the first time was indeed... not a glitch. But the fact that this game has no save system. I had to restart the game twice because the game was glitching so bad... and if that's an issue in your game don't make me restart everything your game decides to not work.

I get that the game is short. If I hadn't run into glitch after glitch after glitch I bet you can beat this game in under and hour.  You honestly shouldn't NEED a save system.

But either this game is glitchy because the dev didn't care to clear up glitches or it's full of glitches intentionally to mimic the frustration of playing an actual claw game.

Either way... you need a save system.

Again. I feel bad recommending against it on the sale price of 89 cents. Or even the full price of $3. But it's just so damn glitchy that it's too frustrating to be enjoyable. Clawfish offers itself up as a simple and relaxing intermission, a sort of vibrantly coloured vignette of claw machine game and fishing in some sort of dreamy train station across the ocean. It promises three different machines with a total 23 variety of fish with a full game experience of less than one hour. How does it fare?

Clawfish is a small arcade simulator with a focus on colorful atmosphere. It was released June 11th, 2021 by solo developer David Czarnowski with music by Robert Kilpatrick. It's self description is self aware and explicitly labels itself as having a gametime under one hour. Personally my first playthrough ran 30 minutes which included 100% of achievements, total playtime after recording footage for this video will likely still be sub 1 hour. This very short playtime will undoubtably cause upset with some people but lets keep in mind this game is intended to be more of an art piece to chill with. This is my reminder to take a breath and soak up the mood.

The game begins when you take your first step off a train onto Clawfish station after a brief dialogue introduction. From here you're prompted to "Release all the fish and get on the train." Exploring the immediate area there are a few interactables in the form of rocks to skip, benches to sit on, 8 hidden buckets with fish to release and several flyers posted to the wall.

The flyers plastered across various walls mostly present small anecdotes about advertising - your favorite beer, an overly sweet coffee brand, etc. There are a few small messages that I'd consider lore such as the maintenance worker marking his vacation and then never returning...

Now what we are here for, claw machine fishing. Each of the three functioning crane game cabinets sits next to token machines. Each token machine use grants five tokens, which translates to five tries at the claw or drinks at the vending machine.

The Lucky Lake machine functions about how you'd expect. Use WASD to move the claw and then when you're ready to drop it on your fishy prize press the SPACEBAR. This machine features five lake fish.

Hopping on the boat located just a few feet from Lucky Lake we can sail over to the Wild Wetland machine. Wild Wetland functions similarly to the last machine except that we'll also have to click it again to make it GRAB the fish. This machine features a total of eight wetland fish.

Taking the boat in the complete opposite direction (or swimming I guess) leads us to our final machine - Colorful Coral. This machine will drop its gripper as soon as you let go of the WASD controls. It features ten tropical fish to catch.

After playing all the machines you can return to the original platform and check if the train has returned. Getting on and taking a seat will complete the game. There are also 14 steam achievements to gain though it is very likely you managed to collect them all in a single playthrough if you sought out to explore.

The sound and music in this game are great. It's slow pacing tones blend perfectly with the machine reward tunes and it really sets the atmosphere - only rivaled by its graphical style. The whole experience is a sort of hyperbright dream sequence and I can definitely see myself coming back to this just to hangout for some respite when I have a head cold.

One minor criticism I have is that the models of the fish aren't indicative of what they are as each fish only varies in size. It would be nice if each had its own unique model at the very least after being released from the machine as I'd love to sit and watch them all swim around in the ocean.

Typically I view the constant expectation of more content and pestering about games being abandoned with frustration here I believe it is justified if not by the small playtime but because David Czar is on record via steam discussion speaking of further updates to the game. Unfortunately for us there seems to be radio silence on the status of update since August of 2022. Other commenters mention he had been posting developer progress via Twitter as of looking now that seems to of been scrubbed offline. Hopefully someday we will see progress.

During the end sequence I experienced a bug where I had sat down to end the game and been ported outside of the train. This did not impact gameplay in anyway though did tarnish the overall experience as a paid product.

Currently Clawfish price sits at $2.99 with frequent 50% discounts to $1.49. In my opinion its worth it at this price given you understand and expect what this game is.

Overall I enjoyed my experience with Clawfish and it's biggest downside is that there isn't more of it. I hope someday at the very least it receives updates or maybe even a sequel with a more grand scale.

While going for that, aside from the wonky controls, fishes randomly dropping from the claw while it's moving or stopped, and the very bad boat mechanics, I encountered two more bugs! I caught two fishes at once and one of them hovered over the drop-off thingy, then slowly swam back from thin air to the Claw Machine. Another thing: Sometimes dropping the claw right on a fish would work, other times it would keep swimming, then when trying to predict where a fish would move, sometimes it would move normally and end up getting caught and sometimes it would simply freeze in place and make you miss, so frustrating.

I put over 200 hours in when the game first released, but the longer I played, the more annoyed I became. Decided to reinstall and give it another bash ... but it's just as annoying as it was, with apparently no meaningful updates.

Pros:
- The soundtrack is nice
- The 'NASA-punk' aesthetic is excellent
- The shipbuilder is very good (small caveat - no way to track or wishlist ship parts from different sellers)
- I liked the 'perform tasks to unlock ranks' of the skills
- The shooting was decent.
- There's a good selection of weapons, spacesuits, helmets, etc.

Mid:
- The writing is somewhere between dated/uninspiring to good. Main quest is essentially Skyrim, but some of the side quests/faction quests were enjoyable.

Cons:
- Loading screens. Leave your ship ... loading screen. Enter your ship ... loading screen. Enter a small shop ... loading screen.
- You don't land or launch your ship. No in-atmosphere flight. Most space travel is done via the map/loading screen.
- No seamless on-foot exploration. The game loads a terrain 'tile'. Get to the edge of the tile and it will need to loading-screen you into another tile.
- Insipid exploration. I don't mind long hikes (I love No Man's Sky, so I'm happy walking discovering stuff) but buildings & settlements are copy pasted from a 'pool'. Seen one particular layout, it will be *exactly* the same, down to loot *and* clutter.
-No catalogue of flora and fauna I've scanned.
- Inventory management is dated, cumbersome (no pun intended!), and gets in the way of crafting. If you are a resource hoarder like me you and your ship will be encumbered all the time. The only 'vanilla' workaround I found was using a seemingly infinite-storage in the basement of The Lodge, and going there to do all my crafting.
- The crafting is a massive downgrade from Fallout 4. For example, you have to spend resorces to craft iron sights, and the attachment you are replacing just disappears. This is the same for most weapon/suit mods. Having limited-roll legendary stats in a single player game is frustrating ... just let me build my loadout how I want!
- The NPCs and companions look terrible. Their faces all look 'flat' complexion-wise ... like a texture hasn't loaded! Nothing like subsurface scattering, etc.
- The companions were a bit predictable, boring, and their 'barks' are annoying! Jackie Welles is only in CP2077 for a short time, but man is he memorable! Nothing like that here.
-No transmog. Look the love of a suit/helmet/boostpack but it's got crap stats? Tough! What a shame, as there's some great-looking gear.
- The major settlements are more akin to small hamlets than "cities".
- Performance is hit and miss. From smooth 60fps, to stuttery 28 - 54fps for no apparent reason. No amount of changing settings I've tried has managed to stabilise performance.

Summary:
Starfield is a game that feels very dated; if it had released around the time of Fallout 4 it would have felt a bit more of an achievement. Coming after the writing, characters, and world-building of games like Witcher 3 or CP2077, Starfield is just stale. Coming years after the seamless universe exploration of No Man's Sky feels like indifference or (dare I say) incompetence from Bethesda. I can't help but compare Starfield to 2 games that I love and have aforementioned; CP2077 and NMS. Those games had horrendous launches, yet the studios put their shoulders to the yoke, pushed multiple meaningful updates, and have made their games financial and critical successes ... in contrast, Starfield is essentially the game it was at launch and feels a bit abandoned - Bethesda's 'updates' have focused more on paid mods (although they did add a moon buggy, and recently enabled in-system cruise, it's nowhere near enough in my book). It's a shame, because I would have loved this game to become fun. I've never finished the main quest, nor have I played either of the DLCs, and I don't have the motivation to do so. After giving the game another 20 hours or so over the last couple of weeks, I'm going to uninstall it, and excepting a major update that changes the issues I've experienced, I don't think I'll ever play it again.

[list]
