Shipbuilding is honestly my absolute favorite part of the game. I love coming up with new ideas and making crazy ship builds come true.

[h2]The Bad[/h2]
From how Starfield came out, you can tell a couple of different things: It's clear that the game changed directions several times during development. This is evident in the systems that went into the game, only to be taken out again, but leaving behind traces. 

Fuel economy is a good example. Originally, fuel was meant to be a resource you had to manage. In order to go deeper into the unknown, you'd have to actually secure sources of fuel. The further you got away from settled space, the more this would be a challenge. This got toned down to basically nothing. Which takes us to the next system that got newtered.

Outposts were supposed to serve several purposes. Extraction of fuel and raw resources, automated processing of said resources, and enabling you to build a network of outposts, allowing you to reach the furthest corners of space. That's all still there... except, it no longer has a real purpose.

There's no actual need to ever touch the Outpost building system any more. With the de facto removal of fuel economy, and the lack of a proper place to sell bulk goods, there really isn't any reason to use these.

On top of that, the way that Bethesda has implemented procedural generation means that no matter how far out you travel, you will always run into human-built structures.

[h2]The Technical[/h2]
The technical aspect of the game deserves its own section. It's pretty much part of "The Bad", but it's all related to the engine, so I will tackle it here.

Bethesda uses their own game engine. Originally, they used an engine called "GameBryo", which was then forked, and later evolved into "Creation Engine". Starfield uses Creation Engine 2.

First, there's the loading screens. Starfield has a lot of them. This is entirely due to how the engine handles loading world spaces. Kind of. More on that later. Just know, that vanilla Starfield will have a lot of load screens, so you'll want to have it installed on an SSD.

Second, there's dialogue screens. In modern games like Cyberpunk 2077, characters will move around and emote while talking, and it adds so much to the believability of the scene. In Starfield, the game "pauses", and you zoom in on the face of whoever you're talking to, and stay there. Just like in Oblivion.

So why use an engine that's obviously old and outdated? Well, the Creation Engine does two things that other engines struggle with:

First thing: Every item in the game is simulated and has full physics. The game remembers it all. Hundreds of thousands of objects. And it actually handles it pretty well too. One of the cornerstones of Bethesda Open Worlds is being able to interact with pretty much everything in the world, and that's something that Creation Engine handles better than other engines.

Second thing: Moddability. This is quite possibly the greatest strength of the engine. It's very moddable. The process is more evolved now, but at the base level is the same as it was aaaaaaalll the way back in Morrowind from 2002. This means that there is a modding community with 24 years of experience being able to work on mods for Starfield, creating new content, stories and gameplay systems.

Which brings me to the last thing I want to mention: [b]Engine limitations are strangling the moddability of the game.[/b] Without going into detail, there's a hard-coded limit in the engine that means you can only install so many mods before the game gets wonky and unplayable. For a game that lives and dies on moddability, having this limitation is absolutely disastrous. I ran into this limit myself, and it almost caused me to quit playing.

[h2]The Saving Grace[/h2]
In a word? [b]Mods.[/b]

Every single issue that I've mentioned above? They can all be fixed with mods. Even the engine limitation on mods can be fixed with mods.

Work is currently ongoing to make landing and takeoffs from planets completely seamless. These have loading screens currently. Work is also ongoing on making... everything else seamless, including building interiors and worldspaces. The things that modders are able to do with this engine are frankly amazing.

Technical fixes aside, there are also some absolutely fantastic story mods out there. I played several of them during my latest playthrough. One of the standouts is "Watchtower" by Kinggath Creations - A mod team so good that they are routinely hired by Bethesda to make mods for them, including the universally loved FEVer Dreams mod for Fallout 4 that came out with the 40th anniversary of Bethesda.

Then there the gameplay-altering/adding mods. Remember the fuel economy I wrote about earlier? Yeah, there's a mod system for that. Want to put a little cyberpunk in your Starfield? How about a hacking system that lets you remote-hack robots, cameras and even other people's space suits? Yep, you can get that too.

[b]The possibilities are endless, and Starfield mods have now matured to the point where you can really tailor your experience to what you love, and ignore what you don't.[/b]

I played this game on PC, and used mods from both The Creation Club, and Nexusmods. This is my recommended way of playing the game. Especially since Nexusmods has something called "Collections" that will let you install curated sets of mods with a single click.

Consoles now also have mods, via Creation Club, but I don't have any personal experience with playing on console.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
It's really taken me a while to get to this point, but I can now say that I love Starfield. Will you love it too? That heavily depends on the kind of energy you're willing to invest into it.

[b]On Steam, Starfield has a "Mixed" rating, and it fully deserves that in its vanilla state.[/b]

Add mods though, and you're looking at a different beast. With my current mod list, I have gotten my game to a state where I love playing it. With mods, the downsides of the game are outweighed by the upsides I get from all the mods I'm running - But it took time to get here.

Looking ahead, the mods coming out will be truly transformative for the game too, so this is definitely not the last time I voyage into the Starfield.

A Disappointing, Bug-Ridden and Utterly Boring Experience

Starfield is one of the most disappointing gaming experiences I've had in a long time. For a game that promised so much, it delivers remarkably little. What should have been an immersive space exploration RPG instead feels like a collection of unfinished ideas held together by loading screens, repetitive gameplay and an astonishing lack of meaningful content.

The game's technical state is frustrating, with bugs, glitches and inconsistent performance constantly getting in the way. It's hard to become immersed in a world when you're regularly reminded of how broken and unpolished parts of the game are.

The biggest disappointment, however, is the complete lack of engaging storytelling. The narratives feel uninspired, the characters are largely forgettable, and the dialogue rarely gives you a reason to care. There is very little emotional investment, very little tension and almost no sense that your choices have any meaningful impact. For an RPG, that's a pretty serious failure.

Exploration, which should be the heart and soul of a game like this, quickly becomes a tedious chore. Countless planets feel empty, repetitive and devoid of anything genuinely interesting. Quests become predictable, activities feel copy-pasted, and the constant travelling and loading screens make an already dull experience feel even longer. Things got a little better with Freelanes, but it still feels like a game that is mainly played in menus.

Ultimately, Starfield suffers from a fundamental problem: it's simply not fun enough to justify the time it demands. It has a massive universe but very little worth discovering, plenty of content but very little worth experiencing, and all the ingredients of an epic RPG without the soul to bring it to life.

A game this ambitious should inspire curiosity and excitement. Instead, Starfield mostly inspires boredom and frustration. A huge universe wasted on a painfully shallow and forgettable experience. 

Starfield has raised concerns for me regarding BGS's future and the direction the studio has taken since Skyrim, as each subsequent release appears less complex. Observing how studios such as CDPR and Warhorse have built on Bethesda's formula further emphasises areas where Bethesda falls behind. I hope the next Elder Scrolls title will mark a positive turning point for the studio.

Man this game is such a weird bummer.  I don't wanna feel like I'm just jumping on the hate bandwagon, but I really tried to give it a fair shake.  First of all, it's been 4 years since release, so they've had *plenty* of time to fix all of what I'm about to say.

It's incomprehensible how this UX could have come from humans who tie their own shoes in the morning.

The gunplay is probably this game's strongest aspect, and it's just bad, but like, regular amounts of bad, I guess.  Why put thin-railed handrails all throughout the game, for example, if no care is given to them having proper hitboxes? The story and plot beats I've encountered have all been disappointing, and the dialogue writing ranges from ok to rancid. How would that even make sense?!?  Every bit of "lore" feels so haphazardly slapped together.  And then the dialogue bugs!  Everybody interrupts each other all the time! None of this has been thought through at all!  I know that's a silly nitpick, but with the variety of nonsense assets in this game, it's clear it was a big priority to make things "different" because weird = scifi, and yet it all feels so incredibly phoned in.

And then there's the fact that...  this was supposed to be a SPACE GAME!  And yet, there is no spaceflight!  You can fly your ship around a given local area, just for the purposes of having space combat, but you can't actually fly *to* anywhere...  the moment you want to so much as go from a planet to its own satellite, well, that's just a teleporty loading transition. # ⭐ STARFIELD — 9.5/10
One of the best games I have ever played in my life.

Starfield is genuinely a top-tier gaming experience. I can confidently say it's one of the greatest games I've ever played. The story is phenomenal, the exploration is incredible, the combat is outstanding, and the progression system is extremely satisfying.

However, there's one major problem preventing this game from being a perfect 10/10: the bugs.

### 🌌 Exploration — 9.9/10

For a space exploration game, Starfield is almost perfect.

The universe is massive, and there's an incredible amount to discover. Most of the important planets offer multiple activities, locations, and opportunities for exploration.

Yes, some planets feel empty, but I genuinely don't understand why people consider that such a massive problem.

It's space. Not every planet is supposed to be populated.

Think about it logically. Even in reality, you wouldn't expect to find civilians, settlements, or massive outposts on every extremely hot, freezing, or otherwise inhospitable planet.

Some planets being barren actually makes the universe feel more believable.

Of course, a few locations could have benefited from additional content, which is why I'm giving exploration a 9.9 rather than a perfect 10.

### 📖 Story — 10/10

The story is absolutely phenomenal.

I'll admit that I experienced some boredom during the middle portion of the main storyline. A few missions felt slower than I would have preferred.

However, as the story progressed, everything started coming together beautifully.

The later missions genuinely elevated the entire experience, making the journey worthwhile.

By the end, I was completely invested.

### ⚔️ Combat — 10/10

The combat is outstanding.

You have an enormous variety of weapons and playstyles at your disposal:

- Shotguns
- Assault rifles
- Pistols
- Sniper rifles
- Grenades
- Explosive launchers
- Laser weapons
- Special powers and abilities

There's so much variety that combat rarely gets boring.

My only criticism concerns the powers. Even after upgrading certain abilities to their maximum level, some still deal disappointingly low damage.

I believe fully upgraded powers should feel significantly more powerful, especially considering the effort required to improve them.

Nevertheless, the overall combat experience is fantastic.

### 📈 Progression & Leveling — 10/10

One of Starfield's greatest strengths is its progression system.

Leveling up feels rewarding, unlocking new skills is satisfying, and developing your character gives you a genuine sense of becoming stronger.

The progression system kept me engaged throughout the experience.

This is exactly how progression in an RPG should feel.

### 🐛 Bugs — The Biggest Problem

Now, this is where I have a serious issue with Starfield.

I cannot stress enough how frustrating the bugs are.

We're talking about bugs that can genuinely prevent you from progressing through missions.

I really wanted to love Starfield.

I've spent hundreds of hours wandering through Skyrim and Fallout, getting completely sidetracked by random caves, strange NPCs, and stories I wasn't even looking for. Going into Starfield, I expected Bethesda's biggest and most ambitious world yet. Instead, what I found was a game that somehow feels both enormous and strangely empty at the same time.

There's no denying the scale. Thousands of planets, dozens of star systems, ship building, outposts, factions, companions, and enough content to keep you busy for hundreds of hours. On paper, it sounds incredible.

The problem is that bigger doesn't always mean better.

A lot of my time in Starfield felt like I was travelling from one objective marker to another. Talk to someone. Fly somewhere. Pick something up. Return to the original person. Repeat. Bethesda games have always had fetch quests, but previous games hid them behind engaging exploration and world design. In Starfield, I often felt like I was working through a checklist rather than going on an adventure.

The comparison to Skyrim is unavoidable. In Skyrim, I'd set off towards one objective and end up spending three hours doing something completely different because I stumbled across a ruined fort, a dragon attack, or an interesting side story. Some of my favourite moments happened by accident.

In Starfield, exploration rarely gave me that feeling. There's certainly a lot to see, but so much of it feels procedurally generated that the excitement of discovery wears off far quicker than I'd hoped. I spent more time navigating menus and fast travelling between loading screens than genuinely exploring.

That's a shame because there are things Starfield does really well.

Ship building is fantastic and easily one of the best systems in the game. Creating a ship that feels uniquely yours never gets old. Combat is also Bethesda's best to date, with gunplay that feels far more responsive than anything in Fallout 4. Visually, the game can be stunning too. Some planets genuinely made me stop and admire the view.

The faction quests are a mixed bag. The UC Vanguard storyline is probably the strongest content in the game and shows what Starfield is capable of when it focuses on storytelling rather than scale. Unfortunately, not everything reaches that standard.

The DLCs haven't really changed my opinion either.

Shattered Space finally allowed us to learn more about House Va'ruun, one of the setting's most mysterious factions. The problem is that despite the interesting setup, the story felt surprisingly restrictive. For a game built around player choice, most of the major outcomes felt largely predetermined, and my decisions never seemed to have the impact I was hoping for.

The Starborn Armada DLC was an even bigger disappointment for me. The faction itself seemed interesting enough, but the content never gave me a real reason to care about them. There was very little meaningful backstory, not much exploration of who they actually were, and most frustratingly, no real option to properly join or align with them. It felt like Bethesda introduced a potentially interesting faction and then did very little with it.

That's probably my biggest criticism of Starfield as a whole.

There are so many interesting ideas, factions, locations, and mysteries scattered throughout the game, but they often feel underdeveloped. Just when something starts getting interesting, the story moves on before you've had a chance to become invested.

In the end, Starfield is a good game, but I don't think it's a great Bethesda game.

It's one of the biggest worlds they've ever created, yet I often felt less compelled to explore it than I did Skyrim's single province. There are more planets, more systems, and more content than ever before, but somehow less wonder.

For me, that's Starfield's biggest problem.

It's a galaxy that's vast in size, but often feels empty in spirit.

I discovered Starfield in July 2026 and finally completed it after over 200 hours. I honestly don't think I've ever spent this much time playing a Bethesda game!

==========The negatives==========

-A slow start:
Compared to Fallout or The Elder Scrolls, it takes quite a while to get into the game. I spent my first 15 hours feeling a bit lost, especially when it came to managing loot, resources and money. Watching a few YouTube guides made a huge difference to my experience.

-Way too easy: 
A recurring issue with Bethesda games. You can get ridiculously powerful gear within just a few hours and breeze through even the final boss.

-Not enough space combat:
Shipbuilding is one of the game's best features, yet there are surprisingly few opportunities to actually use your ship in combat.

-Underwhelming quests:
Aside from the Crimson Fleet, UC Vanguard and main storylines, most quests felt rather forgettable. The excessive reuse of procedurally generated locations doesn't help either.

-What's the point of outposts?
Unlike Fallout 4, I struggle to see their purpose. With unlimited storage at The Lodge and resources readily available from vendors, there's very little incentive to build them beyond farming XP.. Considering outposts don't have unlimited storage.

==========The positives==========

-Freedom and exploration:
That classic Bethesda feeling of developing your character and making your own way through the universe.

-A grounded sci-fi universe:
I really appreciated Starfield's realistic approach to science fiction. The bulky spacesuits, believable technology and overall aesthetic make its universe feel like a plausible evolution of our own, rather than an over-the-top sci-fi setting filled with flashy, nonsensical designs.

-Fantastic shipbuilding:
I had a blast designing my Class B ship, followed by my first Class C ship after 100 hours, which took me around six hours to build!

-A clever New Game+ system:
It fits the universe surprisingly well. I would have loved something similar in Fallout 4 or Skyrim!

==========
Final thoughts
==========

Despite having more negatives than positives, Starfield is still a game I'd happily recommend. Not all the previous points carry the same weight, and Bethesda's open worlds remain something special.

If you've been dreaming of a game like Starfield since Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger in 1994, that's a 32-year wait for your ultimate space-faring fantasy to take shape

1994 — Wing Commander III

Cinematic storytelling, memorable characters, branching decisions, and the feeling that you were a pilot in a living sci-fi universe.

2023 — Starfield

Your own spaceship, distant worlds, exploration, faction storylines, and the freedom to build your own life among the stars.

What I love about that comparison is that these games scratch slightly different parts of the same itch. Wing Commander III made you feel like the star of a cinematic space opera. Starfield lets you inhabit a science-fiction universe and decide what kind of spacefarer you want to be.

And if you've spent decades imagining what you'd do if you could actually step into a universe like that, Starfield's appeal goes far beyond shooting pirates or completing quests. It's the idea of climbing into your own ship, flying into the unknown, landing on an alien world, and making the adventure yours.

I'm curious about one thing, though: what was the big dream for you back in 1994?

Was it the cinematic, character-driven space opera of Wing Commander III, the freedom to explore a vast galaxy in your own ship, or the fantasy of actually living in a believable science-fiction universe? Because those are three different dreams, and Starfield comes closest to some of them in very different ways.

I've thought about writing a long essay about all of the things this game did right and wrong, putting it in bullet points and all that, but I then figured that these sums up this game pretty well:

The core idea seems to be quite straightforward: this game is your typical Bethesda experience that was meant to be shared with the community, for the people to pour their creativity alongside what the devs made, yet it has nearly zero pull and appeal to make most of them commit to it. I'm not sure if its the creative direction or if the team lacks what the previous ones has, but everything that this game offered, outside of it's technological advancement (graphics, support for new tech, higher fps support, etc) is watered down and worse than what its predecessor has, this game has less story, less agency and less uniqueness, and due to all of that, it also has less community support.

The story is so watered down and short, the writing is safe and sterile, conflict felt fake at times and your choice doesn't matter the majority of the time, a far departure from the previous title's immersiveness and freedom. And then there's the gameplay, it's been improved but the loop is downright attrociously repetitive, majority of the things you encountered during exploration are procedurally generated, but they only made 1-2 templates for all of them, which means, everything you encountered will only have 1/2 variants, once you found an abandoned military base, you've found all of them, same enemies, same layout, same loot table. When this is all they have to offer in the base game, I can see why most people aren't necessarily interested into putting more work on it.

TLDR: I enjoyed Starfield enough to put a lot of hours into it and give it a thumbs up! That being said, the game also have one fundamental issue, let me try to nail it in one sentence: The concept behind Starfield is great and Bethesda designed a huge universe for it, but this huge universe is way bigger than Bethesdas ability to fill it with enough meaningful content.

Lets return to the expectation part, because I think it's important if you are thinking about getting the game. Bethesda sold the game as a huge universe full of content and exploration. I think many players were probably expecting something in the line of Skyrim where the world is packed with discoveries, distractions and surprises for almost every step you take. Starfield is obviuosly not Skyrim, but this particular difference is what I think causes most disappointment. Its a huge difference between filling a limited map with handcrafted content, and to do the same one hundreds of whole planets. This is exactly where the concept and the gaming experience collides, making the game very wide but shallow. 

Bethesda has been doing a lot of what I think they do best, which is the handcrafted exploration formula combined with often great storytelling. There is a lot of that in Starfield too but when it's stretched thin over a whole galaxy it just gets diluted. I think this game would have got way better off starting with a much smaller universe of maybe 15-20 or so explorable systems that could later have been expanded.

But again, I enjoyed the game. Not just because of lowered expectations, but also because many of Starfields individual ingredients are actually great. Some questlines like Vanguard/Crimson or Ruyjin are excellent, and some of the handcrafted locations are just as atmospheric and engaging as they come in a Bethesda game. I also found the shipbuilding challenging and fun once I got hang of it. Base building was a bit too space restricted and basic for my taste, but I somewhat enjoyed it anyway.

Personally I did not really have a problem with the loading screens or space jumps. I would say that also comes more from what you expect the game to be, and as long as I get good content at my destination, I don't mind. Some mention waiting time on loading screens, but I did not experience much of it. Hardware thing?

One sad thing is that once you are done with the handcrafted content, the game is no longer interesting. There might still be hundreds of planets left to explore, but finding identical facilities and layouts across countless planets is simply boring and eventually you just give up on it. Standard missions are also very repetetive. 

I will probably try modding next, let's see if I can squeeze a few more hours out of the game. :)

That being said this isn't a bad game its actually fairly solid IF you realize it isn't Fallout 4 or Skyrim or Mass Effect or Cyberpunk or Outlaws its Starfield and its does pretty ok at that.

What I like, right out the gate it doesn't have that Fallout 4 latency you experience just loading the game. Its crisp and prompt when loading and the world is just boom there, its dirty its dingy and I don't want to be there. 

A level 1 noob with dreams of conquering the galaxy and in short order a level 2 noob with a borrowed and quite possibly stolen ship and off to explore the unknown. After a short visit with the nice people naive enough to give me same said ship I'm off to the races.

39 levels later I'm a ranger, a tracker, a pirate, a corporate fixer, a privateer and a security officer and I have super powers but most importantly I'm my own boss I fly where I want when I want and do whatever I want when I want. I can't think of any game that just lets you actually explore without the main quest progression not breathing down your neck and that makes this game special.

The UI as anyone who has read other reviews is very clunky ridiculously clunky but if you take the time to start messing around with it and experimenting it actually has some pretty good tools stashed behind a lot of frustration but they are there.

The ship build UI can give you fits but it actually makes sense when you get into building big ships and I have a very big ship 80 meters long 4 decks high and around 60 meters across and it handles like a star fighter because I'm one of .9% of players who discovered some very cool toys stashed in game to make your ship ridiculously op which is sad really considering how long the game's been out having a gizmo that wipes out 20% of ships mass is very very useful especially at level 5 when i found it.

The NPCs.... This isn't mass effect so the core NPCs aren't shall we say as irreverent but they can be chatty a little too much sometimes Sara really needs to stfu when I'm negotiating with my pirate buddies or any criminals in general and her tendency to throw a fit and walk off can be inconvenient but I'm too lazy to switch gear between my minions so its really on me not her I could swap her out for someone whose more morally ambiguous. Piper in fallout and Sara should start a club to whine about my "crimes."

There are 4 types of NPCs in game; core who have "personalities" and back stories personal quests etc some who become followers or you deal with regularly. Generic type A can serve a function like ship or out post crew shop keeps or quest related generic B are filler exist to populate the world and not good for anything but being a crowd to enhance immersion.(the last group you can modify in settings to really make your cities come to life max it out and your computer might fry but you won't be lonely.) 

Finally bad guys; A type or as I like to call them target practice are just that. Bad guys B are a little more complex some of which will speak with you and may or may not actually be bad guys I don't want to drop spoilers but I've had more then one unanticipated conversation in game.

Quests yes there are tons and I mean tons of fetch quests and most are just that but some if you take the time to look around and or talk to NPCs along the way can actually lead you down some very cool rabbit holes.

Combat is good shooting someone in the face in no oxygen environments does massive crits and blinds as it should and it works both ways not pleasant but I'd call it fair.

Loot there's so much loot in this game its ridiculous but you spend so many credits it balances out I can never seem to just hold onto 100k credits without blowing it all on some new toy.

"The skill tree" is complex(sort of) and confusing(very) and every time I add a point I feel I need 5 more before what I blew on this point makes a difference but it eventually catches up and your toon feels like its learning something useful.

I'll update this once I get into the expansions and deeper into the game in general.

It took me 3 years to finally decide to finish playing the main quest of this game. It took me this long to decide to sit down and commit to finish it because the first 15 hours is such a painful slog. 15 hours is a long time for the game to feel somewhat enjoyable. 

The first part of the main quest is a tedious, repetition of flying somewhere and mining a shiny rock out of a bigger rock after downing some mobs. I hated it. The second half the main quest does get much better and have a couple of probably the best main storyline quests they've ever made. The second half of the main storyline really saves it. I did a few of the faction questlines and I thought they were pretty good too. There's a ton of side quests, most of them are forgettable.

I felt like companions were much more fleshed out here than the previous games and even some of the dialogue was good or decent.

Lore-wise, this game is so light on lore that it never gave me the curiosity to look up anything about it. It basically feels non-existent. I think its a difficult job to live up to the vast lore of Elder Scrolls and Fallout, but it feels like they didn't even try here.

This is probably the prettiest game they've made in this genre, the art and the sounds are amazing. I have no complaints here.

Customization options are pretty great. The shipbuilder was a huge plus and unique although a bit annoying to use, and all the weapons and armor are customizable but locked behind perks and materials like Fallout 4. This felt more of a grind to get the mats though so I didn't get to customize as much as I did in Fallout 4.

Pretty good QOL features.

I was disappointed in combat the most. Special abilities are pretty cool, but they've basically haven't innovated much in this area other than that. It feels like the same-old gunplay (possibly even worse than before) and melee isn't interesting at all.

I was interested in seeing space in my customized ship and ship battles, but after a little, it got old so quickly. Most of flying around isn't interesting and the battles aren't exciting at all. It kinda feels like theres not much happening in space despite many of the systems being settled on.

In quantity, theres a lot to do in quests, outposts, grinding materials, customization, and discovery. I just think they dropped the ball on providing a good baseline of quality or enjoyment or innovating on previous gameplay elements when taking on a new IP.

I'd recommend only if you want something mildly interesting that you can sink your time on and its on sale. To me, it was mediocre.

They clearly went with quantity over quality and you can feel it after a few first hours.

The amount of planets is incredibly large but very rarely do they contain anything important on them.

Additionaly each of them is procedurally generated and it is impossible to explore them fully because of the sheer scale.

Pairing that with Bethesdas' obsession with repeatable quests it makes it uncear which ones are important and which ones are pointless fillers.

I expected a cool space exploration game, instead I got a game where 90% of planets are empty dead rocks, 9% is filled with never ending quests that feel pointless and only 1% is actually worth doing.

It's annoying and made me stop asking vendors for jobs, because I can't be sure if it will be worth my time.

I'm probably in a minority in this but if somebody is like me this is your warning.

Also don't get me wrong I'm stil going to play it because I paid for it. I'm just saying that anything beyond faction and main quests is a 50/50 to be just trash repeatable.

At first, i had my doubts about this game and was skeptical because of the backlash this game was getting but in the end i decided to give it a try.

First of all the character creation was a lot better than i expected, the sliders and options allow you to create some really good and unique characters and also some freaks if you want to, but the best part of the CC is the option to select your background and character traits, the backgrounds are quite simple, it's mostly for role playing and offers you some starting perks, you can say it's kind of like Morrowind and Oblivion classes. The more fun though has to be the traits, there's a great selection of traits that give some unique moments and interactions, Such as Dream Home that allows the player to have a house but you have to pay a weekly mortgage or pay it off in full, Or you can start by having a bounty and bounty hunters are trying to claim it or you can have your character have parents that have dialogue and unique interactions on planets and some quest lines and also provide a starting player apartment for free.

Another thing that i want to point out is that said background, traits and perks can add new dialogue options that can help with quests. Also if you decide that you no longer want a specific trait you can have them removed by certain NPCs for role-playing reasons, such as if you chose the wanted trait you can pay your bounty at a tracker alliance agent or if you have alien DNA you can get "cured" by doctors.

I am not going to talk about the main quest other than that i personally enjoy it to avoid spoilers but i will say a few things about the side quests and faction quests. 

As is typical of a Bethesda game there are a huge amount of side quest with multiple ways to complete them, you can persuade your way to completing some quests, you can find alternative ways that the game doesn't tell you or you can just do the classic and kill your way out, and some of those quests are some of my favorites in any Bethesda game for instance one of my favorites has to be the crimson fleet/sysdef questline where you work undercover to take out the pirate faction of the game while hunting for the ultimate loot in the galaxy, you can also doublecross sysdef to join the crimson fleet unlocking the pirate playstyle.

Also another that stand out to me was the UC Vanguard questline, I love the introduction, where you're introduced to the lore surrounding the Colony War and the ship Simulator. The Ryujin questline that to unlock it you need to submit a résumé to a company, after that you attend an interview and get the job, at first, it seems mundane but each mission you complete you climb the corporate ladder and the missions become more like a spy movie than a standard office job. 
Or some hidden facilities that hides some surprises that i don't want to spoil, and more. 
One thing to point out is depending on your traits, background and your factions that you joined you will get more dialogue options that may help you to proceed some quest. 

As typical Bethesda fashion there are a lot of random encounters some of those are: a dispute between a sentient ai and suits, Space shanties, a creepy woman that should be in a horror game, ship's extended warranty and more.
I also love the outpost and housing in this game i spent a lot of hours building an outpost for harvesting resources and for housing, you have access to so much junk items in this game that seem useless but can make your house or outpost be more alive, also the fact that you can rotate objects in your hand is really helpful. 

Now the shipbuilding, i have spent a lot of hours and credits in the shipbuilding trying to build ship of my own design or just ships that exist in other games and movies like the Pillar of Autumn the Millennium Falcon and Normandy, you can do a lot of things with the shipbuilding but it is difficult in the beginning and the ui is not helping. 

Another thing to note is the attention to detail put into this game like the gravity of every planet is almost accurate to how they are in real life also the gravity actually feels right and not just normal g and zero g, also the way the time passes in planets it's mostly accurate with some exceptions, also the planets, moons and sun are actual 3d objects that actually orbit and are not just a 2d skybox, that seems like a small detail but it's really nice to see for space enjoyers. 

The combat is pretty solid, nothing too fancy just fun enough i can't complain, there are some scenarios were you can utilize the physics of the game like you can grab a explosive barrel and throw it at enemies and make it explode also the zero g combat is really fun. 

Also the graphics are very beautiful and add that with the simulated 3D planets you can witness some truly beautiful sights, i have spent more than a couple of hours using the camera mode adjusting the filters and settings to capture a lot of pictures, that isn't anything new but there is something truly relaxing and therapeutic to just try to capture a really good picture  while surveying a planet. 

Of course like any game there are some negatives like i really don't like that when you shoot in public or next to NPC's they don't react at all, i also do not like the use of crowd NPC's they don't do anything just aimlessly move around say a few things and look really ugly i get that they are used to make the cities more alive but i don't like them, also i feel like the enemy ai could use an upgrade. 

Overall, I think Starfield is a pretty great game with a good selection of quests, locations, and mechanics. you can truly spend hours doing whatever you like and playing whatever kind of character you want. There are negatives, sure, but there are plenty of positives, too. If you focus only on the negatives, you're probably going to have a bad time. But if you approach it with an open mind and appreciate what it does well, you can have a truly unique experience.

[h1] В какой-то момент мне начало казаться, что генерируются не планеты, а диалоги... [/h1]

Помните Cyberpunk 2077 на релизе? Технически всё было крайне плохо, но капец как интересно. Starfield ощущается примерно так же, только неинтересно.

Объективно у игры есть хорошие стороны. И не просто хорошие, а переломные для многих любителей космоса — это визуальный язык, стрельба и конструктор кораблей.

Сотни пропсов, парящих в невесомости; до мелочей проработанные станции с потрясающим освещением; масштабнейшие локации для эпичных мультиплеерных зарубов, которых вы никогда не увидите; настоящий gun-porn в лучших традициях Cyberpunk 2077 с прокачкой и модификациями. А вишенкой на этом великолепию идет блочно-модульный фит кораблей, в котором можно утонуть на многие часы.

И давайте ещё раз закрепим про визуальный стиль, чтобы стало понятно, куда ушли 10 лет разработки — стилистика и исполнение выше всяких похвал. Пока другие студии делают стилизованную сай-фай мультипликацию а-ля Marathon, Bethesda проработала каждую дверную ручку.

Но... Зачем-то в перерывах между «красиво пострелять, залутать и прокачаться» завезли диалоговую РПГ. И завезли так, что лучше просмотреть пару лишних экранов загрузки, чем ритмично, с паузами, «прощёлкивать» абсолютно все диалоговые окна. 

[h1] Много загрузок, говорили они. Нет посадок на планеты, говорили они. Устаревший движок, говорили они... [/h1]

Первое, что сильно бьёт по глазам, а потом и по рукам — интерфейс. Бывает плохой UI (Grim Dawn) или сложный табличный «мониторинг всех систем» (EVE Online и 4X-стратегии), но Starfield пошёл дальше и решил не отображать ничего, а взаимодействия со звёздной картой (да и в целом навигация по меню) не оставят равнодушным даже шестипалых.

Десятки неочевидных решений перемещения по системам и посадках на планетах, невозможность следовать по простроенному маршруту неоткрытых систем — разработчики просто не понимали и явно не тестировали свой продукт. Ибо даже запутанный (визуально) интерфейс EVE Online решает самые сложные «задачи со звёздочками» в несколько кликов.

Управление — это отдельная песня, и речь о назначении и переназначении клавиш. Неотключаемые «зажатия» клавиш на клавиатуре в 50+ свободных кнопок и неразрывно связанные двойные действия на один бинд кнопки просто выше моего понимания разработки такого рода продуктов.

Это настоящая диверсия продукта. И Starfield 2.0, который якобы был, должен начинаться не с переработки игрового мира, а с переработки интерфейса.

И если вы еще не устали зажимать Escape, то геймдизайнер со сценаристами знает, как вас развлечь. Вы же любите буквы? У них «есть их много для вас». Сотни часов аудио-нарратива, лица, города, гильдии — никто и ничего не имеет никакого смысла. В какой-то момент мне начало казаться, что генерируются не планеты, а диалоги...

Ну кто играет в игры Bethesda ради сюжета, он скорее зарисовка. Прощёлкали диалоги, посмотрели цели миссии — ну дайте пострелять! One of the best things about Red Alert 3 is watching a battle move from land to sea without slowing down. An Allied Riptide can carry infantry across the water and drop them behind a base while the defenders are busy watching the road. Even the shoreline feels worth fighting over. With buildings and ore expansions out on the water, a navy can threaten the economy that keeps your opponent’s tanks coming.

The three factions each have something fun to learn. Soviet Twinblades can carry tanks across the map, Allied Cryocopters can shrink them, and the Empire’s Mecha Tengu can switch between ground combat and dogfighting. Those abilities make small fights surprisingly involved. They can also make a big battle feel like a lot to juggle, especially when you’re trying to use the right ability while keeping an eye on a second front.

The campaigns lean all the way into the absurdity. Tim Curry delivers the Soviet premier’s speech about escaping to space with a straight face that makes the whole thing even funnier. Every campaign mission is built for two commanders, and playing with a friend makes it fun to divide up the work and see whose plan falls apart first. The AI co-commander can make those same missions feel more rigid when you’re playing solo.

**9/10.** Red Alert 3 is easy to recommend if you like fast base-building strategy and factions that reward learning their quirks. The cutscenes are worth watching for Tim Curry alone. The battles are worth replaying until checking the water becomes second nature.

Red Alert 3 is a very serious military strategy game about time travel, alternate history, naval warfare and global domination.

The Soviet Union has time machines.
The Allies have advanced technology.
Japan has giant robots.

Somehow the most dangerous weapon on the battlefield is still my inability to manage my economy.

You can build a perfectly respectable military force, carefully position your units and prepare a coordinated attack.

Or you can build 40 tanks and send them directly into the enemy base.

Both are valid strategies.

The naval combat is also surprisingly good. Apparently the solution to every strategic problem is to put more military equipment in the water.

And then there is the Empire of the Rising Sun, which looked at conventional warfare and decided that giant transforming robots were probably more efficient.

Honestly, difficult to argue with the results.

[h1]Recommended[/h1]
Red Alert 3 is completely ridiculous, knows it's ridiculous, and that's exactly why I still enjoy it. You have transforming tanks, armoured bears, giant robots, psychic schoolgirls and Tim Curry delivering one of the greatest lines in gaming history. What more do you need? 

[h2]PROS[/h2]
[list]
[*] Three factions that genuinely feel different instead of being reskins of each other.
[*] Loads of memorable units with some completely stupid abilities, in the best possible way.
[*] The campaigns are cheesy as hell and packed with live-action cutscenes.
[*] The cast is ridiculous. Tim Curry, George Takei, J.K. Simmons and plenty more.
[*] Naval combat is much more important than in previous Red Alert games, with plenty of amphibious units.
[*] Co-op campaigns were a brilliant idea and still make the missions fun to replay.
[*] Skirmish is still great when you want to build a massive army and completely flatten the AI.
[*] There are loads of mods available if you want more factions, units and complete conversions.
[*] The soundtrack still goes hard.
[*] It has the exact sort of stupid humour I want from Red Alert.
[/list]

[h2]CONS[/h2]
[list]
[*] Getting older mods working on the modern Steam version is sometimes an absolute pain in the arse.
[*] Some mods require specific game versions, launch commands or extra fixes.
[*] Online functionality obviously isn't what it once was.
[*] Pathfinding occasionally makes you question whether your army has collectively suffered a head injury.
[/list]

[h2]OVERALL[/h2]
It's old, cheesy and completely over the top, but that's Red Alert.

As a long-time fan of the series, the game feels far too childish and colorful, with an aesthetic that resembles a cartoon/anime rather than the alternative world war we loved in previous C&C games. The biggest issue is how the visual style and the bizarre units mechs/robots completely destroy the atmosphere. The gameplay also suffers from poor design choices, especially the horrible co-commander system that forces you to cooperate with an AI that often does more harm than good. This partner ruins much of the fun by blocking your strategies or wasting resources. Additionally, the maps feel far too small and cramped, which removes the possibility for proper tactical expansion. The new method for ore mining is also a major letdown ,fixed mines is far more boring than the dynamic ore fields we had before. When you add the fact that units die far too quickly in combat, you are left with a gaming experience that feels stressful and superficial instead of epic.

That being said, the game is not without its merits. I actually like the mechanic of being able to build entire bases on water, which adds a unique layer to the strategy. The only other thing that actually works as intended is the fantastic cast of actors. The live-action cutscenes featuring stars like Tim Curry , J.K. Simmons and Andrew Divoff are a clear highlight and provide the game with the charm it otherwise lacks on the battlefield. In reality, the game is okay for what it is, but it simply should not have been a Command & Conquer title. It feels like a different game entirely that has been forced into a franchise where it doesn't belong.

I get dragged back to this game a lot for a lot of positive reasons, however, I can't say that the reasons are for the fact that this game is polished, stable and cohesive.

This game is a very, VERY messy experience. Chaos ensues everywhere and I struggle with controls often. There's no proper guide on game mechanics and first hours into the game will be very confusing and can ruin your first impressions.

There are orders and objectives, however, they don't feel rewarding most of the time and don't feel like they progress your campaign. The units you can control are mostly braindead (same can be said for enemy forces) and you'll be mostly doing everything on your own.

If you're very passionate about how AI is used, you'll probably be put out of the experience by AI made voicelines.

The game is mostly fine nowadays in terms of optimization, but last year it was worse, and I still encounter odd freezes or softlocks.

HOWEVER,

You've got the whole map of the Vietnam, its cities, villages and bases everywhere, all of which you can capture (if I'm not mistaken. Perhaps there are some permanent ones too.)

You can create your own outposts. I've spent lots of time figuring out where to put a nice base for artillery support or where I can cut off a major supply chain (one time I got it right, the whole base immediately became captured and piles and piles of trucks and tanks appeared as pure slaughter ensued. However, the enemy supplies dropped to 1% xd)

You can use trucks, tanks, boats, aircraft, artillery (without proper aiming, so you have to manually adjust where you wanna strike), AAs, etc.

You can control other teams across the map when you rank up enough, which I suppose introduce some strategy into the mix, but so far I'm yet to find any usefulness out of the feature.

Graphics are not the best, but charming and can look quite nice in some places, but I like how nature looks like.

Long story short, there's a LOT of content that is present, giving the game a potential of being a very fun and addicting odd, silly sandbox FPS game, but the developer is yet to put the pieces into the places. It's a very ambitious game and it's a lot of work just for a single developer, who is still updating the game, adding new content. But, I REALLY wish that the developer would focus on main core mechanics of the game, which are still raw and unpolished. It's nice to see new units or new fire support, but without a proper core, they would all fade into just novel distracting features that will only highlight many problems of the game.

Let me start by commending the sheer amount of ambition realized here. So much of what you've heard is true about the depth and width of features to offer, all done by a single developer. But it kind of ends there as most if not all of them come off more like a proof of concept instead of a realized design. I've seen a lot of indie games fall into this trap of feature creep. Devs who don't expand their production by hiring a working team, fine in itself if you can manage as sometimes that does have its own benefits. But as the features added are piled on more and more, with nobody to ask you if you should rather than could, you add a significantly greater technical debt to the game that one developer alone would take forever to fix. Even if we assume no vibe code was used to outline the structure, you raise the risk of breaking so many older scripts and systems that once worked because that is the nature of how games that build their foundations out of spaghetti crumble. That's probably the reason why you might notice a common complaint is lack of attention to polish, since fixing the debt would be glacial at this scale.

As for the gameplay/design itself, I have a few issues.

(1) Lack of Clarity | No surprise this being set in the Vietnam War, foliage & asymmetrical warfare is inevitable. That's all fine if my disadvantage playing the US would be that the Vietnamese have better camouflage (it was literally the NLF's greatest strength). But where the problem really lies is the lack of any ambient occlusion, which basically darkens parts of the game scene from the ambient light. The weird Gouraud shading makes it so you can walk straight into wooden spikes that are right there on proud display around a base because the lack of contrast makes nothing about it different from the rest of the ground textures. Same goes for snakes, who are unusually quiet. In fact, that reminds me...

(2) Sound Design | Either stupid loud and never shutting up, or you get one-tapped by... I don't really know to be honest. There's just that many hazards you can stumble upon out in the jungle, and almost none of it gives you a sound or even a hit noise to point out something is close in the area with you.

(3) Preservation (Or lack thereof) | I hate this one so much. Everything is out to kill you. And initially that might sound realistic when you consider the amount of friendly fire in collateral bombings, but WHYYYYYY does it have to be dropped on every single squad of 2 malnourished farmers I come across???? In fact, the entire logistics of this game I refuse to believe is real on the tab menu. No matter what you do, everybody seems to have a bomb shoved up their punji for almost every minor inconvenience. It also circles back to problem 2 where no sound of a grenade hits the ground, or that the RPGs in this game sound like opening a soda bottle more than the weapon that can butcher you for daring to stand behind or using indoors. I'm not asking you blow up cows in Thailand to achieve immersion, I just need a better way to know there's an Anti-Personnel guy without having spontaneous combustion. I pray to anyone attempting hardcore mode, because you're going to get one tapped by barbed wire stuck half way into the ground and trees. 

(4) Progression & Pacing | I'm gonna lump the 2 in one as I find they have some overlap. There is almost no breathing room at any point you play in your career. You could be 4 villages away from the nearest active skirmish, and guess what? This looks like a good time for Napalm, cowboy! Enjoy that recon mission we gave you 5 minutes ago, because we'll bomb everything to Hell & back, yet SOMEHOW NONE OF IT IS DESTROYED! You just kinda go to point A then B and make the flag go to you, I hardly find a reason to stay in villages or build bases when none of it has a benefit for the long term.

Leveling is also just the worst. Probably the most obtuse feature in the game. None of the skills or attributes are explained in the slightest. The manual is not out, but that really should be the priority if you are going for this much depth. I don't know how to level some, you just guess, others feel useless, actually I can barely tell the difference in skills. Nothing feels like it makes a difference, and without any information what it does do, I'm taking virtual diet pills. Past the haha warcrimes skill, what does any of it actually do? Just like with money or village loyalty, I have barely a use for it, and don't see why I should?

(5) AI | Not that kind, although the choppy vocal fry in the lines AI loves to do does start to feel like Chinese Water Torture. This is about the NPCs.

Besides the friendly squad somehow getting lobotomized compared to the early release builds, both friendlies and enemies feels like babysitting a daycare while the Combine are raiding Earth during the 7 Hour War. Seriously, did you get a wizard to curse this game so my team is always eating glue while Delta Force snipes me with an RPG-7 through a 2 pixel sightline at night under 50 km of foliage? This is some black magic, it actually kills me how intentional it feels at times. And of course everybody has a rocket of some kind, so they just spam what seems like a basically infinite supply of the stuff in a random ditch. Meanwhile, I can't get my squad to stop clipping into every building at every garrison. I literally have witnessed 4 of them die before leaving spawn because of a hovering snake, come on!

And they spawn, OH MY GOD they never stop spawning! Not in the out of bushes and trees way, I mean I could watch a US pilot manifest 2 inches behind me during a base capture. There's a new platoon every 10 seconds, no matter how many bases or supplies you destroy. Logistics are like skills in that sense, you can't even tell if it's actually in the game or just a placeholder, it's that bad! They just keep spawning. It never feels like less, you just have to stalemate until you get lucky really. Doesn't help they never miss. I'd honestly would prefer it if you had them shoot more often between volleys, but increase their aim spread under different factors like distance, time of day, or weather. Because if they're not going pro E-sports on your backdoor, they'll sit there for 20 seconds picking their nose, even if you get in their face.

(6) Survival | It's not too annoying. But I would like something of a stomach rumble or lip smack, even just having more lines saying you're hungry or thirsty, because right now you sometimes forget to press H. And that happens a lot because I'm obviously not going to feel the hunger IRL to be aware of the matter.

Medicine is still not really anything special. Looks like they'll expand it later, but I kind of dread the idea of bleeding and infections if I'm fighting aimbots and flying elephants that make no footsteps. Nothing more to say besides more mechanics with no indication of how you feel, meaning more annoyance.

That's all I have to say. I mean, we could talk about the other maps being a 2nd game; but that stops being cool when the core game can't even stand on its own, so i can't be bothered. Otherwise you'll get some good fun out of it for a time, but try to play it any longer, and it starts to feel like that one friend who tells the same joke everytime. It only serves to waste your time and sanity.

I launched this game and thought "Wow this is pretty fucked and buggy as hell." And frankly it is. But shocked by the amount of content I found in the game.

There is a kind of huge skill system, mental health system, patriotism, hunger, thirst, need for cigarettes. I could go on and on. I just kept playing it for some reason as I started to get the handle on what the hell was going on. I played as an Infantry Squad leader patrolling and finding Vietcong tunnel systems in need of destruction, Artillery positions hitting Da nang, I went back and played for a while as a gunship pilot getting radio calls for emergency support, I flew a F4 Phantom again with messages about units in need of urgent support, I returned to the ground and found a road heavily used by the NVA. So I built an outpost to disrupt them. Calling a airdrop of supplies to start building, and having more brought in by a C-47. I put barracks, a mess hall, a bar, an armory, guard towers, bunkers, helipads, and even some artillery emplacements. I eventually had it well supplied and self sufficient enough it could hold its own against the AI and I moved on. I assaulting major NVA strongholds calling in paratroops or infantry platoons by helicopter to help take and hold it. My tour is in its last 60 days before I can go to Da nang and catch a flight to Saigon to fly back to my characters home state. But obviously I will be back for a second tour.

Now all that being said while this was happening the game really is an incredibly buggy mess. The flying is pretty bizarre, the NVA will just being running about, Your squad doesn't follow you properly, massive area's seem to just blow up in massive explosions with no obvious caught or effect. Airstrike called in down really fall quite where you want them, Tons of clipping through the ground, trees, etc etc. Technically I could command other units in the area and direct them to attack objectives but its probably the most annoying and frustrating interface to deal with and very little instruction. There are systems in the game like mental health, armor, camo etc but I have no idea how well it actually works and as much as I would love to lead a squad stealthfully through the jungle like a couple of LARRPS the AI squad is pretty horrible and unreliable, and I am not even sure those stealth mechanics work. AI seems to just constantly scream in terror at most times even just standing around not under attack at a fire base.

The game looks very silly and can definitely be pretty silly at times. But what's hiding underneath is the perfected formula for making an actually fun single-player milsim sandbox that has been eluding larger studios for decades. 

The main thing this game gets right over others is leaning into the open world nature of the map. Instead of building a massive map, only to not utilize it at all by splitting the game up into a bunch of story missions set at specific locations (looking at you Arma), this game's whole shtick is that the war is live and happening independent of you everywhere. This not only makes the game more unpredictable, but also makes it far more engaging. You're not just thinking about getting to the next mission now, you're looking at the war situation and deciding where to go and why. Not to say missions don't exist at all in this game, because they kind of do. You'll receive orders from command occasionally, but they pretty much just tell you to go somewhere and do something that you could actually expect to be ordered to in a war. No cutscenes, no fantastical over the top scenarios, just regular gameplay as usual.

The AI squad you command is also pretty easy to move around and isn't completely brain dead to the point of needing every little action spelled out for them (again, looking at you Arma).

If you're into single-player shooters and milsims, absolutely buy this game. The cost is cheap and the developer is constantly improving the game with new updates.

Vietnam War: I'm Wiggin' Out, Man.

In the indie game sphere, passion projects are a dime a dozen. We are conditioned to presume any game pumped out by a small dev team is done with the hopes and dreams of making their idea a reality. We are [i] also [/i] relatively certain that those ideas won't be fully manifested properly. It's not intentional, but for every project that succeeds in its goal, there's just as many that end as either a game dev crashout or a middling failure. The road to Hell is paved with games that got too popular too fast, and who's devs flamed out under the pressure. A series of Braid's, Yandere Simulator's and FEZ's that linger on digital storefronts like dust in the wind. I viewed Vietnam War under this same lens, because every idea that it mentions seems [i] a bit [/i] absurd. An open world simulation of the Vietnam War that lets you do anything and everything is a hard sell, and surely it wouldn't work.

And it doesn't, but it's one of the most amusing games ever made.

Vietnam War is an open world first person shooter that allows you carte blanche to fight in the Vietnam War, and that includes Cambodia and Laos as well. You are a pawn in a grand and elaborate attempt to make the entire conflict run on Unity, and it is a circus performance each time I play this game. And I say this with 30 hours on the clock, you'd expect to understand what kinda stuff the game can throw at you by then but NOPE! Each and every time I play, the game finds a new and exciting way to break my skull open with the butt of a Type 56 AK. It's an astoundingly stupid game to play, and I say that as a term of endearment. 

Enemy AI? Completely bonkers, you will watch hordes of Vietcong and Pathet Lao run across open jungle to get mulched by an attack helicopter. They're also really good at getting stuck, so shoot any body you see a few times to make sure they're actually dead. Friendly AI? Also bonkers, do not, under any circumstance, trust an ally in a vehicle. You will suddenly get struck by a UH-1 that spawned in, clipped another UH-1 and drops two burning hulks of Bell Aircraft parts directly on your basecamp. NPC's? Manic, I keep being kissed by random Vietnamese women and I don't know why. I will watch them ram a 2CV into a M113 APC without a care in the world. They're not fazed by the concept of the war being fought around them, nor the problem that an ongoing insurgency in the town they're driving to raises. They merely exist to let me harass people on ID's and buy cigarettes. And when you think the game is over after playing as the US Army, Marines, Air Force, Army and Marines Helicopter Corps, SEAL's, SOG [i] and [/i] Air America, you get to go home.

To find that the dev has rendered an exceedingly large USA homefront map that you can [i] also [/i] do things in. Grow weed and sell it to the Hell's Angels, hit the oil rig and strike it rich with a claim, dig up random Mesoamerican artifacts that augment your comedic amount of stats. Buy a nightclub, finance that nightclub with bank robbery. Get involved in random massive riots that turn Kansota into Vietnam. There's more layers of content in this game than most Triple A releases, and every single time that I think we're done and dusted with features, the devs add another. He adamantly refuses to stop adding things to this great and mighty quasi-functional salad of a game, and I'm all here for it. Every instinct in my head tells me that we shouldn't keep adding things, and yet I'm [i] fascinated [/i] by each thing tacked onto this game. It's a manic, bipolar experience of a game that barely works, crashes constantly and amuses me to no end. So it's just like the Vietnam War.

What I thought I was getting was a goofy cartoonish Vietnam War game to mess around in for a bit. What I didn't realize I was actually getting, but what I got was one of the most in-depth, realistic, depressing, and dare I say moving depictions of war in any video game. You might think I am on drugs, but I am not. This game may not look like it on the surface, due to the graphics and relatively simple animations, but don't let that deceive you. This is a game that prioritizes gameplay and depth over graphics, which is something that is sorely lacking in my opinion in the modern gaming industry.

On the US side, you will see all the horrors of war. You will see your fellow soldiers burnt to death as a result of Vietcong (VC) molotov attack, rogue napalm, or fuel storage explosion. You will be pinned down by a VC MG nest, and call in for Huey gunship support, only for it to get taken out by a SAM on the other side of the hill you had no idea about. You will grow paranoid of the creatures of the jungle, who may be harmless but may at any moment turn aggressive on you. Despite this, you will gain the loyalty of a dog, and do your best to protect him, but it will disappear on a random mission. You will get saved by a friendly medic, who moments later is taken out by an enemy sniper. You will be ambushed by disguised VC soldiers hiding in villages, and amidst the screaming and chaotic firefight that follows several innocent villagers will be killed. You and your squad will be victims of friendly fire incidents, probably many times. Of course, you will also wield the full arsenal of the US military, from battleship barrages to B-52 carpet bombs to attack helicopters to flamethrowers, to kill as many "bastard atheist Commies" as possible - in the name of their freedom and liberation.

But underneath all the horror of the war lies an unmistakable sense of brotherhood, purpose, and in a sense, freedom. The constant radio chatter, the patriotic music broadcast everywhere, that medic running to you when you get wounded, the random rifleman in your squad that constantly complains about being tired, or the radioman swearing he totally isn't drunk. You feel like part of something big, and even though you barely know the faceless people fighting alongside you, you share a common struggle, a common fear, and a common goal. The 60 Victory Points (the real objective of the game - to capture them all), they send you on what feels like an epic and dangerous mission across the entire map, even into Laos and Cambodia. Some are much harder than others to get to, but this just makes finally getting to them more satisfying.

Then, after your quest for all VPs is complete, you are able to return home (all VPs took me about 40 in-game hours/5 in-game years with mostly default settings, but after your first year of service you can return to the states). But after killing thousands of VC soldiers, liberating even more innocent villagers, traversing the entire region multiple times over, the grand hero's welcome home - it's never there. Instead, you are welcomed home with the deafening silence of a busy airport terminal full of nameless faceless strangers who don't know you, don't care about you, don't acknowledge you, and don't know what you've been through or seen. You can take the bus downtown, where the constant radio chatter and/or patriotic music is replaced by the distant noise of a protest against the war you just returned from. Maybe that protest even turns violent, and a protestor is killed. Your grand goal of liberating Vietnam is replaced by a forking road with many options, but ultimately they all revolve around the basic need to make money. You can stay with the feds, and work for the FBI, including putting your skills to the test spying in Siberia. You can keep it more simple, and work for local law enforcement, start a farm, or purchase a business. You can also fall into a life of crime, and spend your days hiding from the government like you used to hide from the VC. Or, in this game the War is neverending, and if the jungles of Vietnam ever call your name, you can travel back to Saigon and re-enlist.

* Absolutely massive map of Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia, with hundreds of handmade cities, villages, enemy bases, other POIs
* Massive map of a, shall we say alternate US, consisting of Hawaii, New Texico, W. Ashington, Coloradaho, Wyomingtana, and Kansota, and part of Ohiowa, with a bit of Canada and Mexico near the borders
* Siberia map related to certain post-war careers
* Tons of weapons with unique behaviors, characteristics, animations, etc...there are a lot that are not available at simple armories and you will find them scattered around the map, hidden in random crates, etc.
* Tons of vehicles of all shapes and sizes - civilian vehicles, military jeeps, tanks, AA trucks, scout helicopters, attack helicopters, transport helicopters, small planes, attack planes, jet fighters, boats, etc.
* Helicopter flight models feel shockingly good
* Cockpits and interiors of vehicles, they are basic but functional
* Base building available basically anywhere outside of pre-existing bases, decent number of options for buildable structures currently
* Just tons of random small features that make the game feel so immersive despite the visuals - interacting with villagers and buying from them, finding and befriending stray dogs, random jungle creatures some of which are hostile, getting makeshift modifications applied to your equipment, VC propaganda directed at US soldiers, the need to clean your guns often, the random dialogue from your character and other characters, both in-person and on the radio, and a lot more
* About 10 different career options on the US side (different branches of military, affects starting location and random mission types, among other things)
* Option to play as Vietcong which has different gameplay from the US in many aspects, but obviously no "post-war" gameplay like the US does, at least currently
* Probably the most important thing, this game is being worked on actively and the dev has a discord where you can discuss the game and suggest additions and report bugs

Cons:
* Allied AI is pretty moronic but, this review was drafted 21 August 2026 and just today (22 August) the dev released an update that addresses this issue somewhat
* Optimization could be a bit better, particularly with smoke/fire effects - when an area gets carpet bombed or napalmed my performance seriously tanks, and my computer is pretty good too I think
* Some hitboxes are kinda buggy, I believe this was also somewhat addressed with today's update but I have not tested
* Just general jankiness, which is frustrating at times, but not a dealbreaker to me and like I said this game is very much WIP - just go read the update history and see for yourself
* The player's character climbs stairs/ladders so damn slowly lol, considering how fast and long he is able to run it makes no sense
* I wish there were more radio dialogues, or squadmate dialogues, just more dialogue lines in general. Some more variety would make it feel more alive but I love the dialogue that is in the game currently
* Day/night cycle, glad it is in the game at all, but it is largely just day/night right now, there is not really a smooth transition between the two with a dawn and dusk it is more just day one moment and then night the next
* Options for the Vietcong post-war, in a then-unified Vietnam with no foreign military presence, dealing with the fallout of the war...if it's already a thing I missed it but if not that would make the VC option more alluring, currently the US side has more content because of the stateside/post-war thing

Vietnam War is an extremely well thought out open-world military simulator. It packs a lot of content, though it has several drawbacks. Here's my review filled a couple of things to consider before buying the game.

There's a shit ton of content in this game. You could play as the Americans and the Vietnamese (both the north and the south, if I remember correctly). Specifically, you could play as most branches of the military, including the Army, Navy, Air Force, VC and more. Not only that, but the game also comes with an expansive map, covering all of Indochina (Laos, Vietnam) and even featuring Hawaii and the mainland US (these two are available after completing a tour, usually 1 in game year to complete). I also would like to add that military equipment and vehicles from both sides are also complete, for the most part.

Though, when it comes to drawbacks, there are several that has to be pointed out. First is how unoptimized and buggy the game is. The software crashes often, especially if you were to operate any aircraft (including helicopters). Though if you save the game often, and stick to land vehicles, you'll be alright, albeit a bit tedious and bothersome. Second, despite what the game looks like, it actually requires a decent PC to run. Playing the game with a device below the recommended/minimum specifications is not recommended.

Overall, I still do think that this is a game worth playing. Even though its "kinda" buggy, I think that janky-ness has its charm. It has a lot of potential given the content we're given, and if the developer were to ever fix these problems, then that would be great.

Vietnam War is, with no exaggeration, the most schizophrenic MilSim I have ever played, and I say that with nothing but love. 

To put it into perspective: I had started out somewhere in the middle of the jungle with a village a few clicks away with a whole 11-strong team in tow. My squad had a company preacher in it arbitrarily giving sermons and quoting the bible with Text To Speech voicelines. I begun trading with one of the civilians after entering the village when we were all ambushed out of nowhere. The company preacher took a bullet square to the face and died right in front of me, but somehow he continued to preach post-mortem and I could hear his sermons everywhere I went, including after I got separated from my team in the ensuing chaos. I spent some time wandering around in the jungle till I got attacked by an angry monkey in the wild, killed it, then listened as my character called the angry monkey a "Goddamn atheist communist." The company preacher continued his gospel in my character's head until I wandered into a US Base where I was able to buy and eat a hamburger from a Vietnamese Chef, when US command decided it was time to call a napalm strike on their own base all because a single Vietcong guy was out on the wire taking potshots at an artillery cannon. The napalm killed a good half of the soldiers stationed at the base then I took a bite out of the burger as my character mutted "Man, this is crazy" to himself in a very monotone voice. I left the base and eventually got killed by a VC sniper before waking up in some other US Base where I was confined to a wheelchair to move around. Thankfully the wheelchair was all-terrain, as I was able to scale hills with an M60 despite being crippled.
