The game is promising, but it is far too buggy at the moment. I'll start with the compliments and end with complaints.

For the good: This game has a lot of promise, but that's the operative word: "Promise". It is fun to play initially, but the constant bugginess starts to get extremely annoying extremely fast. I love the open world concept, the arcade nature, the multiple expertise area (Infantry, Armor, SpecOps, Armor, Helos, Aircraft), and the objective systems. It is insanely fun to saturate an objective with bombs, rockets, and guns and then capture the point while fighting off the stragglers. The game's difficulty is a good balance, and you cannot just run and gun lone wolf and expect to live. The amount of different aircraft and vehicles in this game is awesome and extremely enjoyable to play. The detail applied to presenting the cockpit/interior of vehicles is impressive for an arcade game and the varying loadouts that can be applied means that each platform can provide varying approaches to attacking objectives. I personally enjoyed loading up 500 lb and rockets onto an OV-10 and saturating NVA strongholds with munitions. The F-4 Phantoms show promise with the old TV guided bombs, and they fly insanely fast. Lastly the scale of the world and the detail of the regions is an awesome touch. 

THE BAD

1. Bore sight on the vehicles is wildly off. 3rd person crosshairs will be perfectly centered on target and when zoom is applied, the optic is wildly misaligned; I'd estimate nearly 5-15* of traversal. It makes engaging fast moving infantry with a tank coax super annoying, as the misaligned slew is disorienting and reacquiring targets is spatially difficult. 

2. Vehicles keep double spawning on top of each other. I have died multiple times due to 2 of the same helicopter spawning atop each other, which will cause the first takeoff to most assuredly flip over and crash; Luckily I wasn't playing hardcore mode (Permadeath aka no respawns), but this bug makes hardcore mode unplayable. 

3. Region loading: While it makes sense to chunk the game up into boundaries, this is impractical if you are attacking an objective that borders 2+ regions. It is super annoying and unplayable to be in the middle of a nose down rocket dive and then suddenly the game freezes while the region loads. And for reference, I am running a 4080ti. If I'm having this problem, so is everybody else. And it happens every single time. 

4. Air strikes via radio: the air strike drops right on top of your position, not a configurable distance, nor an offset with a bearing from your position. Right on top of you. Order in a B-52? Well, you better be in the middle of the enemy base or else its wasted... and you're running for your life so you don't get fragged. Also, you can't control the attack vector, which is crucial for a good strike. 

5. Ammunition effects: A 500 lb bomb and its lethal radius is considerable. While this game is not milsim, it is disappointing to drop dummy 500 lb bombs essentially on the target while moving at mach jesus and then paradropping in to find the area of effect to be comically small. Same for high explosive/frag rounds on the tanks; I was defending a FOB from NVA attack, and there was a group of 5 infantry in the open in a loose formation all within ~5 meters. I placed HE in the middle of the group and it only dropped 2. Beings that ammo is limited (you can RTB to a pad and resupply) this should be fixed. 

6. Great for infantry, armor, and helos.... not so great for fixed wing aircraft. While it is playable, the fixed wing aspect is somewhat limited as the land is quickly obscured in a ground haze if you climb too high. This doesn't prevent you from conducting strafing runs, but it does prevent the pop-up, nose down dives that CAS conducted in Vietnam without getting disoriented on where the target is. Once again, fixed wing is playable, but it could be much better. Also, the F-4 phantom flies like a bat out of hell true to form, but it does make the game quite laggy when trying to use free camera slew. Also, the fixed wing physics of flight seem like it's just helicopter physics applied to a fixed wing aircraft; Not a game breaker, but it is odd to essentially do a tail slide drift in an OV-10. I found it difficult to use the L/R mouse movement for aileron control, so I resorted to Yaw (via A& D) and Pitch (up/down on the mouse) and it worked pretty well. 

7. Customizable controls: Remapping is a necessity. I don't like having to rapidly flick my mouse just to roll my helo to stay upright, and I would like to remap other items to different hotkeys; I don't use smoke grenades, but I was constantly reaching to hit "0" and then "1" to heal, and also "9" and "1" & "2" for rations and water. 

8. Resupply/Repair points: Only complaint is fuel is not automatically applied, and fuel cans are oddly absent from around helipads/airfields/ground vehicle spawn points. This is the least of my complaints and somewhat easily remedied by running around the base like a moron looking for an armory or a random spawn of jerry cans, but it is annoying -especially since the repair point has fuel cans stacked around it that you cannot interact with. 

Once again, great game if the Dev keeps at it. I will probably keep playing from time to time, but it is far too buggy to pour a ton of my time into at this moment. Best of luck to the Dev and I hope he continues to evolve this awesome idea.

I first came across Demonologist while browsing Steam. The store page immediately caught my attention with its dark, atmospheric presentation and the promise of a co-op horror experience focused on identifying and exorcising evil spirits in cursed locations. It looked interesting enough that I decided to dig a little deeper before committing. 

I watched several gameplay videos and trailers to get a clearer picture of what the game actually offered. After seeing the Unreal Engine 5 visuals, the investigation mechanics, the variety of equipment, and the tense, unpredictable encounters, I thought it looked genuinely fun. At that point I went ahead and purchased it. I also gifted a copy to a friend so we could experience it together. We both jumped in and immediately enjoyed the game.

It took us a little while to fully figure out how to complete a map successfully the first time learning the evidence gathering process, the map-specific objectives, and the proper way to perform an exorcism required some trial and error but once we understood the flow we managed to get it done. That initial learning curve felt rewarding rather than frustrating.We are now 8.8 hours into the game and still have no complaints. Both of us particularly love the graphics, which stand out as some of the strongest in the co-op horror genre thanks to the detailed environments, lighting, and overall atmosphere. 

The leveling system provides a satisfying sense of progression as new maps, equipment, and options unlock. House customization (the ability to upgrade and personalize the safe house between missions) adds a fun long term goal and a personal touch between tense investigations. And the jump scares are excellent well-timed, varied, and genuinely effective at keeping the tension high.

Overall, Demonologist has been a highly enjoyable co-op horror experience for both of us. I would recommend this game to anyone looking for atmospheric ghost-hunting gameplay with strong visuals, solid progression, and memorable scares.

I'm not one to review games on here, but I figured after all of the change I would decide to weigh in. When I first started playing Demonologist a while ago I loved it, and I refused to play other similar games because I enjoyed this game that much. 

Unfortunately, in February 2025 there was an update about a "major overhaul" that was coming, and then by October 2025 there was finally an update after nothing, with a few screenshots of a new map, but that was it. The supposed major overhaul largely was supposed to focus on optimization, however, since then the game continuously crashes, even when running it without and upscaling or NVIDIA frame gen on, it still crashes pretty consistently. As soon as you turn either of those one, I was lucky if I got through a single round without it crashing. It was sometime around the update that finally came in January 2026 when one of the maps (Bedlam) that would frequently drop to 30 FPS at times like hunts, was finally fixed, even though this map was introduced in late 2023.

Since then, any updates have been entirely based on adding new achievements because they added a new map, with no forethought on the longevity of the game. An easy example, is anyone who has played a video game before would easily be able to recognize that adding tiers to your tools or prestige levels. And although I'm sure some people will say it's just copying another game, a tier list for weapons/tools and prestige levels has been around for decades, so it's definitely not copying anything. But, here we are, with another update just coming out about this new map, with again no forethought in sight. I played the game today with some friends and in the first game it glitched where I couldn't see the items in my hands so we had to restart, and then the second game the other players were sliding around, sometimes even facing me with their head turned around unnaturally facing the other direction because that's actually the direction they were facing, even though the game clearly wasn't registering it. Years later, and not only has the game not actually improved, it's gotten worse, to be completely honest. Each new map introduces more bugs, but the dev is too hard-focused on bringing in a new map rather than just adding some small fixes and other longevity changes to promote people to do more than install > get new achievements > uninstall.

So, although I've put a decent number of hours into this game, I can say that >95% of it came from before the start of January 2025, and anything after that has been to get achievements and play it for an hour or two with friends a handful of times, but ultimately, I just do not recommend anyone gets this game right now. Maybe in the future the dev will start focusing on the things that need to be focused on, but given the years that it has been, I don't see that happening.

It looks really good and is inherently much scarier than the other ghost hunting game, plus includes the ability to exorcise the ghosts. But that's about where the positives end.

The maps initially look nice, but after playing the same map a few times, you'll know every jump scare and learn that events that happen are "just because" and have nothing to do with the ghost. It gets repetitive and old pretty quicky. The tools and by and large inferior to Phasmo in how they function, which is sad because the art style for them is fantastic. It feels much more "Supernatural" and less "Ghostfacers" (if you know, you know ;)) I like the concepts, but finding a ghost is entirely trial and error and not any sort of process. You can very easily have the wrong tools with you when it decides to drop a clue, and it won't drop it again as best I can tell. One thing it does that phasmo should really adopt is being able to use your breath to find the room. It lets you save a tool slot until you are ready to check the temperature, or even find the ghost without a thermometer.

I've played several maps a few times now, and I just don't have any desire to play the rest. It runs fine, and other than a handful of times where it didn't drop evidence, it ran fine without any crashes. The exorcisms have some enjoyable animations, but don't expect anything complicated. It's basically a treasure hunt on a timer, and that is disappointing. Unlike Phasmo though, you generally can figure out the secrets without having to use the wiki, and that is a plus to their overall level design.

If you are absolutely into ghost games of all kinds, you'll probably really enjoy it for your first time when you finally complete a map and remove the ghost. I did initially But unless you enjoy repetitive jump scares that have nothing to do with the ghost, you'll probably get bored with it.

So much potential if the jump scares would have been sincere ghost actions and not pre-scripted to always happen. That simple change, very well might put this over the other ghost games, but as it, it knocks it down significantly.

19 hours in, and I’m still afraid of the jumpscares.

Demonologist starts deceptively quiet. The atmosphere and environments already feel eerie, but once the noises begin and the ghosts start stirring up trouble, things can get intense.

The investigations are surprisingly challenging. Some ghosts play tricks on you, others are difficult to detect, and your team often needs to split up and use different strategies to gather evidence. The equipment matters too, what you use and where you use it can make a real difference.

So don't forget your candles, cameras and etc!

The maps are another highlight. Each feels unique, with different environments, sounds and scares.

It’s definitely at its best with friends. Hearing your friends scream might honestly be half the experience. 😂

My main criticism is progression. I’d love something more personal and shared between the team, something like working together to buy and upgrade a house or headquarters, rather than progression mostly feeling individual.

If you’re a group of scaredy-cats who enjoy jumpscares, teamwork and the idea of hunting down and exorcising ghosts, Demonologist is absolutely worth a look.

[h1]TOO LINEAR[/h1]

Arcadie: Second-Born is an interactive text-based novel set in a low-fantasy world. It tells the story of a prince/princess fighting for a better future for the Kingdom of Arcadie. 
I’ve always had a small problem with this type of game - the writing needs to be excellent, or at least engaging in some way, because that’s really all it has to offer. There aren’t many writers who can truly make that work. Adding even basic visuals and audio would help make these games more accessible and appealing to a wider audience (like Roadwarden).
When it comes to Arcadie: Second-Born, I have [b]very mixed feelings[/b]. The writing’s fine, but the pacing drags, and while the romance can be fun, the whole thing feels more like reading a book than actually playing a choice-based game. It’s just too linear to stay engaging.

Unfortunately, [b]I can’t recommend Arcadie: Second-Born. It’s not a bad game, but it falls short in too many areas to truly stand out.[/b]
For a deeper look at the story’s problems and inconsistencies, check out grubby justin’s review.

[b]Story[/b]
I want to avoid any spoilers, so I’ll keep this short. The game starts with a VERY obvious "plot twist", and from there it’s basically on rails - your choices don’t really affect the important events. On top of that, most of the story is about preparation, while the actual action is fairly brief. That can work in some games, but it requires a good balance, which this one doesn’t quite achieve. 
The pacing is also problematic. It’s fine at the beginning, but as the story progresses, there are increasingly large time skips, or entire chunks of the story just vanish. It feels like the authors rushed to the ending, cutting out too much along the way. This had a negative impact on the finale, which ended up feeling anticlimactic and sudden. 
There are also moments that don’t make much sense, like the council of nobles that could apparently vote you out as monarch... because why not. 
The romance was probably the highlight of this game. The characters themselves aren’t particularly unique - they’re actually pretty cliché - but the flirting and love scenes were genuinely enjoyable. Will’s romance was my favorite. At first, they weren’t interested in starting a relationship, but seeing those walls gradually come down was really satisfying. Cyril’s route, on the other hand, didn’t stand out as much in comparison.

[b]Audio & Visuals[/b]
Just text and no audio. 

[b]Technicalities[/b]
No issues.

At the same time, however, I was able to play my character in a way that suited my preferred choices.

I wish there was more feedback on my choices. For instance, I went for a bratty and playful character, and beyond a line or two of dialogue in reply to rowdy statements, nobody really reacted long-term to my choices to be saucy and immature. That's the bad news: this Twine game is not particularly good at being a "game." How is it as a story?

Fortunately, it's pretty fun! I like the fantasy theming, and the writing is good and competent. I wish the magic system was more well developed. And I almost yearn for the story to be a little longer. But what I got was nice enough. I enjoy the framing of being the "second born" in a royal line, as it leads you to make decisions that seem self-serving and selfish, but become slightly consequential later. Also, the narrative is great at throwing twists. Every time there was a twist, I was pleasantly surprised by the direction it was taking the story. If there were any complaint, it's that some of the romance options are very heavy handed; however, that complaint is so mild, it's hardly worth mentioning. It's also nice that, regarding romance, lewd scenes are always gated behind a "fade-to-black" command, so if you want a PG-friendly experience, you don't have to witness the characters getting frisky.

All in all, this was well made and competent. It's an interesting and entertaining choose-your-own-adventure, and definitely worth the admission, despite its brevity.

[h1] Elegant, Character-Driven Drama [/h1]

There are three aspects to Arcadie: Second Born that make it special to me.

[b] 1) Restraint [/b]
This author has a deft touch; they seem to know some common pitfalls and take care to avoid them. Thus, the cast is modest, the scope of the story isn’t too big, and none of the ideas are too outlandish. The prose may appear rather basic, but that’s why it works; it’s not bogged down by excessively detailed descriptions, flashbacks or monologues. It leaves room for your imagination to fill in the blanks. All of this made the whole thing so much more immersive. 
As an aside, this was written to be stand-alone, so you’re getting a complete experience. How refreshing! I will add there’s now a sequel in the works, though. I’m interested to see how they’ll continue this story.

[b] 2) Characters [/b]
The small cast works greatly in the story’s favour. While some side characters don’t get much time in the limelight, all the major characters have their personalities established quickly and efficiently, and they’re further fleshed out over the course of the story. Your two main companions (and romance options) are especially stellar; they differ in opinion but aren’t diametrically opposed on everything. They feel real and internally consistent. Their personalities make sense within the world and the political positions they inhabit.
A lot of ‘show, don’t tell’ is used for the characterisation as well. Much like the prose, characters won’t communicate every nuance or inner thought. A pause or something left unsaid can reveal something, too. When they do choose to say something, it will be relevant and based on their personality and worldview.
My only criticism here is that your two main companions can—rarely—feel a little similar in ‘voice’, but this is usually compensated for by body language or plain old context. And, failing that, there’s the strong character establishment to fall back on.

[b] 3) Agency [/b]
This interactive novel is more of a linear one; you won’t make sweeping changes to the plot or the world. It’s more about dealing with the crisis that’s thrust upon you early in the story. There are stat checks, but they’re not intrusive and the results feel like the consequences of roleplaying a character. That roleplaying is the real focus; this is where your agency lies. You craft your character’s personality through what you say and do. 
Those same choices also affect how your companions see you. Yes, this matters; they have agency too! I’ve loved experimenting with this system. Your companions can like you as a person, but not as a political figure, or vice versa. They have their own thoughts and feelings, so they may choose to agree to disagree, or to decide something is a bridge too far. I find this very compelling.
Obviously, the limits of an interactive novel written by one person still apply. The author can never account for every roleplaying option, but I’ll say they did their best to include a lot of them. I was pleasantly surprised with my options in almost all scenarios, especially when the lack of stat checks allowed me to be as consistent or as fickle as I pleased. 
To be thorough, I’ll say there were two instances where I sorely needed more options. There’s a scene with two prisoners that feels too brief and doesn’t give me the chance to roleplay it how I want. The finale also feels narrow; I understand it’s tallying up your roleplaying up until that point, but it’s the only time I feel the plot takes precedence over characters. Despite that, I think the ending is satisfying and fits the story well. 

[b] In conclusion [/b]

Arcadie: Second-Born is a captivating text-based interactive fiction game available on Steam and Google Play. While it might not dazzle you with graphics or sound, its rich narrative and character depth make it worth exploring.

[h3] Gameplay Mechanics [/h3]

The gameplay mechanics are familiar for fans of the genre, resembling other interactive fiction titles. While nothing stands out as groundbreaking, the experience remains polished and engaging throughout. The game draws you in with its narrative and character interactions rather than flashy visuals.

[h3] Story and Characters [/h3]

The story is a heart, featuring multi-dimensional characters and unexpected twists. As you navigate the world, the relationships you build feel genuine and realistic for most of the journey. However, the ending left me feeling unsatisfied, almost like a cliffhanger that didn’t tie up loose ends.

[h3] Pros and Cons [/h3]

[b]Pros:[/b]

- Complete and polished experience
- Fresh take on fantasy interactive fiction
- Engaging characters and relationships

[b]Cons:[/b]

- Anticlimactic ending with no real closure
-Decisions felt inconsequential, leading to a frustrating narrative disconnect

[h3] Overall Impression [/h3]

I thoroughly enjoyed my six hours with Arcadie: Second-Born, but the lack of closure in the ending was disappointing. It’s a game I’m glad to have purchased for the experience, even if the finale felt rushed and anticlimactic.

[h3] Final Thoughts [/h3]

While the journey through Arcadie: Second-Born is well-crafted and enjoyable, the conclusion left much to be desired. If you’re a fan of interactive fiction, it’s worth a play, but be prepared for an ending that may not meet your expectations.

Arcadie is an engaging and immersive interactive novel. The story is fine even if it treads rather familiar ground but its character development and interaction where this work truly shines. The plot is standard fantasy fare dealing with assassination/betrayal and the subsequent conflict within a kingdom. Very much to the novel's advantage the protagonist starts off as a royal spare bypassing the stereotypical chosen one cliche and giving the player ample opportunities to define their character in an organic way.

Arcadie does a creditable job of weaving the plot together. In truth though the political and military machinations take a back seat to characterization. I can think of few games (if any) that have created such compelling supporting characters. The romance(s) are well paced and feel earned and rewarding (even if the two romance options are unequal in terms of depth and level of engagement). Indeed the dialogue and character development are engaging enough that I have replayed the game/novel multiple times much like rereading a favorite book. 

There are occasional grammatical/compositional errors or awkward word choices that I suspect are down to the work having been written in another language before being translated into English. However, the mistakes were rare enough to not detract from my enjoyment of Arcadie: Second Born.

All in all, I highly recommend this work.

That's all you need to know if you don't like spoilers, but if you don't care, or if you already know how the story goes, then here are a bunch of my nit picks.

You never feel powerful. You have a vile of the most powerful magic blood in existence, the thing that is meant to make you a myth, a legend, something people will be talking for eons about, and it does nothing. I am aware it gives you more mana, but other than that, it does nothing. She wasn't entirely unreasonable. Like, yea, she was blood-lusted, but if you were supper cautious or overly prepared, the game should've rewarded you, perhaps not with your sister surviving unscathed, but with her still alive. I would've totally loved playing as the second fiddle to a furious empress who can't fight anymore, and would've saved the game from the third nit-pick I have.

Deus ex machina, a term that everyone knows. So, if the writer knows it, then why did they put a blatant example of one in it? Like... there's no explanation to it. The game itself disproves the theories of the only guy who knows stuff about magic. Not only that, but the dialogue does as well. I'm usually a pretty big fan of CYOA books, and even more than that I'm a huge fan of political intrigue, medieval fantasy and games about governing but despite my best efforts Arcadie just isn't a very good CYOA book. The big issues here are the actual impact you have on the story, the quality of the writing, horrible characterization and pacing as well as a complete disconnect between the events of the book and what makes sense for the world.

To start your choices in the game don't exactly have much real impact, yes you'll see an extra scene or two, get a different line here and there or change the ending, but the game consistently feels like you're on rails from the beginning, in fact the entire first act until the battle really feels like you're just a bystander to events. Sure its intended to be that way and you get more freedom later on but that doesn't mean its fun, you end up just witnessing events and only really giving your opinion on those events rather than changing them and creating an interesting divergent path. This is one of the biggest problems in the game. There's a huge emphasis on a wide variety of responses and while it helps you differentiate who you're playing as, the real impact of these choices only serves to change the context you view events in rather than actually changing the events themselves. This tends to make the story feel very hollow since you constantly are asked for an opinion or some input but again it only makes you feel like a bystander to the events rather than a catalyst for them. I played for about 6 hours and I really only saw a couple events occur that actually felt like I caused them but these were extremely few and far between. 

The quality of the writing left a lot to be desired, unnecessary details are thrown at you and scene changes are done so swiftly that you barely get any sense of the scenes you find yourself reading. Descriptions either become so simple as to leave you unimmersed or so detailed as to bore you since the writing isn't particularly evocative or immersive except for the romance and smut which is actually quite good.

The pacing is easily the biggest flaw with the writing though, I've played many CYOA books and even the subpar ones can coast by on a simple premise even if the pacing isn't great. The problem with Arcadie is that its aiming to do so much without anywhere near the amount of competency needed to actually write a good political thriller or epic fantasy so it just falls on its face. In Arcadie things just sort of happen in the game, again with very little player discretion. One minute you're in a council meeting then suddenly there's a ball, then you're at a fort preparing for a battle and then right back at a council meeting. This all happens with virtually no buildup or time to digest anything, it feels like the player is just being flung from scene to scene without any care taken to immerse the player or let the text breathe. This jarring feeling characterizes a lot of the book and its one of the bigger reasons why the game feels so linear especially when the events that occur seem like they should be under your purview. In the end the pacing just feels like the author had too many ideas and no idea how to gracefully transition between them while giving the player agency over that content.

Another thing I really didn't like was the characterization, most of the main cast were very one note and largely fell into some basic archetypes with very little nuance. They aren't entirely cookie cutter but upon meeting the character you get their entire vibe virtually immediately, this left so little mystery about the main romantic interests and really flattened them as characters and if not for the well written smut then the romantic interests would be entirely uninteresting. The supporting cast, if you'd even say the game has any is also quite bare bones. A haughty noble, a righteous revolutionary, its all really too simple and boring and if the game were merely some fantasy epic or whatever it'd be more excusable but in a game clearly trying to evoke the ideas of political intrigue it just makes everything so unbelievable and lifeless. Complexity and nuance was really lacking from almost every character in the book. The lack of nuance was worst with your sibling, who from the very beginning was made out to be a complete warmonger without any real redeeming qualities. In isolation this would be fine but every character is like this, feeling entirely one note and as a result, forgettable.

Finally the book has a weird amount of immersion breaking stuff in it. For starters there's the leader of the nobles' private council, a character who just seems so out of place. When you first meet him he mocks your dead sibling, challenges your right to rule and positions himself against you no matter what you do. It feels like a complete parody of a noble. The kingdom of Arcadie is a very militant and authoritarian institution, yet this schmuck openly questions you like it wasn't horribly dangerous. Furthermore, apparently this council he leads is both unknown to the masses yet actually responsible for appointing you the monarch? Yet earlier, Cyril tells you that no matter what they'll support you since you're the monarch? Very odd. I know the character is meant to show you the vibes of the nobility, that they just want to undermine you for their own power but like, it comes off so outrageously out of place that it knocks the legs out of any political intrigue you might've expected. Then there's the Aether chandeliers and stuff you find everywhere but yet apparently only the royal family have ever been able to actually use Aether, so what are your family just enchanting a bunch of chandeliers? Are these really old ones? Or is there some other way these are made? It just feels so odd introducing this unique magical force that is rare and apparently your sibling is the only one who can reasonably utilize it within centuries, yet these light sources are everywhere. There's plenty more out of place things like your character being so extremely ill-equipped to run a country because of 2 whole children your parents never thought to prepare you alongside your sibling, or a conversation with a foreign monarch going from heated difficult negotiations to him rolling over without the slightest push back just because you said some tough words. The game just feels like someone wanted to write a cool story about being a monarch with political intrigue and choice and skills and whatnot but had such little understanding of how all this would actually work, everything just feels so one note and lacking almost any complexity at all.

Anyway, I spoke plenty now. Finishing off, the UI is pretty good though I would've like a sepia theme like what Choice Of Games has. I also really appreciate the ability to save and load which I think is kinda necessary in games like this so its a very welcome addition. Beyond that I can't say much praise for the game, though again the romance and smut scenes are a definite highlight.

Gameplay: 8/10
Visuals: NA/10
Audio: NA/10
Replayability: 8/10

In a world where PC gaming no longer stands on the edge of the frontier in terms of innovative technology and ground-breaking graphics, games such as Arcadie, Second Born that take a more basic and dated approach to storytelling serve as a great reminder that the content and passion of a product is worth more than impressive graphics and immersion. The story was extremely interesting, and willing to cross lines that can only be crossed in games where developers don't worry about pleasing audiences or creating that feel-good happy ending. While it is a simple text-based novel, the Choose-Your-Own-Adventure aspect is so present that it differs from classic reading by letting you explore many options to forge your own path, while still having good and consistent world-building to have you along.

Visuals are neutral for me, as while I did not expect animations or cutscenes of some sort, character portraits or complimentary artwork could have been used to flesh out some of the more defined characters, although I understand that highlights specifics may have broken the immersion for people who may imagine the characters in a different way. On another note, I do wish you could change the text color, as I was playing at a very late night and the contrast between the text and background was blinding, but that is a rather trivial complaint that was easily remedied.

The complete lack of audio is an interesting choice. While I think some people might hate this and choose to not play due to the dead silence that persists throughout, I put on the Witcher 3 complete soundtrack which in my opinion enhanced my immersion and the atmosphere. I find that this game leaves a lot of aspects out and I'm starting to believe that that was on purpose, in order to allow another layer of depth to the choose your own adventure aspect.

As for replayability, my first play through took just over three hours to finish. You are allowed to go back pages and change decisions, as well as save and load to your heart's content. If you know you are not going to want to go through everything again, I think the save/load method should allow you to get through most of the content you were hoping to see without committing another three hours to the game. As in terms of actual story differences, I cannot say how much each playthrough differs, but when I clicked on the community page, I had another ending quite different than mine spoiled to me by some idiot who put spoilers in a post title. I won't say exactly what the post was, but I'm happy as it looked like they were dealing with a rather unfortunate outcome.

Another thing I would like to touch on in terms of replayability is romance. It is what drew me into playing this game, and I did not even end up doing anything romantically related at all, because I was too busy saving the kingdom. Romance is completely optional and customizable, and the creator makes it clear that romancing a character is not a linear path as what most games are (eg: pick this dialogue in this scene to start the romance) but rather is a split path that allows multiple opportunities to make your move, meaning that if something seems out of character to you or you feel that more imposing matters are at hand, you can move past that point without being locked out of said romance. 

To make a short story even shorter, Arcadie Second Born is well worth the full price and feels like what new-generation storytelling should be, where we can bend the narrator's choice to our will in order to create stronger attachments or simply create different perspectives. If you like/liked to read, and perhaps feel like enjoying some medieval fantasy on your down time, you will like this game.

[i][u][b]Arcadie: Second-Born[/b][/u][/i] is a completely texted-based choose-your-own-adventure (CYOA) novel by [i][u][b]Arcadie & Utopie.[/b][/u][/i] 

In [i][u][b]Arcadie: Second-Born[/b][/u][/i], you play as, yep, you guessed it, the second-born child of the D'Arcadie line: the Royal Family. Your elder sister, Ariana, has The Gift: the ability to control and use aether. Your bloodline is well known for it, but it's become very rare. The fact that your sister is the first aether user in over three hundred years, shines a great light on her. She is the future Queen too. These two things combined make Ariana special to your parents and while she's showered in praise, you are always in her shadow. Despite this, you were still given the best education possible and are allowed more freedom than your sibling. 

Your kingdom, Arcadie, is at war on almost all sides of the border. Your lands hold a great deal of fertile land and others want it. To some people, the King and Queen are seen as warmongers, forcing their loyal subjects to fight for their own selfish desires, instead of actively trying to compromise and make peace. However, one of the commanders of your armies does manage to broker a peace treaty and this is where the novel will start. You can guess that things don't go as smoothly as planned. 

The plot was spaced out nicely: more often than not, flowed at an acceptable pace. Things move realistically for a mission that has a time limit to it. There isn't much I can say without it spoiling the story, but prepare yourself for twists, turns and an emotional journey. 

As for the characters, you can choose your characters' gender and that of the romance options (RO), catering them to your preferences. You are also offered a few basic cosmetic customisation options for the MC: hair/skin/eye colour etc. These are used for some flavour text throughout the novel. You can choose your forename but for story purposes, your surname will always be D'Arcadie. 

What you can expect:
[list]
[*] Two main ROs, a minor and a secret one.
[*] Main romances develop at different speeds: a slow-burn and a faster-paced one. 
[*] Main ROs have different tastes, personalities and things they like/dislike: they feel like individual people. 
[*] Minor RO is more of a fling.
[*]   Sexual content is completely up to the player with a fade-to-black option, and another for a bit more detail. 
[/list]

My one grievance with the ROs is their age. It's not something I'm often bothered by but story-wise, they feel a bit young to both be commanders of your armies. I'd have expected persons of an older age/more experience to hold those positions. I assume the decision to make them young was to be able to keep their age close to the MC, who is in her early 20s. That's sort of the average for novels like these I believe.

I found the world to be crafted in a way that added interest to the story of a thriving country that is forced to fight for its land: the reasons made sense. All of the characters were fully fleshed out with their own backgrounds, motivations, desires and reasons for doing what they do. I felt as if a lot of care and attention went into making this CYOA novel: it really showed in the amount of pleasure I received from reading it.

Most of the CYOA games I've played in the past were from the more well-known interactive fiction provider Choice of Games/Host of Games: [i][u][b]Arcadie & Utopie[/b][/u][/i] have already beaten their platform, in my eyes, with the quality of life options they have implemented into their own software. A save and load system, and although it only has a few direct saves, it also gives you the possibility to make saves directly to your pc, outside of the game, that you can name yourself. They also provide a back button, a simple thing but it adds so much more freedom. As with any text, it isn't easy to decipher the meaning behind the words sometimes, and choosing an option you perceive to have a certain tone, only for it to actually have a different one, can make it feel very out of character for you. Just being able to pick through the choices and see which you prefer, or sating your curiosity, offered a lot more enjoyment to my reading.  

Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed my first playthrough of [i][u][b]Arcadie: Second-Born[/b][/u][/i] and was very glad about what I received for my money's worth. I'm not often a fan of war-related stories but the well-designed world and characters very much pulled me in and ensured that I stayed too. I would more than recommend this to anyone who enjoys interactive fiction, thinks the story sounds interesting, or perhaps fancies playing through their very first choose-your-own-adventure title.

This is a pretty brutal story, but one I quite enjoyed and happen to think is worth the price of admission and time invested. I don't feel the need to hold my big conclusion for the end, that's the takeaway, but I'll expand on that.

The story is complete, but leaves room for more, rather than being a nugget of a story that demands a sequel to provide any sense of resolution.

The characters are distinct and well written, interesting, endearing, whether as villains, friends, family, lovers, or whatever part they play in events. That extends to your own character, who can be competent and play an important role in events while giving you, the player, room to develop them as a person in the way that you desire.

The story makes it clear that your character has lived in the shadow of the elder heir, but at no point did I feel that their place in the story was fully eclipsed by it or that they were lacking in agency. Events unfold along a particular path, sure, but only inasmuch as you cannot control the world around you, you are always afforded agency with how you react to events as they unfold, and the choices you make feel meaningful, and have an impact on the other characters swept up in events, both in the moment and in the long term.

There were definite moments where the progression of your skills felt like they had an impact and were recognized within the world, but it never felt like a grind, and the opportunity cost of focusing was rewarding without becoming paralyzing.

The pacing of the story was also good throughout, giving you chances to breathe and develop relationships and an understanding of the world between pitting you into frenetic, perilous circumstances that reach satisfying climaxes which build as they go. Giving you time to process what happens without dwelling so long that you lose interest. The prose is engaging and always pushing you forward, being concise where needed and expansive where justified, varying between those in a way that is satisfying as a reader while also always providing you the opportunity to engage with it on your own terms through your choices.

The romances are satisfying, at least the ones I pursued, there seemed to be other options that might appeal to other people that I wasn't interested in, and I see that as a good thing.

I am very happy with this and look forward to more, whether they decide to continue with this world and character or if they try their hand at other stories. As I said before, this is very satisfying as a standalone but leaves fertile ground for a continuation, which is a very difficult line to walk that many fail at.

I’ve long anticipated the release of Arcadie: Second-Born, having eagerly tracked its progress since the first uploaded demo. I enjoyed reading through the novel then, and I’ve enjoyed the finished product all the more.

Arcadie: Second-Born is a superlative work of interactive fiction. Not only is the novel well-written and emotive, the author has moreover done a magnificent job of employing the conventions of the genre to their fullest and most effective use. 

The narrative expectations constructed prior to and during the novel are convincingly sold to the reader and then abruptly subverted in a way that does not feel contrived. The interpersonal relationships into which the player character can enter—romantic, familial, and platonic; friendly and adversarial—are (depending on the relation) authentically tense, sweet, and solemn. The skills in which the player character may specialize all feel meaningful, as their selection bears not only where skill checks are present, but also enables the selection of certain choices and reveals unique bits of dialogue. In other words, the skills act to shape the personality of the player character themselves. The different ways in which the story can conclude feel appropriately distinct, based on the different, contrary emotions to which they’ve given rise when I played through them.

Above all, I appreciate that the author has written a story that is memorable and has created a setting that is emotionally and intellectually captivating. Having played through the novel on multiple occasions, I’m not only satisfied but am also possessed by a burning curiosity about the history and geopolitics of Arcadie and its surrounding states, in addition to the fates and philosophies of many of the novel’s characters.

To anyone who’s a fan of fantasy settings involving the use of the pen and the sword, in which you can interact with a host of different characters, many of whom have realistic and sometimes fascinatingly profound motivations and philosophies, and in which your choices feel meaningful—I would recommend Arcadie: Second-Born.

The game has a linear plot, but this is not necessarily a bad thing. In this case, I think it's a positive thing, because the title is about what it's about, which is the story of Arcadie's second born.

The writing style is just right, I didn't have any problems reading and understanding it, which is something to be thankful for. 

The pace of the story in general is good and steady, and most importantly, it has no humdrum or unnecessary moments that could affect the pace. 

I think all the characters are particularly well done. They are not walking stereotypes, and they are not perfect either. The fact that the different characters have their positive and negative points, and the fact that they are imperfect and make mistakes, I think that's what makes them human, and helps a lot in the immersion of the story. 

Another point to take into account is how customisable the MC is through the options presented to us. Not only in terms of actions that affect the story, but also in terms of the MC's personality and reactions to events. The author has been very detailed in that sense, and it's something that has really entertained me.

I think she also does something that a lot of authors don't dare to do, or don't want to do, and that is to allow for character development. You can start with a naive, good-natured character, but the choices allow you to lose your head over the course of the story, and change radically. Apart from that, the MC can be heartless if he wants to be. 

The issue of the romantic relationships you can have with other characters, I think that's also done quite masterfully. Because it's not just an add-on for getting into bed and doing hand-holding, but it can also affect how certain aspects of the story go, depending on those relationships. To the point, that you can have romances with the characters, as a way to manipulate them for your plans. 

Overall I think it is an interactive game that is well worth buying and playing. Because of how customisable the MC is, it has significant replayability, so it can offer hours of gameplay.

Eris Dysnomia is a 2D action RPG that blends side-scrolling beat 'em up combat with light role-playing elements and an adult-oriented presentation. Developed by Above a Damage Tile and published by Kagura Games, it follows Eris after she becomes trapped in a dangerous land filled with hostile creatures. Rather than building the experience around extensive dialogue or complicated exploration, the game quickly establishes combat as its main attraction, giving players a selection of melee attacks, weapons, and combinations to master while progressing through its stages.

Combat has considerably more flexibility than its straightforward appearance initially suggests. Eris can use punches and kicks as basic attacks, but changing stances gives her access to additional weapons, including a scythe and a firearm. These abilities can be combined rather than treated as completely separate fighting styles, allowing players to construct longer attack sequences. Maintaining a combo becomes especially satisfying when several enemies are present because positioning, timing, and choosing the right attack all become increasingly important. The result has a noticeable arcade influence, rewarding players who experiment instead of repeatedly relying on one dependable move.

The scythe is particularly useful for giving the combat a different sense of reach and impact, while the gun introduces a ranged alternative when approaching an enemy directly is inconvenient. Mixing these options with Eris' physical attacks gives battles a pleasant sense of momentum. There is an enjoyable learning curve to figuring out which attacks naturally connect, how enemies respond to particular moves, and when changing tactics is more effective than continuing an existing combination. The controls and mechanics are accessible enough to understand quickly, yet there is room for players to improve their execution over time.

Progression is divided across multiple stages, with some choice regarding the route Eris follows toward her objective. This prevents the adventure from feeling like one completely rigid corridor of encounters and provides a little additional incentive to explore what the game offers. Enemy variety also contributes to the pacing. Different opponents require changes in positioning and attack selection, while encounters involving several enemies make crowd control more significant. The combat is generally strongest during these busier situations because players are encouraged to use more of Eris' available moves rather than settling into a repetitive pattern.

Visually, the game uses colorful 2D pixel graphics complemented by anime-inspired character illustrations. Its presentation is deliberately modest compared with larger action RPGs, but that simplicity suits the side-scrolling format. Characters, attacks, and enemies are generally easy to distinguish during combat, which is particularly useful once encounters become crowded. Mature sexual material and nudity are also prominent elements of the game, making it firmly intended for adults. However, the adult material does not completely overshadow the gameplay, as the underlying combat system offers enough interaction and mechanical variety to stand on its own.

Players expecting a deep traditional RPG should adjust their expectations accordingly. Character interaction, world exploration, and elaborate build customization are not the central focus. The experience is better understood as an action-focused hybrid with RPG elements supporting a beat 'em up foundation. Its relatively compact design also means repetition can eventually become noticeable. Many situations revolve around defeating another collection of enemies, and players who do not enjoy experimenting with combos may find the structure becoming predictable sooner than those interested in mastering the fighting mechanics.

The game's lightweight 2D design results in modest hardware requirements, making it accessible to PCs that would struggle with demanding contemporary releases. Steam Cloud and Family Sharing are supported, and the game is designed as a single-player experience. Steam Deck compatibility is officially categorized as Playable rather than fully Verified. Performance with the default graphics configuration is considered suitable, and the game can run successfully on SteamOS. However, handheld players should expect compromises. Some functionality is not fully accessible through the default controller configuration, touchscreen interaction or a community controller layout may occasionally be useful, and text entry can require manually opening the virtual keyboard. Some interface text may also appear small, while certain prompts can display keyboard, mouse, or non-Steam Deck controller icons. It is therefore functional on the Deck, but the experience is less seamless than a fully optimized handheld release.

Eris Dysnomia ultimately works best for players looking for a relatively focused action RPG where fighting takes priority over elaborate storytelling or expansive exploration. Combining punches, kicks, stance changes, scythe attacks, gunfire, and extended combos gives its combat more substance than the game's small scale might initially imply. The stage-based structure and mature content will narrow its audience, and repetition prevents the experience from reaching greater heights, but the responsive action and opportunity to develop increasingly effective combinations provide a solid foundation. For players comfortable with its adult themes and interested in pixel-art beat 'em ups with light RPG characteristics, it offers a surprisingly involved combat experience.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The weakest aspect of the game is its lack of story. There isn't even an excuse plot or an intro that explains who the protagonist is, who we are fighting against, and why it seems everyone has depraved intentions towards the protagonist (we can figure out the last one by ourselves just fine, though). [h1]Gameplay[/h1]
In contrast, the gameplay is solid and features a good variety of game mechanics, so visiting the tutorials is a must to get the most out of them. Each level is split into smaller segments in which you beat enemies left and right and obtain the souls you need to learn and upgrade skills and buy items from the merchant. They are randomized and give you the option to choose between three of the following types: a long road with easy enemies, a short one packed with easy foes, a healing onsen, a room full of aphrodisiacs and easy enemies, and a short one full of harder opponents and more souls to obtain.

Another fun mechanic is using MP to switch to Scythe Mode or Gun Mode. Scythe Mode allows you to dish melee damage in a wide area, making it easier to deal with groups of enemies, while Gun Mode lets you shoot bullets in rapid succession as if you were John Wick himself. Transforming lasts a few seconds, so players must use it sparingly to not run out of MP at the worst moment possible.

Furthermore, the lewd aspect is neatly integrated into the gameplay. Players have to distribute ten sensitivity points between the character's erogenous zones and choose a main fetish that'll affect gameplay in one way or another, be it making her randomly start masturbating when attacking enemies, unlocking a skill to reduce your HP to 1 to make it easier to see defeat scenes, and so on. The art was even better than I initially expected. The main character and the different foes are well-drawn, and the animations are smooth. They also added eye-catching effects to give more flair to the attacks and the protagonist's horniness, including an option to turn off some of them in case players find them excessive. As for the sexual content, the game covers a wide range of fetishes such as breeding, masochism, masturbation, exhibitionism, and other less prevalent ones.

[h1]Verdict: Great[/h1]

That feeling never gets old.

“Knock it off, will ya?" said the very believable 20 year old neonate vampire protagonist..
".. I'm actually on the internets gramps, I don't read James Joyce's 'Ulysses' like you do"
I halted myself for a second in regret as I uttered those words.
Like in a Ally McBeal episode from 1997, I knew my riz was going bad fast.
This was clearly not the time to circle the wagons.
I didn't want to come off as another random broad holding up the corner like I owned the block.
Not taking the L this time.

In the old era of buttons on the phones, landline calls and vhs glory, people used to role-play face to face, with gatherings, especially when it comes to Vampire: The Masquerade, which is even one year older than me myself. Game, that required tons of books, dices and mindset creativity, has evolved through passages of time, technology changes and audience, to the point - where we are welcomed by more digital variations, the "modern" way of role playing, hidden behind the facade of what visual novel is about. 

Vampire: The Masquerade - Reckoning of New York, is one of the few games in the online games from an entire series, that explores the dark corners of the famous Big Apple. Through necrotic eyes. By actions and their consequences. With a lot of blood spillage guaranteed. Yet, it is also quite of a refreshment for any connoisseur of the entire franchise itself, thanks to the reassured exploration of wampires world, their hierarchy, society, families, abilities, and only the developers knows what else could possibly be there.

This episode, was a little bit of a slow journey. The one, that allow us to learn more about deception. To get properly introduced to how certain class is looking like from the practical point of a view. To sense "how would it be" if we choose one or another character, in order to understand better their perspective of "unliving". 

It is not a title, that you should expect fireworks from and tons of rapid changes. This is an episode, that explores communication, secrets, lies, political frictions as well as how much one decision leads to one another, in terms of faliure or sarcastic win of the certain boundaries. Both characters in the game, show us two new clans in further "light" so we can re-experience old fashioned RPG. So we may understand more this world, by receiving another one bit of it. 

People who complained, truly miss the whole point of the franchise, where each one new game release, gives us something different, yet centered around certain society and area. While more titles are yet to come, we will move on within time from one location to another, while finally understanding better each one fraction bit by a bit, by simply having that chance via various storytelling. Not every legend has to have an end which is good or bad. 

Padraic and Kali are a proof for that. Are we certain that they will end up one day in passionate romance, starting from enemies and going from it to lovers? Can we be sure that they will not be more like nemezis to themselves and they not gonna end up sabotaging their clans? What about the vial? Voices? Other secrets that are yet to come or be burried? This uncertainty gained through ending variations, is another one lesson for us players: To appreciate the moment, change, with the expectation of what is about to come yet.

Maybe Padraic survives and evolve? Maybe Kali will forgive him? Maybe they both will loose an ancient blood, ending up in good or bad hands? Only time will tell [ehkhm, ehkhm or devs kindly please] what is going to happen, and if we will see these two in the future episodes, just like we had a chance to see the Julia again.

Sincerely not horrible.

Let's be clear, I don't hate this. If you're coming here for a continuation of the ongoing saga of the NYC kindred in VTM, you'll get that. Lots of familiar faces, lots of court drama, lots of vampire goodness. If you're here for the VTM and WOD world, you get that too, with a bit of edge and flair. This is certainly an improvement over Shadows, which was an absolute travesty; this is at least competent, and a decent story, if not the most exciting.

The big issue here is, once again, the change in writing style. Coteries was refined, exquisitely written; Shadows was a fucking mess, and is better forgotten. How does Reckoning fair? Not bad, but not good. The writing has turned from EMO EDGE into Teen YA novel. The story has abandoned pomp and bombast, which VTM stories are known for, in favor of witty quips in a style reminiscent of Marvel. Our character is plucky and spry, but because the entire story is (mostly) delivered from her perspective, we're basically stuck in the brain of a cranky 15 year old who thinks she has the whole world figured out. She's a fun character, but kind of exhausting, because the authors felt the constant need to have her back-talking, quipping, and huffing. I love me a brat, but a brat this girl is not; she's more just frustratingly annoying, and doesn't exactly have a redeeming personality.

The story itself leaves a bit to be desired as well. Because we are playing a Ravnos - effectively transients in the VTM vampire world - we're graced with a very unique perspective. But it feels like, outside of the initial first chapters, the game doesn't really know what to do with Kali. There is a fun twist near the end, where she gets embroiled in things larger than life, but even then, the climax is... kinda dumb.

Part of the problem in all the dullness and blandness is that things just kind of work. Any time our girl gets in a fight, she auto-wins, even against far more skilled opponents. Any time she's threatened, someone else deus-ex-machina's her to safety. It didn't really ever feel like she was under threat after chapter 1. This makes the action scenes fluffy, and the tension she keeps ranting about within internal monologues hollow. "This is so dangerous, what do I do?" she says after super-humanly destroying a group of baddies.

And again, the story here isn't actually surprising. It's shocking in the same way The Maze Runner is surprising. "It turns out, THERE'S A BIG TWIST!" But the twist is kind of easily understood, and not that shocking, and you're like "okay," and all the characters are like, "cool, that's fine." It almost feels like nobody actually takes the story seriously, so it's hard for me to take it seriously too. There is a second route, but I admit, the wavering writing makes me hesitant to explore it.

The art style is.... a choice. Most people will refuse to play this likely based on the art style alone. We've traded moody, painterly styles to whatever 2D/3D homunculus-thing you wanna call this. To be clear, I don't HATE it, it's not bad inherently. It just looks uncanny, almost AI-generated. It's sad, because all the work that went into these portraits could have just been spent making high quality art-portraits, like the previous games, and they would have looked infinitely better. But oh well, I don't want to harangue upon it too long, because I think it's easy to hate them, but they're sincerely not horrible.

But that's the problem with the entire game. "Sincerely not horrible" is not a ringing endorsement. The story is good at parts, and bad at parts; the art is not bad, but not great; the mechanics, yet mentioned, don't really seem to matter. This is a very middling game, which is sad, because I do genuinely like the story. I just don't think that the people telling it were competent enough to give it the love it needed.

The first game, although not very good, had a great atmosphere and cohesive writing, and most of the vampire clans were represented fairly faithfully. The second game was genuinely great. Julia was a perfect protagonist, and the story was phenomenal. But Reckoning has almost none of that.

The art style is different. It's not bad by any means, but I definitely prefer the old style. The soundtrack also seems to have taken a downgrade, but for me, the worst part was the writing. I found myself losing interest in the plot several times. Both protagonists were good, and I really wanted to see where their journeys would take them. Julia returning was also a great addition, but I found myself dragging myself to the end just for the 100% completion.

I also played the other games in my native language, and this is the only one that is only available in English, which made the experience even worse for me.

Totally not worth it. It's sad to have played this trilogy and end up being given this.

better than I expected, given the reviews. I definitely recommend playing through both characters for the full story, and I never thought I'd be invested in a romance in WoD, but here we are. it's cool to get to play as a less-explored clan, and I personally like the visual novel-style.

that said, the art style is a downgrade (possibly AI-generated?) and I'm upset that there was no exploration of why Qadir (bae) suddenly got a massive personality transplant. totally worth it, but only when it's on sale.

Seems interesting so far, but the fact it includes Julia sucks if you played Shadows of New York, as it completely retcons one of the endings, and if you didn't play it then she's just another new character, I hope they at least try to explain later in the game.

Effectively the third part of the New York trilogy of games, Reckoning of New York takes us back to Vampire: the Masquerade in what the licence appears to be the most comfortable with - Visual Novels of all things. Just like the previous two, this one functions perfectly fine as a standalone although you will appreciate seeing established characters. Even if Reckoning doesn't honor previous decisions since there's no save import to work with. Still worth checking out regardless.

New Year of 2024 is almost upon us which should be a time for celebration... unless you're Kali of clan Ravnos who just got accosted up by local Camarilla enforcement and dragged to see the Prince. Not that Kali is innocent, hailing from a clan of con artists and tricksters, but this seems to concern her Sire who is apparently in even deeper problems involving some serious smuggling. Getting a stay of execution under the condition she delivers her absentee Sire to New York's Camarilla, Kali pulls a fast one and gets a sympathetic Caitiff mediator to accompany her, lest she flee the city. So begins a week of nocturnal mishaps featuring Kali and Padraic as they hunt for clues, avoid vampire hunters and navigate the traitorous nature of what they are.

Unlike the previous game this is a far more linear affair with some "pretend choices", that becomes more evident on replay, and I think only ONE genuine decision conveniently a reload away if you wanted to check it out. You'd think that would be a problem in a game with one autosave slot, but not in this case. You just end up going with the flow and realize you're on-rails. Whether you want to have Hunger and Hunter Threat on is an option here. I would recommend playing with both enabled since it doesn't affect things that much and at least you won't spam Disciplines to get out of every situation. Or you will seeing as sometimes it doesn't result in Hunger increase. Neither are serious core features game dies or lives by while going into the extreme negative does net you some unique scenes.

Since I mentioned it, yes. There are two playable characters. Not like the game goes out of its way to hide who you'll play other than Kali, but I won't spoil it for you. Whether it's worthwhile to go through what is largely the same story from a different perspective and maybe 20-30 minutes of new context is up for debate. Bizarrely, this is where the one true choice comes in as that's picking the REAL ending for the game. You get to customize Kali's Disciplines: picking from Animalism, Obfuscate and Presence to cover all the bases, but the other character is locked. There's no RNG involved so as long as you qualify for the Discipline requirement you pass. Be careful as what you pick is what you get given this ain't no RPG showering you with ability points or at every step. I'm almost pressed to say Discipline choices are almost merely flavor if you turn off the above mentioned mechanics.

I don't want to say much about the story or characters since, well, it's what you're playing a VN for. If you're familiar with Vampire: the Masquerade you can pick up on some clues earlier and this is a kind of plans-within-plans setup. Nice to see the old reprobates albeit in different art style, for better or worse. Shame my girl Julia from Shadows didn't have a bigger role to play. If there's a downside to how the game is structured that would be the way entire setup hinges on you liking the polar opposite duo in the lead. Ravnos don't really get to shine in the licence material, quite the opposite actually, so it's definitely refreshing to see one as a snarky energetic girl.

Better than I feared, considering the mixed reviews. Kali caters to a younger audience I guess, but she only annoyed me during Pádraic playthrough. I guess she's meant to be annoying. Pádraic's story on the other hand was quite interesting. I'd recommend you playing both stories for the additional scenes and closure. Cool VtM title, nowhere near the heights of Shadows (who doesn't love Julia?), but satisfying. My main complaint is that I expected more reckoning.

Skip this. Save yourself the coins, the time, the underwhelm.

While the prospect of encountering characters from the infamous and generally underrepresented clans [spoiler] Malkavian [/spoiler] and [spoiler] Tzimisce [/spoiler] may seem enticing, the only qualities to be discovered here are boredom and disappointment. 

Like you, I enjoyed the first two instalments — Coteries & Shadows of NY.
I liked the interactive visual novel format; the atmospheric overlay of graphics, sound; the writing. I liked that there were some interconnections between the separate arcs. Those chapters also had their plot holes and shortcomings, but at least there's a plot for those holes to be in. There was atmosphere; you got a feel for the different personalities you encounter. In part 1 and 2, you possessed, sort of, the ability to make a choice now and then, which in turn flavored the way scenes played out. 

Remember that? Yeah? Now, forget about it.
If you insist on entering Reckoning, you must leave all those expectations at the door.

You will inevitably attempt to finally add some of that depth you were left hungering for throughout the stale experience of your first playthrough by replaying the whole thing with the second, now unlocked character. This won't satisfy you, either. As you feel that last sliver of hope for a game, a story, an experience peel away, you will find yourself wondering if the personal horror you came for was the slow-trickling limbo of this empty text all along.

The worst part is that the writing is simply atrocious. 
It's ... so bad. 
Like, really, not good. At all. 
It's trying too hard, yet simultaneously, it's not trying at all.
Description of view, inner monologue, statement about self, rinse, repeat. 

If this was written by humans, then those certainly weren't the same people that were involved in the previous parts; perhaps those writers also wrote while crammed into an overcrowded space, with no sleep, time constraints, and no editor to oversee the output. Perhaps those humans were teenagers, with no creative writing practice. The characters are less than two-dimensional. The story is rudimentary. There's not much there to spark your own imagination. Without engaging details, ideas, or the overall feeling that something was happening, reading often felt like a chore. What mostly kept me going was sunk cost fallacy in the sense that I refused to believe that this sub-franchise would tank itself this hard, and, well, I kept pushing on, kept waiting for things to take off. 

Instead, the other shoe dropped: The other side of the story is almost worse. Have you ever watched a movie wherein the potentially more interesting side character who barely gets much screen time finally gets their own feature, and that's when you realize that those small doses of wide angle shots peppered with their presence brought more intrigue and room for imagination? Or felt the impact of that particular, sobering sense of let-down when you found out that the skittish, standoffish, quiet, cool guy isn't actually brooding over his own depth, but that he instead simply doesn't have much to say about the few thoughts that he actually has? That's what the replay was essentially like for me.

My advice? Keep that money, take it to a store, buy some socks and a bag of googley eyes. 
Attach the latter to the former — whatever play you come up with for your puppet vampires will be so much better.

My carpal tunnel is acting up now, and all that for a game that didn't provide a fraction of the fantastic storytelling in, say, Werewolf: The Apocalypse, The Book of Hungry Names.

As long as you understand it is a short novel (about 6.5 hours), with some art and some rare dialog "choices".  Because I enjoy the VtM world, playing a somewhat "young" Ravnos lady, and because it stimulated my imagination for a possible tabletop RPG game, I enjoyed it. 

While the past games were a bit darker, diving into the dark psychology of becoming a vampire, this one follows two relatively "young" vampires that are rather cute and humane.  They are a young Ravnos lady (a clan of Gypsie-like vampires) and a gifted Malkavian who apparently has no clan.  The writing is fun and good for the first parts but, near the end, some character plots do not hold up at all. 

When you finish the game once with Kali (the Ravnos), you can replay as Padraic, which is a very different perspective, but you have to do the whole story again (which I will not do).  I am told you get an actual choice at the end of Padraic's viewpoint. 

[b]Do not buy if you want gameplay or any form of actual choices[/b] : it unfortunately does not give you any real choices, utterly zero, not even in the end where they could easily have given us choices without needing to write any consequences.  The only options you have are ...

a) which flavor of vampiric power, out of three, will you use in some scenes, 

b) which three flavors of dialog, though they usually all are the same in reality ; like a moment where I had three ways of saying "No" (I kid you not), 

and c) you get opportunities to hunt or some side-events before doing the main events.

Extra : if you read it a second time as Padraic, you should get a choice at the end. 

EDIT / ADDENDUM : 
After giving it some more thought, I concluded I should not give this one a pass (I should not recommend it), mainly because a) the lack of actual choices is too steep, worse than in the previous "games", and the gameplay is mainly an illusion; b) the way vampires react to the main plot makes little sense and this is compounded by the lack of significant dialog choices and even less any actual choice; and c) the art feels lazy, with only a few scenes and rehashing portraits from past games.  If you want a decent novel in the VtM world, buy a good book.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Reckoning of New York is a difficult one to score. On one hand, the presentation is excellent: the artwork is a definite step up and truly stunning, and the individual characters are very well done.

However, the story was not as engaging or likable as the previous titles, which was a disappointment, especially after how much I enjoyed Shadows of New York.

My biggest issue, and what really brought down my enjoyment, was the missed opportunity with the dual playthroughs. While playing as Kali, I felt intentionally kept in the dark, and I was excited to play as Padraic to fill in those blanks and get a complete picture of the events. Unfortunately, playing through as Padraic was basically a repeat of the same story with almost zero new insight or context filled in. It felt irritating to essentially play the same story twice with no real benefit.

The game then ends on what feels like an inconclusive note. While the art is excellent, the lackluster story and unrewarding second playthrough made this a less satisfying experience overall. Perhaps Shadows set the bar too high.

I’ve just finished VTM: Reckoning of New York for the second time and honestly... I’m disappointed. The writing style was either painfully clumsy or overloaded with “fancy” vocabulary that made it feel like a slog rather than an immersive story. Clicking through dialogue often felt like work, not play.

The dialogue choices barely count as choices. Most look like this:

Please! | Don’t! | Stop it!
Reynard! | Reynard? | Reynard…
Duh. | I could switch back to rude. | Haven’t you noticed?

These aren’t meaningful options... they’re just punctuation swaps? Even worse, the protagonist sometimes shifts tone completely out of nowhere. You might start a calm conversation with a Thinblood and suddenly your only choices are to threaten them, use a power, or get physically aggressive for no reason. It feels forced and inconsistent with the tone of the scene....

Lore consistency isn’t much better. Playing as a Ravnos, you’re supposed to change your resting place every night for seven nights... yet by night three or four, you’re back sleeping in the same spot. There are no consequences, no tension and almost no acknowledgment of it at all. She just felt a bit ill.

To be fair, my first playthrough was fun because I shared the ending chapters with a friend, he voiced the male protagonist, I voiced the female. That made it genuinely entertaining, but that’s credit to us, not the game.

Now, about the second protagonist, Pádraic (spoiler warning here!):
He’s introduced as a Caitiff, but it’s painfully obvious he’s actually a Malkavian. His shirt literally features a broken mirror (the Malkavian clan symbol) and his belt has Jesters on it... Later on, the game confirms it but by then, it’s not a twist... it’s just stating the obvious.

And speaking of missed opportunities: Pady has a D20 ring that he spins whenever his “Malk voices” overwhelm him. If he rolls a 20, they quiet down. But what happens if he rolls a 1? We never find out. That could’ve been a brilliant interactive moment! Imagine being able to click the ring yourself, taking part in his little ritual. Instead, it’s just another piece of flavor text that goes nowhere.

You can only unlock Pady’s route after finishing Kali’s, which sounds good in theory. But in practice, it means replaying the same story beats again, just with slightly altered dialogue and “crazy Malkavian” voice snippets. You get to know where he was at those moments you were alone with Kali... and some other background stuff.
Even worse, the game re-explains basic terms like Fledgling and Hound in the glossary, despite the fact that you have to finish one playthrough to even unlock the second.

In the end, Reckoning of New York felt more like reading a linear book than playing a roleplaying game. My choices had almost to just no impact and in 8 out of 10 cases, I wouldn’t have acted like Kali did. That’s a real shame, because the previous two entries: Coteries of New York and Shadows of New York, had genuine potential. Julia, the protagonist from Shadows, was especially well-written and memorable in my opinion.

Great potential, poor execution. A story that forgot the “role” in “roleplaying.”
