This VtM visual novel sure is a great addition to the previous ones (CONY and SONY), with a unique feel, being more contemplative and tragic in tone, also with some sprinkles of existential horror.

I enjoyed the visual aspect of this novel as I did with the previous novels in the series - dark, brooding, and dangerous nights in the streets and the underbelly of NY - although I have to admit that the rendering of some characters felt somewhat off, like pasted-on cut outs. The music underscores the overall atmosphere well - an interplay between silence, ambience and darker tones to hammer the sense of danger home. The main theme, especially, is an underrated jewel: it's full of melancholic tunes mingling with light glimmers of hope, interspersed with an occasional moody violin, like twists of fate. I also adore the fact that the main menu changes its appearance based on the progression of the story: Having the other character appear once unlocked and the room changing from dark to light based on one's choices - I love this attention to detail. It's a small touch, but has a tremendous impact on the overall atmosphere of the piece. Choices therefore do matter, and get their visual representation once you reach the end. They are, however, perhaps more implicit - very much in line with the larger explored themes - it is the internal choices which determine who the characters are - more than their outward approaches to issues and dialogues.

One of the frequently voiced criticisms is the open-endedness. Every VtM novel so far has been open-ended and it makes sense - once certain choices are made, it is up to the characters themselves to write their own stories, so to speak. My only beef with the novel was the initial character selection. I understand that the Ravnos represented the latest addition to V5 at the time this novel came out, but I did not endorse the fact that I had to play one, and a character (type) that I sincerely dislike at that - the perpetual "oh-so tough", whimsical, ill-mannered, ungrateful child. But, though the character felt on occasion very stereotypical, the story itself was definitely well-written and the character I sincerely disliked at the beginning slowly grew on me. The writing also takes care to reflect the characters' identity in the description of scenes and wording of the choices offered. It truly feels like observing the story through their eyes. In this regard, extremely well done. Once I finished the whole story from both perspectives and seen where the different choices took me, I actually feel that the characters complete each other well, and the initial restriction in character selection makes sense to me. 

Another feature that makes this VtM piece unique, as hinted above, is that the other character offered in fact represents the other side of the same coin - you get to experience the same story through their own eyes and thoughts. Their perspective and the scenes shared by both storylines were portrayed in realistic ways, underscoring the differences between the characters' world views, values, feelings and thoughts. One could link some passages in the second perspective precisely to certain moments and feelings experienced by the main character in the first one. It illustrated well how feelings and behaviours can be easily misunderstood, built on the ongoing mystery, and added depth to the overall experience. The combination of these two perspectives therefore makes this visual novel a well-rounded piece, definitely worthy of the whole VtM New York series. Its lens just seems to have a more contemplative filter on, highlighting things larger than individual (un)life.

So, all in all, if you liked the previous ones and are looking for some moody evening reading, I'd definitely recommend this one too. As always, it's a special joy to see the characters from the previous novels (Coteries of NY and Shadows of NY) evolve, but this piece would work on its own well enough if you haven't read those.

Vampire: The Masquerade – Reckoning of New York offers an intense, narrative-driven dive into the dark, brooding underworld of the World of Darkness, blending vampire mythology with a gritty urban setting. Developed by 
Draw Distance, known for their strong storytelling and atmospheric design, this game takes place in a richly detailed version of New York City, where vampire clans vie for control, alliances are fragile, and every choice carries deadly consequences. It’s a game that caters primarily to fans of the Vampire: The Masquerade franchise and those who appreciate deep narrative RPGs, but its complex storytelling and morally grey characters can captivate any player interested in immersive, mature storytelling.

Set in the early 2000s, Reckoning of New York thrusts players into the role of a fledgling vampire caught in the web of political intrigue between the city’s powerful vampire factions. The narrative unfolds through a mix of exploration, dialogue, and decision-making that directly shapes how the story progresses, who becomes your ally or enemy, and ultimately, what fate befalls the city. The game excels at creating an atmosphere of tension and paranoia, where trust is scarce, and every interaction is layered with subtext. This ambiance is enhanced by the game’s moody soundtrack, voice acting, and detailed environmental design, which together evoke a sense of lurking danger and ancient power beneath the city’s surface.

One of the game’s most impressive features is its character development system, which allows players to customize their vampire’s abilities, feeding style, and clan affiliations. This RPG element isn’t just window dressing; it meaningfully impacts gameplay, dialogue options, and combat tactics. Whether you choose to embrace the brutal strength of the Brujah, the manipulative finesse of the Ventrue, or the shadowy guile of the Nosferatu, your playstyle will influence how you interact with the city and its denizens. This customization encourages replayability, as different clan choices open unique storylines, quests, and endings, providing varied perspectives on the vampire underworld.

Combat in Reckoning of New York blends strategic decision-making with visceral action. It’s not a button-mashing affair but requires players to carefully consider their vampiric powers, positioning, and resource management. Feeding mechanics add another layer, as maintaining your character’s blood pool is vital to survival and effectiveness. Combat encounters often feel tense and high-stakes, with environmental hazards and enemy behaviors demanding adaptive strategies. While not revolutionary in design, the combat system complements the story-driven nature of the game, providing just enough challenge to keep players engaged without overshadowing the narrative.

Narratively, the game shines in its exploration of vampiric themes such as eternal struggle, identity, and the balance between humanity and monstrosity. The writing is mature, nuanced, and often philosophical, reflecting the franchise’s reputation for tackling complex moral dilemmas and personal horror. The dialogue is rich and often cryptic, forcing players to read between the lines and understand the motives behind each character’s words and actions. The branching narrative structure ensures that choices have weight, leading to multiple endings that reflect the myriad ways a vampire’s journey can unfold in the treacherous cityscape.

Visually, the game captures the noir aesthetic of Vampire: The Masquerade well, with dimly lit urban environments, rain-soaked streets, and shadowy interiors that evoke the gothic horror roots of the series. While not hyper-realistic, the art style balances stylized character designs with detailed backdrops that bring the city to life. Lighting and weather effects contribute significantly to the mood, underscoring the feeling of isolation and danger that permeates the vampire existence. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, facilitating smooth navigation through dialogue trees, inventory management, and combat without breaking immersion.

Despite its many strengths, Reckoning of New York is not without its flaws. Some players may find the pacing uneven, with slower sections focused heavily on exposition and dialogue that can feel dense or overwhelming for those new to the lore. The reliance on textual storytelling means the game demands patience and attention, which might alienate players seeking a more action-oriented or fast-paced experience. Additionally, certain side quests and story arcs occasionally feel underdeveloped or repetitive, lacking the depth and payoff of the main storyline. Technical issues, such as occasional bugs or frame rate dips, can also interrupt immersion, though these are generally minor and patchable.

Overall, Vampire: The Masquerade – Reckoning of New York is a compelling, atmospheric RPG that successfully captures the spirit of the World of Darkness. It offers a rich narrative full of intrigue, horror, and complex characters, wrapped in a moody urban setting that feels alive with danger and secrecy. Its layered storytelling, meaningful choice-driven gameplay, and customizable vampire protagonist make it a rewarding experience for fans of dark fantasy and mature RPGs. While it may require patience and familiarity with the source material to fully appreciate, it stands as a strong entry in the Vampire: The Masquerade lineage and a noteworthy title for those who enjoy deep, immersive narrative adventures.

Possibly the most middling of all Vampire: the Masquerade visual novels so far. Hard to hate, harder to love. I wasn't a big fan of Coteries of New York, but I loved Shadows of New York. This one slides right between the two in terms of quality.

Being a VN, the story is obviously the main focus. In this case it's perfectly fine. The overarching mysteries were engaging enough that it made me want to continue reading and the consistent pacing of each night/chapter made it a smooth ride. It was nothing spectacular, just perfectly serviceable. The characters on the other hand, a little less so. Kali is basically a Marvel character, constantly throwing out quips and trying to be quirky and clever, while Padraic, the sidekick/secondary protagonist, is a pretty standard strong, silent type (but with a nerdy, pretty boy flair). Obviously this dichotomy is supposed to make them work well together, and I suppose it does well enough, but it also makes them each feel more like caricatures than real people.

In terms of "choices matter", there are none here. The previous two entries were already extremely limited in this way, but somehow they managed to remove even more player choice with Reckoning. Frankly this wasn't a negative for me, as I assumed this would be the case going in, but fair warning to anyone with higher hopes.

Lastly, the art and music. The standout here is the background art. It's as good as ever, with New York looking muddy, dishevelled, and beautifully moody. It reflects perfectly the world of Vampire: the Masquerade. However, the character art REALLY drops the ball. It contrasts starkly with the background, being overly polished and clean. Well made on its own, but inappropriate for its surroundings. Everyone looks like an airbrushed doll who doesn't fit in with the world behind them. Less offensively, the music is entirely forgettable. After the incredible soundtrack of Shadows of New York, I was really disappointed by this.

So all in all, it's perfectly "ok". Due to the cons I decided it errs on the "not recommended" side of middling, but if you're already invested in the New York trilogy, it's worth the read (ideally on sale). If not though, maybe just play Shadows of New York. The connections between these games are meaningless anyway.

Paddy's story is slightly better in this regard but even still largely revolves around new players, introduced at the last minute, instead of the established cast from the first 2 games who's stories I was always more invested in.

The main duo, Kali and Paddy, are likeable and have a fun dynamic- but we don't see conclusions for the likes of Panhard, Qadir, Arturo and Julia. We don't receive any hints about the fate of our character from 'Coteries'. The game's climax is exciting and is more connected to the previous entries, but unfortunately it feels as if the game never truly satisfies in its role as a conclusion to a trilogy. 

With the lack of conclusions we receive the series is, at least, left open to more installments which I hope we receive as both 'Shadows' and 'Coteries' were excellent and this game - whilst disappointing in its context - still presents fun characters and two interesting enough mysteries that I completed both main characters' stories.

I'd recommend Reckoning for those who liked Shadows. The story is good, though not particularly satisfying in the grand, metaplot kind of way; it's quite personal to the two main characters, Kali and Padraic, who both get mostly satisfying conclusions. Replaying the story as Padraic also reveals a number of extra dimensions to the story, because Padraic is more clued into the politics of NYC.
It is not a good game if you are looking for choices or self-expression. Like Shadows of New York, interactivity and choices are minimal, a far cry from Coteries, which I still enjoyed most out of the three (and even that entry in the series was not particularly interactive). It is also not a good game if you find Kali annoying; I got used to her and her dynamic with Padraic is quite sweet but her clueless peppy con-artist persona is hardly a crowd-pleaser. The side-characters are for the most part not very memorable; the only ones with depth are the recurring ones, especially Julia and Qadir. The way Kali's missing sire is handled is not ideal for the story-telling.

Honestly really disappointed with this VtM. I really wanted to like it but it only took 10 minutes of game for me to realize it just wasn't it. I did push through though, because I felt I couldn't really make my opinion on 10 minutes of playtime. I played both characters, did everything. Yet I honestly feel like I wasted my time.

First, the art style. I'll pass the fact that many people, me included, assumed at first that it was AI-generated or at least AI-edited. It apparently isn't and I can get on with that as this style is an art style in itself. I just didn't like it. It has no soul, especially when you compare it to the two previous games. And I don't want to compare but the difference is mad. It's not ugly or lacking in quality but for me, it just simply doesn't fit the universe of the Masquerade. It's too posh, too clean. But I can get behind a change of direction in style so let's pass that.

The scenario is meh. It goes in every directions and none at the same time. If you don't play both characters you will not understand jack of most things, unless you make assumptions. "Yeah but the game is made so you play both characters!", yeah alright I played both and it was still lacking. You don't feel the pressure of vampire society as much as, again, the two previous games. The writing didn't make me feel stressed or scared for the characters or the outcome. 

Speaking of characters, Kali is just unbearable. Whether from first person view by playing her or from playing the other one, she is insufferable. Not once did I feel empathy or sympathy for her situation. I had a hard time with the protagonist from Shadows of New York but this one is a new low. She lack in personality and the writing doesn't give much when it comes to showing the "stereotypes", if I may say, of her Clan. The second character is no better,  I thought I would have enjoyed it but no, painful to the end. Overall I just couldn't relate to them in any way. Not that I had to, but in the end, it was so bland I didn't root for anyone.

Overall, the pressure of vampire politics from Coteries and Shadows is not felt at all in this one, even though you would assume it would just by looking at the events from Reckoning. I felt I wasn't really in the game, that none of my choices had an impact. I know it can be hard to do in a visual novel but still disappointing.

Positive note though, I enjoyed the game mechanics of hunger and threat. I feel like it can be explored more but it was fun to mess with a bit.

Reckoning of New York starts with an interesting concept but it quickly becomes apparent that decisions carry little to no weight. This is even worse in the second character's run which, though filling in some mystery, is basically a repeat of the first character's run but with some additional comments from the character himself. In comparison to Coteries and Shadows, Reckoning falls flat and is a disappointing third entry.

It is definitely worse than the previous 2 games in the series. Coteries of New York and Shadows of New York (and Heart of the Forest) may not have been perfect, but they were the games, that made me think, that some of my ideas probably can work as visual novels, if I ever get to those, while before I did not even consider the genre. If Reckoning was the first game, that would not have been the case.

The main problem is overall inconsistency. The art style, especially when you compare the models (which suddenly required Unity for 3D effects, I guess) to backgrounds. But even comparing one background to another there are some inconsistences that my brain was able to pick-up. They are minor ones, but still. I could have complained that the style is generally different from previous games, and I do not like it as much, but I would have lived with that. Inconsistencies - not so much. Especially that ugly gray line on the albino girl, visible at least in the 2nd playthrough.

Character inconsistencies were also noticeable to me. Not necessarily compared to previous games (can't say I remember much about the recurring characters), but the new ones - definitely. Padraic is the best example, because Kali describes him as kind of "silent" type practically all the time, and notices every glimpse of emotion on his face, but... She notices those emotions in practically any conversation and multiple times, which completely breaks Padraic's character. Kali herself is not that consistent as well, but I am not sure I can get into details here without potentially spoiling some things.

I also did not like the fact that text was now on the right also being a log at the same time. It took too much space, and considering that left side was empty very often, and character models were really small, it felt like there was a lot of wasted space. I think previous games used the available (negative) space much better, which helped with immersion. Let alone them having multiple faces for each character, which also helped with immersion into the story.

What's worse the story itself was not that great. It started in a way that reminded me of my own earlier writing, and I can tell that it was bad. It could have still worked if Kali was an intriguing character with a clearly defined personality, but she was just following the flow almost aimless. Yes, the circumstances kind of forced her, but Julia was also forced into things, and still had her own motivations besides pure survival. Until this game, at least, where she also became 2-dimensional.

The finale of the story was completely anticlimactic, too. It essentially went nowhere. I guess, it was an attempt at a cliffhanger, an open ending, but I am not sure it really worked. It was begging for something more... "Final". I hoped that 2nd playthrough for a different character would add something, but... It made things worse. 85% of it was just repetition of the exact same things as 1st playthrough, 10% - more thoughts of this character (won't tell whom, because devs apparently consider that a spoiler), which do not really expand the character that much, and the rest - some extra scenes, half of which are not even related to either of the characters, feel completely out of place, and the other half is... Mostly inconsequential.

And it ended in the same place. Absolutely same place. Let alone it showed that all your choices in 1st playthrough did not matter at all. Not only for the story in general, but they were not even "remembered" by the game itself, because Kali said some different things from what I chose in 1st playthrough. If I remember correctly, previous games did have proper choices, that changed things. Hey, in-game map made and "skipping night" made sense there, and here it has only 1 option most of the time just forcing you to hold spacebar instead of just tapping it.

The sad part of it is that story could have been saved even in current format. Start with the 2nd character first, then unlock Kali. Remember the choices from 1st playthrough, show only moments when the characters were apart and then you can even use Kali's current ending. This way it would have been, at least, somewhat bittersweet, and not just bland.

Alas, we can't hope for a "Snyder's Cut" here. I do want to support the devs, but unfortunately, I cannot recommend this game, unless you are a die hard fan and it's on heavy discount.

Compared to Shadows and Coteries, the writing here unfortunately falls short. The protagonist is very predefined and the story is really, really railroady. As far as I’ve tested, choices are just flavor and after a few slightly altered dialogue lines, they always converge back into the predetermined main plot. I know many visual novels do this, but here it's especially obvious and just doesn’t feel good.

There are several key moments where decisions would have been perfect for influencing the course of the story and shaping Kali, but the game doesn’t take advantage of these opportunities, leaving you just a spectator on the sidelines. Towards the end, it was almost infuriating how little choice there was in situations where it would have mattered a lot.

Speaking of Kali - for me, she was a truly unlikable character. Impulsive, naive and edgy. A really annoying brat who constantly makes stupid decisions. And you can’t even counteract this because the lack of choice. The tone of writing is generally like a teenage novel with occasional Zoomer slang, which I personally couldn’t get into and I think that just doesn’t really fit VtM well.

The hunger and threat meters, as well as the disciplines, are kinda just for show and don’t really influence the gameplay. Managing hunger/threat was so easy that they might as well have left it out and in the situations I tested, it made no difference to the story whether I used a discipline or not. So why even bother?

However, sound effects, music, art, and UI (apart from the hard-to-read hunger and threat meter) are really well made and help with immersion. Some people say the art looks AI-generated, but I don’t share that opinion. The devs have also confirmed that no AI was involved.

But in a game like this, the core has to be strong - meaning story/writing and also the ability to roleplay, at least a bit. Being able to make meaningful choices, shape the protagonist and experience a narrative that reacts to the players decisions. And Reckoning severely lacks that. This one would have worked better as a book imo. 

Well.. so I could now replay the story from Padraic’s perspective, which might resolve the annoying cliffhanger, but honestly, I lack the motivation to do so.

Conclusion: You're better off playing the previous games and if you still desperately need more VtM after that, then maybe check this one out. Otherwise, you’d be better off with other VNs.

I have played and mostly enjoyed the two previous visual novels in this series, Coteries and Shadows. So when I saw this one I immediately bought it and started playing it expecting more of the same. Why not? Decent writing, an atmospheric and moody presentation, the always amazing World of Darkness. More of the same would be good. Yet halfway through, I abandoned this game for weeks before forcing myself to come back and finish it. Most certainly not a good sign. What happened? How does a 10 hour long visual novel start feeling too long? It's not really the two protagonists the Ravnos girl and "Caitiff" guy. If anything it was mildly intriguing to see a Ravnos, devil-may-care rogue take the spotlight for a change. There is some decent exposition present here and there and the game nails the atmosphere sound wise. So far so good, but it's still not enough.

The first thing I noticed playing this sequel was the shift in artstyle. It's not for the better. While Coteries and Shadows had interesting, stylized character art, Reckoning looks like something that came out of an AI image generator. This damages the otherwise good groove the series has going and even makes some returning characters barely recognisable, but fine, it's a visual novel, if the story is good then much can be forgiven. Well, it's not. There are various plots and counterplots present, including some seemingly interesting character arcs to be explored. On the surface it sounds rather promising, but the game's narrative fails to deliver. The various plot points are resolved too easily or not resolved at all, there is virtually no impactful choices to be made, the main mystery involving the second protagonist feels too much like a pretentious shaggy dog story and the whole experience comes across as vapid. That's ultimately the game's downfall.

It is a shame. It's not that the previous games were masterpieces, far from it, but they were good for what they were. Inessential, but fun excuses to go back and enjoy some more World of Darkness. Somehow, despite being set in that incredibly rich and compelling world, this one manages to be just bland and boring. I can't really recommend this. Not unless someone is a superfan and even then I'd say wait for a steep sale. Hope the developers can do better next time.

[h3] Lamentatio et Laudatio[/h3] 

[u] [b]Prima pars:[/b][/u] 

Ultimum opus in serie New York—Reckoning of New York—aequales non habet normas excelsas, quae a Coteries et Shadows praebitae sunt. In hoc ludo, novitatibus et consiliis obsoletis, quaedam electa male exarata sunt, quae experientiam ludentem turbat. Interface, ad exemplum, partem imaginis obstruit, dum elementa nimis plurima distrahunt et lacerant. Sprites characterum, prorsus in uncanny valley incurrunt, nec animatio suorum gestuum subtilis est, simile quid in ludis point-and-click mediocribus videretur.

Haec omnia, ironice, ludum artis deminuunt. Etiam scribendi genus, quod aliis temporibus elegans erat, nunc turbatur, superfluens multitudine nominum et refertionum culturalium. Quid dicat "Ally McBeal gothed-out…" aut "Nix mihi numquam obstabat"? Haec cadunt in kitsch. Quod pessimum fit c.um omne caput fabulae clauditur cameo vel flashback arbitrario. "Interim", "sex menses ante", vel "nocte antea" – haec omnia valde ineptum inseruntur.

Eventus in hoc ludo ex pluribus prospectibus capiuntur, sed verum insidium occurrit: ut plenum contextum comprehendas, necesse est ludum iterum ludere. Sed inter tot verborum repetitiones, saepe etiam intra monologos interiores, quae nihil aliud quam eadem verba sunt, apparere videtur negligentia. Aliquam multa elementa in secunda versioni (Pádraic’s historia) melioribus elaborari potuerunt, magis distincte rationes inter Anarchos et in Torre Eburnea.

Verumtamen, haec vitia non obfuscant utilitatem verborum, quae in scriptura subtiliter exprimitur. Lingua ricca et complexa, saepe elegans, interdum obscura, sensum certum continet. Scaenae, crudelitate et suspicione repletae, memoriam Vampire: The Masquerade renovant. Sonus, qui a fabulis priores comitatur, ludos ut Bloodlines et Coteries of New York recondite evocans, ambiente lugubri ac opaco, lectoribus non solum spectatorem sed partem universi renditur.

[u] [b]Secunda pars:[/b][/u] 
C.um praevaricatio haec fuerit, tamen, quinam finem obtineret, dubitavi. Fabulae tamen clementer pervagatae sunt, ludos complectentes tandem… Tamen verba scinduntur: non possum quin dicam, hoc opus minus iucundum esse quam prius opera: Coteries et Shadows. Reckoning pauciores fines habet; haec potius minus diversae optiones praebet, quam in prioribus ludis ubi fines iterati erant.

Initium ab Kali, Ravnos primae, nullam fere variationem habet, quicquid sit electio. Istud autem non esse, quod solitum erat in Coteries ubi viri vestri alios socios colligere potuissent, aliae vias pervagandi destinabant. In Shadows etiam diversae optiones loci ultro praebebantur, quod iterum et iterum fruendi experientiam aliter obtinebat. In Reckoning, visiones et colloquia videbantur, in summa, eadem. Solum in Nocte Tertia mirabilis differentia apparet: optio dat te effugere a sensu potentiae.
Si res tantum a Kali dependet, fere reconditum me certis optio haud probarim. Sed pervenit Pádraic; eius fabula profundius se explicat, aliquid maioris curae in fabula. Quamquam celata eius vera clan et consilia immutabilia, confestim intellegimus cur hic solus post Kali ludere liceat. Pádraic, fortasse solus, saltem in fine eligibilis finem habet, qua solis duas vias impleri potest.[u]  [b]Finis recusare[/b][/u] , prorsus meis oculis celsissimus.

C.um sit historia, ut memineris, non tam fortis ut prioribus fabulis Coteries et Shadows comparata, utpote minus curata. Attamen, si vobis fabula solitaria vobis placeat, pulchra et grata quidem erit. Etsi Kali, ut saepe dici potest, irritans est, mihi minime nocet. Pádraic autem, c.um sua obscura et mysteriosa indole, potius magnum impactum facit, et fabula eius universum totum profundius illustrat.
Etsi pars artium mutata, ipse stilus a prioribus fabulis discretus fit, mutavit. Backgrounds tamen, satis pulchri, ludi atmosphaeram servantes. Sonitus etiam minus frequentatur, ut antea fuerat. Hic tamen, si priora ludos ludere potuisti et fabulae de New York te decipere possunt, tunc haec opus sit admodum satisfaciens.

Sic, Reckoning of New York non sine lacunis et non solum hic non aequans praeteritis, sed finem suum perducit. Ars quaedam vacillat, sed atmosphaera ipsa manet fortis. the writing is ok but the story mostly just meanders on, if you're dying for more after you played Coteries and Shadows of new york then go for it, otherwise it's probably best to save your money. Tentatively recommended.

## Art
Although from a technical fidelity standpoint the art has progressed, i find this to be a step back compared to Shadows of New York. Characters have a sort of glossy over-pretty look to them and the few characters who dont look like caricatures. Its to the point that i (and many others) assumed them to be bland soulless ai-generated pretties at first. This is especially bad with the first protagonist Kali who looks like she leapt straight out of pinterest. Other characters look like caricatures, Thomas Arturo looks less like a smarmy aristocrat and more like an incredibly mis-cast benedict cumberbatch. Addison Payne looks like a childrens book caricature of a mean old man, lacking any of the menacing dignity he had in the previous games. Qadir al-Asmai has lost all of his charm and seemingly become just a pretty boy in camo pants (which fit his character incredibly poorly).

The only character i liked is prince Panhard, who has adopted a more goth look in this game. 

## Mechanics

The hunger and suspicion mechanics are back from the first game, however they're much more forgiving (you basically have to actively try to get a fail state) and can be turned off if wanted. Beyond that your use of disciplines seems to mostly be flavour text and as far as i can tell there's no really consequences to your actions, other than that if you pick the wrong option you might get an extra scene about the second inquisition being on your tail.

## Story

The story is bland and seems to mostly re-tread old ground metaphorically and literally. As the story follows a similar structure to the previous two games, a young vampire thrown into an investigation beyond them, only to discover at the end that [spoiler]he powers that be knew all along what was going on and where just using them as a distraction[spoiler/]. Unlike in Shadows however you dont get the satisfaction of turning things around on them, mostly your character just limps away with the mcguffin. At no point was i interested in the story or trying to predict what would happen.

The first protagonist, Kali is mostly unlikable. The story can't seem to make up its mind on whether she's a sharp-witted fledgling or just a foolish young girl and she ends up coming off as cocky with poor impulse control. 

Padraic is better but by the time we get to him we're literally re-treading old ground, going through the whole game again from the his perspective. His knowledge offers new insights which to be faire ARE interesting. Except 80% of his play time is literally watching scene's you've already seen play out from the other perspective. His inner monologue is interesting but not interesting enough and i ended up skipping through most of his story just to get to the end.

I was really excited to play this final installment of the new york series, I enjoyed the first two a LOT! But it fell flat at nearly every possible opportunity, here are my major complaints: 

The protagonist Kali is nowhere near as likable as the previous games, and has little personality beyond stereotypes. The second playthrough allows you a glimpse into another characters perspective but it is ultimately a line for line repeat of the first playthrough. 
The dialogue options are severely limited, and often offer no choice at all or a single sentence response before the game breezes to answering the 'correct' option. And the writing of the dialogue itself felt very amateur, like some fan-fiction with unfitting fourth wall breaks or cheesy references. 
The music was nice and atmospheric, but had hardly any tracks which lead to a bit of bland constant repeats of the same 2 or 3 songs, the ambient noise was very nice where it was worked in. 
The plot itself is fascinating, and I loved getting to revisit a lot of favorite characters. But the player is painfully tied into the least interesting part and we are forced to slog through it twice while gleaning very little ambiguous information about the actual goings on in the city that the other games have built up to, and the ending ultimately leaves it vague and open ended simply because our protagonist could care less about what happened. 
One of my biggest gripes was with the changed artstyle, both for the characters and the backgrounds. I'm suspicious it is retouched art that was AI-generated and is inconsistent and sloppy across the board. Though it still fits the mood and theme well enough.

This is a bit of a tough review. Without a doubt, I am of a mind to recommend this game, if only for the rather interesting progression of the state of NYC's unlife. There's a number of perks and trade-offs to this narrative, of which I don't really have much to add from prior reviews of this title. But I will say this: Reckoning is indeed an apt description, and that HAS to score some extra points.

In terms of the overall plot, I can safely say that it is fantastic. Well timed twists (maybe a bit obvious on one or two, but hey, most twists are), a rather well done dynamic between the two 'protagonists', and a good amount of life thrown into the voices of the characters. Additionally, there's a humanity to these characters that is hard to find in the World of Darkness, and it forces far more of a tug on the emotional strings than I have normally come to expect out of Vampire the Masquerade. Now, the voices *do* fall a tad flat in a few times throughout, and there's a couple dull moments (mostly on the 'side quests'), but I left most every scene with questions and thoughts about the future of the story (in a good way, not a 'I don't get it' sort of fashion). The narrative does a rather good job of pulling attention to and from different subjects to keep a good flow of mystery and questions to be answered throughout, and in the end, wraps up the questions of the narrative at hand quite nicely, while still leaving room for the progression of the city's situation through either later exploration or through personal curiosity/creation.

Now, for complaints, I have nothing new, really. The art is undeniably more lifeless and indistinct than that of prior titles, the UI was altered [from prior titles] for seemingly no real reason.... The music was decent, though there were only a handful of tracks (it does a good enough job. You're focused on text, and it doesn't intrude, it's fine). A common complaint that I see that I actually disagree with is about illusion of choice during the narrative. Yes, most of your choices lead to similar outcomes or don't really change your character. Okay? Same with prior titles, and also, you're playing a character. You're not playing you. This is much less a game and much more a story. You're experiencing something, watching it through the eyes of another. It's not really about your choices. Now, prior titles DID have a *bit* of narrative alteration from your choices that is not present in Reckoning, but honestly, given the state of New York, choices are a very pricey commodity for ALL of the characters, even the most powerful, and like many things in the World of Darkness..... Your choices are very often not your own. 

Anyways. I believe I've said my piece. Reckoning is not as strong as others before, and questionable design choices with the game as a digital format annoy me slightly, but overall, I do think that it is a solid piece of storytelling, with a wonderfully tangled web and a good cast of unfortunate characters that must endure within it. It could have been presented much better in the audio and visual space, and perhaps there are some slight edits to the words/phrases themselves that I might have preferred, but to the narrative on the whole? No, I think they did just fine.

As the finale of the trilogy, Reckoning sets the stage for truly reshaping New York, and then it immediately stifles its own potential by giving us the main protagonist who simply doesn’t care about any of that. While major events happen in the background, Kali is on her own quest. For her story to work, Kali would need to be interesting if not likeable, but she just isn’t. Now, I’m not one of those people who think that all vampires have to act like stereotypical medieval monsters. There’s nothing wrong with characters who retain their contemporary streak. I adored Julia. Yes, she was a snarky goth, but there was so much more to her. Julia had a lot of history and personality, we got to see who she was as a person. Now, all there’s left for Kali is mostly just snark. Endless snark.

But that gets worse when you replay the game as the secondary protagonist, Padraic, because that’s when it becomes clear just how much better the game could’ve been. As it stands, his route is not that different from simply replaying/re-reading the game so it’s basically wasted. Which is a damn shame because he is a much more compelling character. Still not as good as Julia to me, I have a soft spot for her, but his inner monologue is considerably more enjoyable than Kali’s. I found myself often pausing during Kali’s route. I went through Padraic’s route in one sitting (and even got to google some cool Irish mythology stuff). What’s more, his character is uniquely positioned to be directly involved in all the juicy stuff. That is so very smart… Expect he can’t actually even witness anything because he has to follow Kali’s story, who is uniquely positioned to witness nothing! You can’t make it up, it’s just bewildering.

Just like the previous two instalments in the series, Reckoning is incredibly linear, more like an illustrated novel than an interactive novel. In Shadows, Julia was compelling enough to make up for it, but in Reckoning, the lack of interactivity is very noticeable. You can’t even stupidly get the protagonist killed in the very beginning, which feels like such a staple of the series by now. The game could’ve at least benefitted from more “flavor” choices. The sort of choices that only affect one or two lines but add interactivity, especially during fight scenes. Padraic actually has a gimmick which adds a flair of interactivity even without those flavour choices. It has to do with how we simply scroll through the text, but I liked it quite a bit. But again, that is something that is locked behind the first playthrough/readthrough. It's almost like better stuff is purposefully locked behind worse stuff!

I wonder if Reckoning was somewhat constrained by its budget. I won’t comment on the art style, everyone already has, but the characters also no longer have multiple facial expressions, which is very noticeable. The game feels like the shortest in the series, with what feels like less side content. Then there’s the ending. [spoiler] Where Shadows improved on Coteries, Reckoning seems to revert back to a more “realistic” approach to its ending where you find out about as much as a regular Kindred probably would. Except why should we play for regular Kindred? [/spoiler]

Despite my frustrations, there are a lot of good elements in the game. Some interesting characters, some fascinating lore concepts, some inspired descriptions. And I truly believe that the game would be better received if Padraic was the main and perhaps solo protagonist, and if the story was centred around his involvement in the city politics. But then it would be a different game, wouldn’t it?

[h1]Reckoning of New York[/h1]
The final instalment of the New York series falls short on standards established by its predecessors, Coteries and Shadows of New York. Questionable choices mar this game left and right: interface, for instance, blocks half the background. It also has too many elements, which is distracting. Going further, many characters barely resemble their older selves; instead, their sprites border uncanny valley. This is not helped by decidedly [i]frugal[/i] animations reminiscent of third-rate point-and-click titles. 

These innovations, ironically, cheapen the game’s artistry. Even writing, otherwise elegant, is stained by a disturbing amount of name-dropping and cultural references; let the phrases “That gothed-out Ally McBeal…” or “The snow never bothered me anyway.” illustrate their kitsch. More than that, every chapter finishes with an arbitrarily assigned cameo. "Meanwhile", "six months ago", or "earlier that night"… the implementation is clumsy.

The events unfolding in this game are captured from multiple viewpoints. The catch is that in order to view the full picture, one must re-play the game. Yet observations and inner monologues are often identical, word to word. Sometimes, repetition appears even in first person—an obvious sloppiness. The similarities, or rather sameness, is too noticeable; the second (Pádraic’s) version could have been crafted with greater attention to detail, adding more to the happenings in the Ivory Tower and between the Anarchs.

In spite of these imperfections, I was impressed by the diverse vocabulary, aptly written descriptions, word plays, and figurative language. Each line is bound by a purpose, at times more obvious, other times obscure. The narrative is rich and complex—ever taunting, leaving readers at unease, pondering what come next. Tension is underlined by gruesome scenes, cold apathy, and distrust in all—the hallmarks of Vampire: The Masquerade. This effect is heightened by a fitting set of soundtracks, reminiscent of both Bloodlines as well as Coteries of New York. Combined with bleak, matte artworks, scenes fully engulf readers in an oppressive, despondent atmosphere. One often feels a part of the universe.

Characters intrigue the moment they are introduced. They are very colourful, distinctive and even polarising. Kali’s antics, for example, estrange people both real as well as fictional. As vexing as she is with her quips and puns, she freshens up this world of undeath by contrasting the old-fashioned Pádraic. She gets to people, and that makes her interesting. Even old reliables such as Arturo, Payne, or Quadir, more enigmatic than ever, come fitted with surprises.

And so, while Reckoning of New York may have misimplemented some of its novelties, it presents an impactful, emotional story. One, I daresay, which towers above many acclaimed titles of this genre.

I have rated the last two games in this series highly - Coteries of New York and Shadows of New York - and recommended them to others. I have also replayed each, the same way I re-read a favorite novel. I am a fan of Vampire the Masquerade. I act as Storyteller for the TTRPG with my friends, and fell in love when I played Bloodlines in 2004. I am also an avid reader, who has played the strictly text-based Choice of Games titles, and who owns beloved copies of the flavor-text ancillaries to the tabletop. I elaborate about the size of my dick to try and illustrate that I leave this review out of an immense love for what I know Vampire the Masquerade can do.

TL;DR - Terrible. Keep your money and your time.

The game menu presents itself with the illusion of choice between two characters: Kali, a young Ravnos whose sire has gone missing or  ??? a presumably male character in shadow. You are forced to play as Kali. If you want to play as the character later introduced as Padraic you have to complete the game one full time with Kali first. This is an apt beginning functionally, as all other choices I have been presented with have also been completely illusory, leading me down the established plot and without meaningful consequence.

The writing feels off immediately. It’s not concise, and riddled with rhetorical questions. Even when they are not written as straight-up questions (of which there are numerous) the prose is meandering and undercuts itself on multiple facets. I saw another review refer to this as “fan-fiction” writing. It's amateur. Either the writer doesn't trust their own ability or they don’t trust the reader to get it and fall to over-explaining. I find myself wondering at the age of the head writer/the team who put this together. Kali’s inner monologue and dialogue are clearly meant to mimic a younger, online, trend-aware vampire. This is not pulled off, because not only are the phrases (yapping, take the L, etc..) clumsily used, but Kali’s voice is not consistently maintained and she makes outdated references or suddenly says something awkward like “knock it off, will ya?” which people don’t actually say.

Here’s an example that sticks out to me: “they are sizing each other up like cats on a hot tin roof.” Why would Kali know that play, given her supposed age and background? Even if she did know Tennesee Williams, the reference is completely out of left-field at that moment and breaks with the overall tone. My actual breaking point was a passing reference to Frozen. We get an overwrought description of the snow, ending with something like “she brushes the snow from her face, but I don’t. The cold never bothered me anyway.” I wish I was joking.

So, the player is ploddingly carried along, reading as Kali ponders choices that the player should actually be making. We are walked through Kali’s narration of “I could do X, but of course I will not for Y reason” for long stretches of time. These are obvious missed opportunities to have the player make a choice in how to tackle the presented situation. The rest of the time, Kali is engaged in dialogue that is just as poorly executed as everything else. It’s exposition at best, and pseudo-snappy/witty/wink-wink-nudge-nudge at worst. Again, fan-fiction.

The player is presented with very few choices, and worse, the choices are meaningless. On one occasion my choice was actively rejected, and I was redirected to the consequences of the other choice within less than a paragraph. This is the TTRPG equivalent of rolling a one and an amateur storyteller saying “you failed, so do you want to try the other way?” instead of spinning that failure into something more interesting or giving it real outcome. Most of the choices presented are just for flavor, how snarky Kali is, or how she asks for a certain piece of information, but the information you get and the actions that follow are the same regardless.

When you meet with a Thin Blood on Night 2, you press her for information about Kali’s sire. Kali offers the other Kindred access to her stashes of blood and supplies (again we should have been able to choose a few approaches to getting this information), but you can act like a bit of a hardass about it if you want. EVEN IF YOU DO, later on Kali’s inner monologue says “I feel kinda bad for the way I acted towards her.”

I don’t get to drive the plot and I also don’t get to decide anything about who Kali is. I've established the writing is bad, so why am I playing exactly?

Background art and ambiance is still pretty good, but I don’t like the art style for the character portraits in this one as much. Aisling and the Prince especially look...weird. Speaking of Aisling, Kali refers to her as “goth Ally McBeal.” Another example of a missed chance to do some actual description and character building passed off to a non-sequitur and outdated reference.

I only made it to Night 2. I kept telling myself to push through and maybe it would start to get good when this scene was over. Okay maybe after this next scene it will pick up. Maybe once we meet this new character. I’m waiting for Godot over here!

The game is divided into two character paths, and after completing the first it falls apart in the second. You replay all the events as the other character of this story, except 95% of this is content you've already seen, asking questions you already know the answer to. Even the inner monologue of this character isn't revealing things about them you didn't already learn towards the end of the first path. The game mechanics, thin as they already are, are also removed from play leaving you with something which features not even the façade of meaningful choices.

When it finished, I was left wondering what the point of this second path was. There's no big revelation, no grand tying together of all the plot threads. It just... ends. It might be the weakest ending yet in a series filled with weak endings.

If you're looking for a game of this type, I'd highly recommend playing something like Parliament of Knives instead. It doesn't have the production values, but wins by every other measure.

Pádraic doesn't really make much sense as a character.  It doesn't seem likely that an Irish romantic would have fought in either of the World Wars or that he would care about the fall of London.  Also Pádraig would be a more logical spelling.  The Ravnos you meet including Kali are all pretty unlikable.  The ending feels like the devs ran out of money, the game has a tonne of built-up running around after a MacGuffin but then just ends without meeting the main villain, making any choices about the MacGuffin or your sire, or seeing New Year's Eve.

All the build-up at the end of the game essentially comes down to stuff that happens off screen and is only described as text.  It would have been more enjoyable if it was interactive and included in full scenes like everything else and if you could leave the city and pick up D'Angelo as a resolution to his arc.

Werewolf: The Apocalypse – Heart of the Forest is also made by Polish devs but is the much stronger game because the writing is stronger and rooted in an area they know intimately, Białowieża Forest, which was interesting and exciting to learn about as a non-European.  The story in Reckoning and the clans involved could just have easily been told in Warsaw and it would have been more engaging writing-wise.  

It would be a stronger game if you were allowed to make more choices about what to do at the end with regards to: your sire, the MacGuffin, and meeting the antagonist.  Seeing New Year's Eve would be nice too.

I've been waiting for this game ever since it was announced. I thought Shadows of New York was one of the best stories in a video game I'd seen in a long time.

I share in the criticisms of some of the negative reviewers, but I'm not going to give this a thumbs down. It's a good game. But I confess that I'm disappointed. I was hoping for so much more.

1) The art style has changed a lot, and I don't think it was for the better. It's a much more realistic style now. It's not bad . . . Shadows was just very moody and evocative in a way that this isn't.

2) I'm not sure what exactly has changed, but the writing's not as good. I don't think it's the quality of the description. It's more that something is missing from the characterization and the ambiance.

3) I was really hoping that the loose ends from the previous two games would be wrapped up. But there are a lot of questionable story decisions here.

The issue with Prince Panhard from Coteries, for example (I'm sorry to be vague, but spoilers etc.), is briefly alluded to in a single, throwaway line near the end of this game. They completely wasted a massive loose end that I was dying to hear more about.

Without spoiling actual details, there is an argument to be made that the big reveals which are happening near the end of this game are so big that none of the loose ends from the first two games even matter. But that's not how it's handled. If you were doing it that way, you would build up the tension, then drop your plot bomb that makes none of the previous games matter. Instead, it's almost like this game doesn't -care-.

The first and second games were all about politics inside the Camarilla. But in this game, the Camarilla are mostly side characters with barely any screen time.

A new subplot about Addison Payne is introduced in this game. But it's never explained and is only alluded to in two brief cutscenes. You can infer what happened. But the problem is that every other juicy plot point is handled the same way. There's a massive amount of story that happens off-scene. A lot of it would have been much juicier than the main story, and could have been made to intersect the main story. Instead, the main story feels like a bunch of disconnected side quests.

For example, there's a whole subplot about Anarch politics. You get hints about what's about to happen, and in the first character's story, you hear about some serious shit going down. I expected to see it play out in the second character's story - it would have been very simple to do. But instead, it happens in a single brief cutscene, and you don't interact with any of the aftermath in the second character's story at all. 

Then there's some backstory involving Aisling Sturbridge. Again - one tiny cutscene at the beginning, and nothing else.

Then there's the villain. You get a big splashy introduction to the villain during the first character's arc. And then . . . you never meet them or confront them. And nothing about the villain's motivations is ever provided to you.

On the bright side . . . I do love some of the new characters.

4) The game locks you out of the second character's arc at the beginning. What I thought was that the second character would be the "reveal" character - where you see the whole backstory revealed, some big spoilers from the first and second games, some loose ends tied up, and maybe an entirely different ending. 

The intro to the second character's arc is done pretty well, and I was excited . . . 

And then I discovered that the second character's story is exactly the same as the first's. Same dialogue, same locations, everything the same. A few additional wry observations while you're watching everybody repeat the same lines, like a vampire Groundhog Day. 

Halfway through I just started speed clicking through it to get to the end. I did not care about catching one or two minor variations on the same story.

It would have been much more intelligent to do this like a Japanese visual novel. Branch the story at a pivotal point. There is a very obvious point halfway through the story where you can do this. But they don't. I don't know why. 

If it changes nothing to play as the second character, why lock it?

5) A lot of people hate Kali. I don't hate her, but just at the level of constructive criticism . . . one of the problems with the game is that the things that make you a Ravnos are not really explained very well. 

I didn't know what a Lasombra was when I played Shadows, but the game did a good job of explaining it to me. That didn't happen in this game.

So, I'm not downvoting this. I just feel like it should have been a lot more . . . it feels like the developers ran out of time, money, or both.

I haven’t watched or followed WWE programming in years, but the sheer depth of these video games manages to hook me nearly every year. Because of this, playing an outdated wrestling game doesn't really bother me and WWE 2K25 is fun far more often than it isn't. As a total package, it serves up a refined, content-heavy wrestling experience that stands out as the best option on the market due to almost a complete lack of competition or alternatives. 

The in-ring action continues the steady evolution started back in 2K22, and this year easily delivers the best, most responsive version of that foundation. Every strike, grapple, and transition feels smooth, and performing your moves feels intuitive. Because the game leans into simulation, it isn't an easy pick-up-and-play arcade title for casual newcomers. However, once you invest a little time learning the controls and locking down the timing for reversals, it becomes second nature and genuinely satisfying.

The match variety here is mind blowing. From standard one-on-one singles to four-way action, the gameplay shines brightest, keeping the control tight, the pacing fantastic, and allowing you to execute dynamic back-and-forth sequences cleanly. However, once you max out the ring capacity with eight wrestlers, the in-ring action can become very chaotic and frustrating. An eight-person Money in the Bank ladder match can drag on for an eternity, where trying to set up ladders, grab weapons, or lock onto the right target becomes a chore when seven other AI opponents are constantly interrupting every action. Fortunately, overall match variety is exceptional, providing a massive suite of default match types alongside match customization rules so you can tweak almost any structure to your liking.

The Creation Suite remains the absolute bread and butter of the franchise. The community creators out there are absolute wizards, crafting ridiculously detailed custom wrestlers, real-world celebrities, superheroes, custom arenas, championships, and movesets. Thanks to Community Creations, you can completely overhaul the game into an AEW, WCW, TNA, or ECW simulator. For anyone who doesn't watch modern WWE, this mode single-handedly gives the game infinite replayability.

The various game modes offer a wide range of quality across the board. MyGM is easily my favorite mode in the game, and one I get completely addicted to. I’ve logged hours—if not days—drafting rosters, managing budgets, executing trades, booking rivalries, and growing my brand. It is addicting and easily the peak of the single-player experience for me personally.

On the other hand, Universe Mode remains pretty much unchanged from previous years, making it a total hit-or-miss affair where you get out of it what you put into it. Showcase Mode, which centers around the Samoan Dynasty this year, continues to be a format I'm just not fond of. The gameplay devolves into mindlessly following objective prompts at the top of the screen for a few hours when I'd much rather rewatch real historical matches, leaving its primary value as a tutorial and a requirement to unlock hidden wrestlers and arenas.

MyRise feels similarly tedious, relying heavily on simulated social media text walls where characters "tweet" back and forth to trigger random matches instead of delivering organic weekly television drama. Finally, MyFaction serves as the game's microtransaction-heavy, gacha-style card mode. Outside of popping in for a couple of easy achievements, I don't mess with it and have zero interest in engaging with its card-pack mechanics.

Because there is virtually no real competition in the wrestling video game genre, WWE 2K25 wins by default—but it earns its keep regardless. While the chaotic multi-man matches, static Showcase format, and text-heavy MyRise mode hold it back from absolute perfection, the refined gameplay, addictive MyGM mode, and unrivaled Creation Suite make it an easy recommendation.

[h1]The Best WWE 2K game currently available on Steam[/h1]

Unfortunately WWE 2K 24 has already been removed from sale... so this will probably be removed from sale sometime next year. If you like the WWE games, I would recommend getting it while you still can.

[h1]Story mode (My Rise)[/h1] 

The main reason I would recommend getting this game is that while other aspects of this game will come back in later iterations (WWE 2K 26 is basically the same game in most respects) the "My Rise" story modes are unique to each title and this one is the best in my opinion. 

Rather than the two paths available (face and heel) in 2K 26, this has three different personalities... and you play through the story as two different characters simultaneously who can have the same or different personalities. You also get different stories depending on which WWE superstars you choose as allies (just don't choose Drew McIntyre because his questline is extremely frustrating and sometimes bugged) and as you can imagine, this adds a LOT of replay value. In fact, I played through the story mode THREE TIMES and I am planning to do it again since I haven't seen everything yet. (Fortunately it has New Game +). 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3795290453

One of the things I really like about this game is that the renegade ending is actually much better than I expected it to be. The last time I remember being this pleasantly surprised by the secondary ending was with [i]Saint's Row 3.[/i]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3804454468

The one problem with the story mode (in common with all the WWE 2K games) is that it can get kind of annoying to complete some of the purely arbitrary match objectives needed to advance... and if you choose Drew McIntyre, this will reach its apex with a match objective which is almost impossible... and is sometimes bugged which means you might have to exit (to neutralize the bugs) and replay it over and over again until you get lucky. I did it eventually but I don't recommend choosing Drew McIntyre. 

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IhW830LEvww

Even if you skip Drew McIntyre however, there is a wealth of content in this story mode so I felt like it was a much better value than the My Rise mode in 2K 26.

[h1]Graphics and Character Creator[/h1]

This game is a slight improvement on 2K 24 (no longer available for purchase) and looks just as good as 2K 26. As a man, I honestly feel like the girls in here are the hottest characters in gaming because they look the most like real people AND some of them look very physically fit and strong such that they could literally survive the Stone Age. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3787901691

As with the other WWE 2K games, the character creator is very deep and it also links to the Community Creations section which not only allows you to share your own creations but also to download characters made by other people. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3792510328

[h1]Business Model[/h1]

I'm not a fan of the cancerous "My Faction" lootbox-based live-service mode (which will definitely get killed after 2K 27 comes out as the "My Faction" mode for 2K 24 is already nonfunctional) but at least the business model for this game is better than that for 2K 26 which is probably why it has a better user-rating. 

This game does NOT use a "Battle Pass" system (unlike 2K 26 which does) and a lot of the things that are locked behind the cancerous live service modes in WWE 2K 26 are unlocked by simply playing the game in 2K 25. 

For instance, I unlocked the unique character "The Manifestation" in this game by simply playing through the "My Rise" story mode". In contrast, unlocking the same character in 2K 26 required getting lucky with random lootboxes. 

[h1]Remote Play Together[/h1]

One thing I really like about this game (as well as WWE 2K 26 and 2K 24) is that Remote Play Together actually works... at least if the host has a good internet connection. (In my case, it works when I host but NOT when my bro does.) This really adds value to the game since it allows you to play coop in Tornado Tag against the computer. (For some weird reason you can't do that in normal online play) and that feature will keep the game alive in multiplayer even after they inevitably remove it from sale and kill the servers after 2K 27 comes out. (WWE 2K 24 is removed from sale but you can still play it with a friend via local multiplayer or Remote Play Together.) 

[h1]Roster[/h1]

I actually like the roster for this game better than that for the successor 2K 26 because that game removed some of the the best-looking characters (like Cora Jade) as well as some of the characters with the best theme music (like Carlito). The roster for this game really is impressive and you can add to that with infinitely many custom characters and downloaded characters as noted earlier. 

[h1]Music[/h1]

A lot of this music is good IMHO (I especially like Carlito's theme track) and you can choose what music will show up in menus, loading screens, etc. by choosing which tracks to play if you go to "Jukebox" in the main menu. This is a really cool feature which I really wish was in more games. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

This is a great game. So much so in fact that even if you haven't watched wrestling in years like me, this might draw you in. As someone who sunk a LOT of time into [i]Tekken, Soul Calibur,[/i] etc. I've found that I like this series much better and this title is the best one based on the three I've tried (2K 24, 2K 25, and 2K 26.)

After 2K Sports decided to introduce a Ring/Scamside Pass for WWE 2K26, effectively replacing content that had been an integral part of the game for years with a grinding system, I had no choice but to buy its predecessor, 2K25, which I had originally planned to skip after not playing 2K24. (The last one I played was 2K23.) Let me preface this by saying that buying 2K25 after 2K23 was definitely worth it for me!

As a classic wrestling fan of over two decades, I can say that WWE 2K25 is the best WWE 2K game in the entire series and plays better than any of its predecessors—mind you. Since the WWE 2K22 reboot, each WWE 2K game has built upon the previous one. The three WWE 2K games—WWE 2K23, WWE 2K24, and WWE 2K25—are the best of the modern era. With the new WWE 2K26, which introduced the Ringside Pass and is increasingly ruining the entire series with microtransactions, WWE 2K24 or WWE 2K25 are the only viable alternatives in 2026 for anyone wanting to play modern WWE games.

The improvements over its predecessors are primarily the minor gameplay mechanics in the matches, such as the return of intergender matches since WWE SmackDown! vs. RAW 2009, and some gimmick matches that have been added (Ambulance and Casket, already in 2K24, and the Bloodline match in 2K25). Of course, the game also has many negative aspects, such as the numerous MyFaction Persona characters, which are marked with many "???????"s on all selection screens and are a constant annoyance, reminding the player that even though they bought the most expensive edition, they still don't have all the content. These methods are a recurring nuisance when clicking through the many wrestlers.

Otherwise, the Showcase mode is a mixed bag. This story is narrated by wrestling promoter and legendary manager Paul Heyman, who has accompanied cover star "Tribal Chief" Roman Reigns in recent years. One of the best gimmicks of modern WWE, no doubt. Unfortunately, the Showcase mode featuring the family of Roman Reigns and The Rock was rather lackluster, and most of the matches were pure fantasy. I would have much preferred real matches from Roman Reigns' Bloodline between 2020 and 2024, rather than this fantasy scenario.

Also, all the matches, except for the Tamina Money in the Bank ladder match, were incredibly easy to play. The ladder match, on the other hand, was a nightmare, requiring what felt like 20 restarts. Paul Heyman nicely explained the intros for each match and wrestler, using old video clips.


Also, all the matches, except for the Tamina Money in the Bank ladder match, were incredibly easy to play. The centerpiece of this WWE 2K game, as in its predecessors since WWE 2K23 (especially since it was more like a demo in WWE 2K22), is the MyGM or General Manager mode. Here, you can choose one of seven brands (RAW, SmackDown!, NXT, NXT 2.0, WCW, ECW, or NXT Munity) and then select your preferred manager (including Eric Bischoff and Paul Heyman). This mode has been enhanced with numerous new features and offers the most long-term enjoyment, thanks to the game's excellent Creation Suite.

WWE2K25 answers many critiques of the last MyRise campaigns and solves them outright, but in the same breath, it creates a lot of new complaints that I hope are address in 26. 

I pretty much exclusively play these games, for the most ironic thing in the world, their story. The MyRise series is a legendary romp through WWE non-canon storylines that at times, really do rival the hype of the actual show. The 2K series never breaks kayfabe, even when it breaks the fourth wall. Overall, the gameplay is mostly the same and the new additions feel minimal or outright unnecessary and not-engaging. But truthfully, they have such little impact on the matches, that the new mechanics are pretty much irrelevant and not worth mentioning.

As always, this game is full of hundreds of hours of content in just single player alone and still has the greatest character creator in gaming. 

But MyRise this time around is a main event finisher with a lot of botches on the way. 

My critique of the last MyRise, despite it being arguably the best in 2K's history, was that it was too long and extremely poor in its pacing. And a lot of its dynamic elements were simply not there, the side content being practically absolutely mandatory. 25's 2K is very aware of the critiques, going so far into metahumour that it makes fun of the last game's male protagonist's hideous shirt. In fact, there is an entire fourth wall breaking moment where the player can recruit their own past 2K custom character cast. 

It is honestly pretty incredible and the humour is spot on. It is so rare to have a game where the devs talk to you directly and indirectly at the same time. 2K really pleads its case and thesis of them simply doing their best, but always being willing to get better, do better and deliver more. They heard the critiques of the hideous casual ware of the last games and gave us the blessing to wear our own clothes. At the same time, 2K uses its previous protagonist characters to answer critique truthfully and honestly, it is hard not to agree with the devs. The games provide a lot of modes and customization options to play the game exactly as you want it, and MyRise was always tailored to its storylines. 

The game itself even suggests that players are at times, very unsure of what they are asking for and that is entirely right. So I am frankly glad the developers knew what to listen to and what to discard as merely baseless criticism or just effortless complaining about a mostly linear storymode. 

That being said, this MyRise absolved itself of many past sins, but indulged in some new ones. It feels like you only play as your protagonists for 60% of the game. Now, there are multiple routes, some very dynamic choices and entirely new lanes of content to explore, but its still frustrating when you spend hours hand crafting two wrestlers for this campaign and then you end up doing 4-5 to sometimes 6! 6! Consecutive cameo matches as an established, existing superstar. If these mini arcs only gave us one match, it would be fine. 

In retrospect, I think people were complaining there was too many original character-focused gameplay in the last MyRise and I sort of get that. The MyRise of 24, for both campaigns, is oppressively, overly long at 30 some hours for a single playthrough of each. Both those campaigns overstayed their welcome by about 40% of their content. But above all, people seemed to loathe the persona focus (which this game rightfully states that its more realistic that wrestlers experiment with personas and I agree), but what made that work was the fact it was still our character at the end of the day we were playing. Some people have residual trauma from 23's THE LOCK, who, yes, is in the game.

2K is aware that despite everything, there is a tremendous amount of nostalgia around their characters and even their mistakes. And honestly, this MyRise's sins are very forgivable. 

The last game had us playing a lot as Psycho Sally, who is either absolutely loved by the fanbase or hated beyond all reason to the point she didn't even cameo here. But I think the solution was not to replace such circumstantial character arcs with establish superstar dramas, even though the nostalgia is surely there for some, they simply overstay their welcome. It genuinely feels like the entire middle third of this game is nostalgic fan fiction instead of the self insert empowerment fan fic drama we play MyRise for. 

In the last MyRise, I desperately wanted to be able to betray our player character in favour of redeeming her via switching to Psycho Sally. Thankfully, the entire concept of 25 is this. Creating two allied characters for the Men's Division and Women's Division and then seeing how they come together and eventually come apart. 

The first third starts off so strong and damn near perfect, but it concludes the Mutiny arc too quickly in the final third. And yes, the concept of this year's MyRise is not just the inter-gender competitions (although it is really great they brought this into the games and its a fundamental asset of the MyRise campaign and overall gameplay) but a Mutiny from NXT, leading to an Invasion arc, forcing Raw and Smackdown into a United Front. Its actually really engaging stuff with a lot less BLOAT from the past MyRises, but its sadly sidelined by so much filler in the middle part. 

And by the very end, the main arc concludes often on a weekday show and Wrestlemania's conclusion feels like a squash match against yourself and its not too satisfying. I know that replaying the game two more times brings us to a more proper conclusion but it is a terrible way of encouraging replayability. 

So, overall, is any of it bad? Nope, it is not even a step back as much as it is just a mid-match botch and a less than stellar main event. Overall, these games are ridiculously fun and I had some genuine laughs with the meta humour, the many, many 2K game original wrestler cameos and the comedic character-route is genuinely hilarious. 

Also, 24 had the worst menu soundtrack in the entire series. 25 is a tremendous front flip forward and has nothing but great song choices. Huge kudos on that. 

All in all, its definitely worth playing if you happen to have it already. And the gimmick of the MyRise is certainly worth a playthrough, just maybe not three.
