If you're looking for a cheap, straightforward tower defense fix or a game where you get to play as the villain, this is the game for you.

Oh My Gore!, developed by bumblebee. and published by Daedalic Entertainment, is a strategy game that takes familiar tower defense mechanics and flips their perspective in a way that feels both playful and slightly chaotic. Instead of protecting a kingdom from invading forces, you step into the role of the aggressor, commanding monstrous armies and carving a destructive path through enemy territory. This inversion of roles is not just a cosmetic change; it shapes how the game is approached, turning traditional defensive thinking into something more aggressive and opportunistic.

The gameplay is built around a hybrid structure that merges offensive wave deployment with defensive planning. Players must generate resources, summon units, and send them along different routes toward enemy strongholds, all while constructing towers and traps to defend their own base from retaliation. This dual responsibility creates a constant balancing act. Focusing too heavily on offense can leave your defenses vulnerable, while overcommitting to defense can stall your progress and allow the enemy to regroup. The ability to direct units across branching paths adds a tactical layer, encouraging players to adapt their approach based on enemy behavior and map layout rather than relying on a single strategy.

A notable feature of the game is its use of champions, each bringing a distinct set of abilities and specialized units to the battlefield. Choosing a champion influences how a mission unfolds, as different abilities can dramatically change the effectiveness of certain strategies. This adds an element of pre-mission planning, where players must consider not only the map but also their own playstyle. While the system introduces variety, it remains relatively accessible, avoiding the complexity that might overwhelm players who are less familiar with strategy games.

Progression follows a straightforward but effective formula. Completing missions rewards experience that can be invested into upgrades, unlocking new abilities or enhancing existing ones. This gradual improvement helps maintain a sense of momentum, especially as later levels introduce more challenging scenarios that require better resource management and more precise decision-making. The campaign offers a reasonable amount of content, and the inclusion of different difficulty settings allows players to tailor the challenge to their preferences.

Visually, the game leans into a retro-inspired pixel art style, but with a deliberately exaggerated and chaotic presentation. Battles quickly fill the screen with explosions, blood effects, and collapsing structures, creating a sense of constant motion and destruction. While the environments themselves are relatively simple, the clarity of the visuals ensures that players can easily track units and threats during hectic moments. The overall aesthetic embraces a kind of dark humor, reinforcing the idea that the game is not meant to be taken too seriously.

The audio design supports this tone, though it is less memorable than the visuals. Sound effects are functional and help convey the intensity of combat, but they can become repetitive over time. Music tracks fit the game’s pace but rarely stand out, serving more as background accompaniment than as a defining feature. This does not significantly detract from the experience, but it does mean that the audio lacks the same personality as the visual presentation.

Where Oh My Gore! begins to show its limitations is in its long-term depth. While the core mechanics are engaging, they do not evolve significantly over the course of the game. Missions can start to feel similar, and once players become familiar with effective strategies, there is less incentive to experiment. The novelty of playing as the antagonist carries much of the experience, but it cannot fully compensate for the relatively limited variety in gameplay systems.

Despite this, the game remains enjoyable for what it sets out to do. Its accessible mechanics and unique perspective make it easy to pick up and play, and its combination of offense and defense provides enough variety to keep players engaged through the campaign. It may not offer the complexity or longevity of more advanced strategy titles, but it delivers a focused and entertaining experience that stands out through its concept alone.

In the end, Oh My Gore! is a creative take on a well-established genre, offering a satisfying mix of strategy and chaotic action wrapped in a humorous, villain-centered package. It succeeds in delivering a fresh perspective, even if it does not fully expand on that idea over time. For players looking for a light but engaging strategy game with a twist, it provides a solid and enjoyable experience.

I like tower defense games but I don't like reverse tower defense at all. This game has both elements. You build towers to defend from enemy waves, but you also have to recruit units to send to the enemies base because the game won't end until their fortress or hero unit is defeated. I probably could've looked past the reverse defense part if the rest of the game was good but it was pretty imbalanced. Of all the units in the game the Minotaur is so grossly OP it basically dictates the entire game once they start to appear. They have high HP and high DPS while doing that same high damage to both units and buildings. This completely wrecks a lot of the game. When the enemy uses them tower defense becomes almost futile. They will walk up to your towers and destroy them in as little as 4 hits, and if the send 2+ at a time there's almost no counter in the early missions, and while towers can be upgraded higher stats it's almost discourage by the minotaurs existence. Why spend 200g to upgrade a tower that a minotaur can still kill in 5 hits and you'll have to spend 400g to rebuild, repairing them also takes too much money and never keeps them alive. You're better off just rebuilding behind them as they work on your other towers. On the other hand when you use them they'll steamroll the enemy as well. Saving up food to put 1-2 Minotaurs in your attack waves is basically necessary to win. 

Other imbalanced things that really took the fun out of it for me were the random event enemies, Woody and Albert, these guys spawn randomly around the map sometimes, they're completely invulnerable, and one shot any unit or tower they come across. Even worse is Woody shows up in the one map that doesn't let you use units so him destroying your towers as you're trying to defend 3 separate lanes while also worrying about Minotaurs is just frustrating. The spells are imbalanced too, the harpy spell just feels superior to me, some levels can even be cheesed because you can spam that spell on the final boss or building and kill it from a distance. Traps are basically worthless, they have the same cost as a tower but they have a limited capacity for damage. Once they do their max damage they clog up and are permanently disabled, you can't sell or replace them, so if you misplaced one early on it could even stop you from maximizing your ground space later in the level. The towers themselves are a mess, for more end game enemies (and the minotaur) they don't do enough damage to really finish units off. The gargoyle tower that are prevalent in most of the steam pictures seems to be the best, it has a high range and when leveled up is one of the only reliable ways to finish off minotaurs by setting it to target high HP.

Lastly the design choices for the game were kind of annoying to me. The game uses devouring pits and dead ends which aren't fun at all. When the game makes a dead end it'll put a pit in it that your units will walk into that kills them instantly and refunds 20% of the food it cost to recruit them. This sucks even on normal levels but one level is a maze that requires you to find 3 temples. This thing has tons of dead ends and the entire mission is just you testing paths randomly, watching your units get eaten, changing to the next path and trying again, it's completely tedious. After that there is a mission that has an insanely long path to the objective and even with the double speed option can take units an eternity to get through. The story is okay the ending tried to be a twist I guess, I didn't really understand what the masterminds plan was or why it had to be done in such a convoluted way. The game translation is a bit rough, there are bits and pieces of broken English but it's not enough to prevent someone from understanding it, that said one line was still in German which was weird.

Oh My Gore! offers a surprisingly fresh take on the tower defense genre. It’s cheap as chips at base price and a total steal on sale, especially given the sheer amount of gameplay you get for your money.

The gory pixel art perfectly complements the narrative and its comedic undertones. Between the in-game encyclopedia and the mission interludes, the writing is genuinely funny—it definitely earned a few real-life chuckles from me.

​​Mechanically, the game doesn't rely purely on defense; there is a heavy emphasis on offensive play, too. This dual approach quickly turns levels into absolute bloodbaths, leaving the battlegrounds completely littered with elf intestines, broken angelic wings, and pools of blood.

Your arsenal will be instantly familiar to any genre connoisseur. You have your standard traps like acid pools and spike pits, alongside a selection of towers. Honestly, the tower designs and mechanics are nothing special—they are perfectly serviceable, which is totally fine, just not groundbreaking.

​For the price, you really can't go wrong here, especially if you're a fan of the genre. Once you figure out the optimal tower combinations, it is relatively easy to cheese the game. But during that initial learning curve—before you break the meta—you’ll have a hell of a time. It is just flat-out fun.

The Rundown:
-Fun game similar to Kingdom Rush.
-*Pretty easy to get all achievements on.
-Short but sweet.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Oh My Gore! is a mediocre gore/horror themed 2D retro pixel tower defense game with an amazing gimmick... you play the "bad guys".  Yeah, it's been done to death.  This is a routine TD where you get pretty free tower placement and a few spells/abilities to dump on mobs as well so you don't get too bored between building towers.  There's dozens if not hundreds of TD's on Steam and this one doesn't stand out. 

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

The artwork here is terrible, it's a blend of old retro pixel "art" used as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics, and some of the most amateurish MS-Paint style drawings I've ever hurt my eyes on.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget to arrange someone who can do graphics properly, or lack of talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result of these decisions.

While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.

The developers didn't design the game for modern gaming PCs, as such the display resolution caps out at 1080p, a very low resolution that became mainstream back in 2006 and became obsolete when 4K entered the mainstream in 2014.  The game simply won't look right on modern gaming displays due to this failure on the part of the developers.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Oh My Gore! didn't appeal much to the people who own a copy of the game, either.  It has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the game didn't really capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is for killing 100 elves, you can get that within 10 minutes of playing (with your eyes closed), but only around 11 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the game.  Hardly a success story, gamers just weren't all that interested in the game.

Reviewing SteamDB to check how popular this game was with players reveals a surprise... there's a very healthy spike in player counts for the game.  But this isn't consistent with the achievement stats, that show only 11 percent of players bothered playing the game for any reasonable amount of time.  How is it possible for this game to have so many concurrent players who weren't even playing the game?  Trading cards.  Players will use card idling software to collect the cards and sell them, but this won't trigger any achievements in-game.  That tells us people only really bought this game for trading cards, and that's a damning indictment of the woeful quality.  A closer look at the numbers shows the game just has a couple of players every week running up the game and idling it for cards, then deleting it.  We must ask how it benefits gamers for there to be so many games like this, with no merit as a serious game, that only generate sales from people idling and selling the trading cards.

[h1] Great Concept, Shoddy Execution [/h1]

First, one thing I want to make clear. This game doesn't take 72 hours to beat, I simply left it on for long periods of time. Second, this is a negative review, so why did I even bother finishing the game? Because I have a compulsion to finish games once I start them unless they are literally unplayable. Don't be like me.

Now, onto the game. This is a hybrid where you build towers and send monsters out of your barracks to attack. The only control you have over the monsters is which direction/path they take when encountering intersections, I really like the idea for the game, but the developers did a poor job of implementing it.

The AI in this game is pretty wonky. You will experience moments where your units will destroy a tower or kill an enemy and then just turn around confused before eventually reorienting themselves and going the right way again. The units also stack on top of each other, so visually you often can't tell how many units are actually in one spot.

Managing towers quickly becomes unsatisfying as well. Many of your towers do not have a range greater than 2, with only one tower with a range of 4. This isn't terrible at first, but eventually you encounter enemies that prioritize targeting towers instead of units. These units are very strong and typically take down your towers in moments. Additionally, the places that you can and cannot place towers often make no sense and prevent you from using them to the fullest. You'll see positions where you want to place a tower, only to learn that this pile of bones or whatever the developer has chosen to add to the map blocks you, or that you can place towers in places where they can never actually hit enemies. There are traps that you can place on the ground, but they damage your units too so good luck using those effectively. Combined with the odd paths created, it just comes off as sloppy, like no one played through the game themselves to iron out these pain points.

Many of the units and towers are useless or at least inferior to others. I was curious if anyone else had this experience and saw that someone beat the game on Hard by using just one unit, the Minotaur. I was already using this unit primarily, but just to test it I did the same. So that's one unit that can likely carry you through the game. The towers are much the same, with the fire towers and gargoyle boulder throwers being the only useful ones you really need. 

The story is already nothing to write home about, and it is made worse by the mediocre English translation. There was one part where the text wasn't even in English for me, but German ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2191628713]Screenshot here[/url]). The story itself is confusing and the ending was very unsatisfying. It's sloppy, and again makes it seem as though no one played through the game.

You may be looking at this game and thinking "This looks interesting, and it's so cheap!" Don't bother. There are better tower defense games and better ways to spend your time and money. Move on and don't waste either.

Oh My Gore! seemed like a game tailor-made for me. I love tower defense, copious gore, and I far prefer being a villain than a hero, especially whenever you can be a necromancer. Oh My Gore! features all of this, but unfortunately, I found it fell far short of what I wanted in terms of tower defense.

Oh My Gore! has beautiful old school graphics, dark humor, and interesting locations and music. However, its problems begin with its lack of direction. Because the store page advertises it as tower defense and I'm well-versed in the genre, I started looking out for pathways and strategic places to set particular towers. It soon became clear that Oh My Gore! is a very weird mix of tower defense and tug-of-war strategy games. The tower defense part of the game is only half (one could argue even less) of the gameplay, and the game doesn't do a particularly good job of telling you what the goal is for each level. For example, one early level tasks you with razing a town, but it doesn't tell you how to do that before it starts sending waves of goodly warriors at you. Do you defeat so many waves of warriors? No. You have to send your own warriors down the same path, get to the town, and destroy particular buildings. You have no control over your warriors or even your hero.

The tower defense part of the game isn't very good at what it does, either. Sure, there are some interesting towers, but nothing we haven't seen in other games of the genre, and the large pathways make it difficult to place your towers in a worthwhile place. The game also gives you traps to play with, but because you're sending waves of your own soldiers down the same path, you risk harm to your own units. Also, traps deplete in health over time (poison pools get smaller, etc.). The towers can be upgraded in a generic fashion (improvements to damage, range, etc., but no upgrade pathways). The game doesn't alert you of this, nor does it tell you that goodly units can utterly destroy your towers until one is already gone. This becomes more of a problem in levels where there are multiple pathways and multiple barracks. Basically, you must fight the flow of enemies on multiple paths, utilizing towers and waves of your own units (who take from the same small resource pool). Making this more frustrating to do is the map navigation, where you must scroll for a while to check on multiple paths and waste precious seconds.

Oh My Gore! isn't a terrible game. It's just not great at tower defense, which is the element I looked forward to most. If you're someone who loves tower defense games with a twist (like Bardbarian, which I also didn't care for), you might like this. But I find that changing the genre to such an extreme degree makes it lose sight of its identity and the main reasons why I play TD games. Oh My Gore! is beautiful, particularly when enemies collapse in giblets and blood overwhelms a path. But try as I might, I failed to have any [i]fun.[/i]

This is a cautious recommendation if you like tower defense but are looking for something a bit different. How 'Oh My Gore!' differs itself from the competition is via the introduction of RTS elements that force you to take a proactive approach to winning, no longer do you sit behind your turrets and wait for the waves to end, you need to recruit your own minions and send them against the enemy's defenses to destroy his shit before he does the same to you. 

Now I'll admit that I've only played a few hours but the game isn't that long overall, it mostly has a 20 mission campaign with 3 levels of difficulty and the primary focus is on it's cheesy retro villain-protagonist-turned-hero narrative and the only aspect of the game I was let down by are some of the core tower defense mechanics. Defenses are just too squishy, most enemy units ignore your defenses and get slaughtered, as they should, but the Minotaur is simply OP. He's introduced early, he ignores pathfinding (ie he can freely wander around the map), and he can destroy even the highest HP towers with just a couple hits. 

There is no hard counter to any of the unit types or classes which leaves me feeling a bit empty when it comes to planning out my defenses. I don't have to consider the downsides to each tower before I place them because, when spammed, the differences are largely negligible, which I personally feel was a sorely missed opportunity. The upside of this is you also have access to the OP Minotaur so the enemy defenses are going down fast as well. 

Aside from that the game is overall fun and enjoyable, the art style is consistent and well animated, the game has a dope guitar-heavy soundtrack and the idea of blending a couple of genres is compelling to me because it's nice to see developers try something new.

Misty Judgment, developed and published by 次元边界, is an atmospheric interactive mystery game that delves deeply into themes of memory, identity, and trust. Set against the backdrop of a contemporary urban environment, it follows the protagonist Qi Yi, who awakens with amnesia amid a series of unsettling murders and conspiracies. The narrative unfolds in a richly layered way, challenging players to navigate through fragmented memories, piece together clues, and unravel not only the external mystery but also the protagonist’s own fractured psyche. This dual focus on psychological exploration and investigative gameplay gives the experience a unique emotional depth and complexity.

The gameplay mechanics blend traditional detective work with interactive storytelling and decision-making. Players are encouraged to explore detailed environments, collect evidence, and interrogate a diverse cast of characters, each harboring their own secrets and motives. The choices made in conversations and investigations shape the story’s trajectory, often leading to multiple branching paths and endings. This episodic format serves both to keep the gameplay fresh and to gradually deepen the narrative, rewarding patient players who pay attention to detail and character nuance. The game balances puzzle-solving with emotional storytelling, ensuring that no decision feels superficial or inconsequential.

One of Misty Judgment’s most distinctive features is its use of full-motion video (FMV) sequences, which add a cinematic quality that elevates the storytelling. Real actors bring the characters to life with nuanced performances that convey tension, vulnerability, and suspicion. The production values are notably high, with careful attention to lighting, set design, and cinematography that amplify the game’s moody and suspenseful atmosphere. This FMV integration creates a seamless blend between gameplay and narrative, immersing players more deeply than traditional graphic or text-based mysteries might allow. The moody visuals and evocative sound design work in tandem to heighten the feeling of unease and uncertainty that pervades the game.

The characters in Misty Judgment are intricately crafted, each adding layers of complexity to the unfolding story. Figures such as Su Yunyao, the sharp and determined reporter; Zhao Yan, the enigmatic painter with a troubled past; and Wen Yishu, the secretive neighbor with ambiguous allegiances, serve as both allies and potential suspects. Interactions with these characters are pivotal, not only for gathering information but also for building relationships that influence the story’s outcome. The game challenges players to carefully weigh whom to trust and when to push for answers, creating a tense psychological dance that reinforces the core themes of deception and hidden truths.

Exploration and investigation are key gameplay pillars, with players navigating a variety of environments from shadowy apartments to rain-slicked city streets. The pacing is deliberately measured, inviting players to immerse themselves in the details of each scene and conversation rather than rushing toward conclusions. This slow-burn approach allows for a gradual buildup of suspense and provides room for players to reflect on the clues and narratives they uncover. While some may find this deliberate pacing challenging, it enhances the game’s immersive quality and supports its narrative ambitions.

The sound design further enriches the experience, with a subtle and evocative soundtrack that shifts tone fluidly between moments of quiet tension and dramatic confrontation. Ambient sounds—from distant city noises to the rustle of leaves—ground the player in the game world, while voice acting delivers emotional weight and authenticity to every character interaction. These audio elements work cohesively with the visual storytelling to create a compelling sensory experience that lingers beyond the gameplay itself.

While Misty Judgment has been praised for its storytelling and atmosphere, it is not without its challenges. Some players have noted that the slow pacing and heavy reliance on dialogue and exploration can feel daunting, particularly for those more accustomed to fast-paced gameplay. The complexity of the branching narrative also demands careful attention to detail, which may not appeal to everyone. Nevertheless, for players who enjoy intricate mysteries and psychological drama, these aspects add depth rather than frustration, making the eventual unraveling of the story all the more rewarding.

In summary, Misty Judgment stands out as a thoughtful and immersive entry in the interactive mystery genre. Its blend of cinematic FMV storytelling, richly developed characters, and meaningful player choice crafts an experience that is as emotionally engaging as it is intellectually stimulating. For fans of detective stories that challenge perception and invite deep involvement in the narrative, Misty Judgment offers a haunting journey through memory and truth that will resonate long after the final scene.

Thousands of unskipable animations that look cool the first few times. The game advertises itself with the "amazing" nemesis system and of course it spams captains like crazy. No matter how many captains you kill, they will keep getting replaced. Until you can dominate them, but even then they'll betray you eventually, so you have infinite amount of captain battles to look forward to. Problem is, you have to listen to their monologues. Every. Fucking. Time. So yeah, literally thousands of unskipable animations just by fighting captains. But even when you try to organize your army you have to watch them roar and slowly walk and shit when they react to your orders. Then there is the arena. Funny to watch it a few times. Super boring to watch if you want to upgrade your entire army. Painful to watch when you send a marksman, because it will almost always try to fight in melee. Oh and I almost forgot, sometimes you need to get some health back and are unlucky to have a worm nearby? Bad luck, because draining them comes with an unskipable animation and when it ends, you'll be hit by an attack that you could've defended against without the dumb cinematic. Or the same thing is happening when a new captain ambushes you mid-fight. Quite often you get hit after his dumb monologue. Highly doubt the devs played their own game or they would've noticed how dumb this is.

Then there is the problem with the controls. Game was designed for console peasants. Every button has multiple functions and the game quite often decides to use the wrong function when you press that button. For example I try to drop down a ledge without jumping to the other side of the world? Press E. Oh but I'm sneaking, so that means E is sneak dominate. Time to jump to the other side of the universe, because there is an orc there barely on the edge of my screen. Amazing. Also it's called "sneak dominate" but it's loud as fuck and everyone is running to investigate afterwards. Rofl. Also during fights, more often than not you're facing a dozen orcs closely hugging each other. You try to jump over one of them. Good luck trying to tell the game which one you had in mind. I'm pretty sure the WASD buttons do the selection instead of the mouse, which would allow you to fine tune your aiming. I once tried to simply hit a caragor pen's gate with my sword. Faced it. Pressed W and simply clicked. My character attacked an orc behind him. Repeated it like 10 times before giving up. Retarded.

Then there are game breaking bugs. Twice I found myself inside a wall after draining or dominating and orc who was standing next to it. First time I fell out of the map and died. Second time I just got stuck inside the wall and had to leave the game.

I spent hours AFK in the game so the ~30 hours is a bit of a lie and I'm pretty sure I've spend hours watching dumb animations I would've rather skipped (especially with the arena fights). And I've found myself quite often being fucking mad instead of enjoying the game.

Okay, I played this game directly after Shadow of Mordor so maybe that left me a little jaded on some aspects of the game, but I will do my best to list all of my issues with the game because there is a LOT I have an issue with, and the moments of fun I did have do not make up for the annoyance I felt with this game a lot of the time.

So, story first, while the story of the first game was not anything special itself, this game's story is also just as unremarkable. If the first game's story was white bread, this game is white bread with butter. But it also suffers the sign of being so incredibly transparent while trying to be a surprise. If you know literally anything about middle-earth, you will be able to call the ending from the very opening cutscene of the game. and while some parts were interesting, like learning the identities behind the previously unnamed Nazgul, that doesn't do enough to make the rest of it engaging.

Next is the general gameplay with the combat, they tried to make the combat more defined into it's own thing in this game rather than a direct copy of the freeflow combat system from the Arkham games, and while I appreciate the attempt, it does fall flat a lot of the time because of the way things magnetise occassionally and wiff other times, and if you try to use a combat finisher or a dodge during the fight, you can almost garentee that Talion will run through the 5 people in his path to attempt it on the one person among them who is either immune to the finishers, or will punish the dodge attempt.

Another gameplay issue I had, and why I prefaced this by saying I played SoM directly before this game, is the skills available to you. A lot of the skills you get in this game either should have been wrapped into the base kit originally such as counters gaining might, or should have been base kit because you literally just had access to those abilities in the last game and this game takes place directly after, such as the combat finisher. I can understand if the wraith abilities were diminished to begin with because of where the story begins, but Talion's actual combat should still be at it's pinnacle up to that moment. It seems that rather than increasing your arsenal beyond what you had previously, you spend the first 20 or so level ups getting back things you should have already had. Now alongside of this is a new addition to the game in the form of aquirable gear, and while there are aspects of this that is enjoyable, I will state my issues with them in a moment.

But that's the moment to moment gameplay, now onto my issues with the bigger picture. The Sieges and fort build ups in the game. I enjoyed the sieges, I enjoyed seeing that by investing time to infiltrate the fortress first and building up an army outside the fort too, you can dominate these raids easily. What is NOT enjoyable however, is doing it 5 fucking times of starting from scratch in a region and building it all up again.

And finally, the big draw of this series, the thing everyone wishes wasn't patented. The nemesis system. So. The pros first. Increased orc diversity in giving them clans and classes rather than just the 5 main weapon types having names, and with the addition of ologs as enemies into the game, also being added to the nemesis system adds a lot more variety in generated orcs. The cons. It doesn't work well. Every orc captain seems to defy death so rather than being a unique occassional thing from the higher tier or more special orcs, it becomes a head ache of 'yay, a fight so nice I did it twice' only this time, because of the addition of adaptation into the nemeses learning your fight patterns and adapting to them, they are even more of a pain in the ass to kill, because another thing is, the nemesis system will not give you all the information you need when going into a fight, even with intel unlike the previous entry. got a defender in front of you were the counterplay is to vault over them? SURPRISE VAULT BREAKER, so you try to stun them instead? NOPE! Frost proof! so instead of engaging in fights half the time, a lot of fights boil down to stealth attack, run and lose detection, stealth attack, rather than actually being able to engage meaningfully. AND THEN THEY DEFY DEATH ANYWAY AND IT DRAWS OUT EVEN LONGER. and this was a consistent experience I had with this system that made me hate engaging with a lot of the captains I was getting.

And that leads into my issues with the gear system. There is an emphasis in this game for collecting the legendary gear from the higher tier orcs to get the full collection to proc some new gimmick to toy around with, the issue is that you then have some gear sets that are actually a detriment to you rather than an aide in a fair few fights because it can randomly proc rage effects on the captain and mean you spend the next 30 seconds to a minute just spamming dodge because they hit like a truck and cannot be countered in that state, so you either have to commit to gear that can actively make your life harder, accept sub par gear and miss out on the effects of the gathered collection, or micromanage your armour and skills every single fight fight, which on it's own isn't fun, but when you add the awful menuing experience in this game to it too, it isn't fun.

And the greatest sin this game commited. IT MADE FIGHTING A BALROG BORING. HOW?!?!?!

So in short. I had occassional fun with this game, but that did not overall counter the sheer annoyance and boredom I got with a lot of this game and the headache of feeling like I could not actually fight in this war and had to just keep running away in a war. The first game may have been barebones and a bit more streamline, but at least the game didn't lie to me and made the mistakes feel like my fault rather than throw me in a fight against enemies I can't counterplay.

The story takes some creative liberties with Tolkien's lore, which might not sit well with everyone.

Overall:

Shadow of War builds on the excellent foundation of Shadow of Mordor and turns it into a much bigger experience. The combat is addictive, the Nemesis System is better than ever, and creating your own army adds a whole new layer of entertainment.

It occasionally suffers from trying to do too much, but the freedom to approach encounters in different ways keeps things interesting.

Highly recommended.

Sid Meier’s Civilization III Complete — A Beautifully Stubborn Classic

Most strategy games make you feel like a god looking down on the world. Civilization III makes you feel like you’re uncovering an ancient civilisation, one decision at a time.

Released in 2001, this game has a personality that many modern strategy games struggle to capture. Its graphics are dated, its mechanics can be unforgiving, and its presentation belongs to another generation. Yet somehow, that’s part of its charm.

Playing Civilization III on my modern HP Snapdragon laptop has been an adventure in itself. Getting a game this old running on today’s hardware isn’t always straightforward. Compatibility settings, unusual screen resolutions and occasional freezing can make the experience frustrating. But once the game gets going, there’s something genuinely special underneath those technical difficulties.

The world feels unpredictable. Borders slowly expand, unexplored territory hides potential discoveries, and every new settlement represents another step towards building something greater.

I particularly enjoy the sense of exploration. Sending Warriors into unknown territory, discovering other civilisations, establishing new cities and watching a small settlement gradually develop into an empire is surprisingly satisfying.

There’s also something wonderful about the game’s atmosphere. Its old-fashioned visuals, distinctive music and detailed Civilopedia give it a sense of history that newer graphics alone cannot reproduce.

And Civilization III isn’t particularly forgiving. Poor decisions have consequences. Expansion takes planning, resources matter, and even a seemingly small mistake can affect your civilisation’s future.

What makes Civilization III special isn’t how it looks. It’s how much freedom it gives you to shape your own history.

It’s not perfect. The age of the software shows, especially when trying to play it on modern computers. The interface can feel awkward, and compatibility issues can interrupt an otherwise enjoyable experience.

But beneath those imperfections is a remarkably engaging strategy game that still has something to offer more than two decades after its release.

Civilization III doesn’t need modern graphics to prove its worth. Its depth, atmosphere and challenging gameplay speak for themselves.

A brilliant, sometimes frustrating, beautifully stubborn piece of gaming history.

⭐ Recommended — especially for players who enjoy exploration, empire-building and classic turn-based strategy.

Civilization III is undeniably dated, frequently unfair, and sometimes exhausting. It is also, in my opinion, still the best game in the series.

My Steam playtime is comparable to what I have accumulated in Civilization V and VI, but that number barely reflects how much time I have actually spent with the game. Long before I owned it digitally, I played thousands of hours from a physical disc that was eventually worn down by years of use.

There is no shortage of flaws. The limited resolution makes the game feel its age, while the AI manages to be both shamelessly cheating and absolutely incompetent. It begins with advantages, appears to produce units from nowhere, and readily coordinates with other civilizations against the player. Despite all of that, it may still ignore an exposed city in order to attack some strategically irrelevant unit nearby.

Combat can be equally unforgiving. Unit strength improves your odds, but never guarantees an outcome. In theory, an elite tank should have nothing to fear from a primitive barbarian warrior. In practice, the RNG may decide otherwise. Losing an advanced unit to something that should barely be able to damage it is absurd, memorable, and occasionally infuriating.

Yet many of the game’s limitations are also part of its appeal. Civ III lacks most of the systems added by later entries: there is no religion, no World Congress, no hex grid, and no one-unit-per-tile restriction. Victory conditions other than domination often feel secondary, and the late game is largely an escalating cycle of production, expansion, and war.

That sounds simplistic, but it gives the game a focus that its successors sometimes lack. In newer Civilization games, I often reach a stage where victory is already certain, yet the game continues for dozens of turns. Armies become trapped in gridlock and cultural or scientific victories turn into extended waiting periods, even if it is clear, that nobody can challenge you anymore. The difficult part is no longer winning; it is finding the patience to reach the victory screen.

Civ III is not exactly streamlined. A single late-game turn can take an hour when enormous doomstacks of units need to be moved individually. The AI will defend its final cities with tooth and nail send wave after wave of units into your territory. To survive, you respond by building equally armies of your own.

It is slow, messy, and at times more like administrative work than entertainment. But it also creates moments that no later entry has managed to reproduce. Few things in the series give you the same dopamine rush as earning your first Great Leader and forming an army.

For all its age and rough edges, Civilization III remains the Civilization game I am most likely to finish—and the one I am always tempted to start again.

They changed so little and yet it plays so much differently compared to Civ 2.  If you wanted to develop tiles in Civ 2, you needed to build settlers and make them work.  Now, every time you take an enemy city, you enslave multiple workers, so each and every turn involves giving orders to literally dozens of workers.

It takes 1 slave 6 turns to build a road, but it takes 6 slaves 1 turn to build a road.  So each turn you move those slaves 1 square up and then the next turn you click "build road" for EACH of those 6 slaves.  I must have clicked "build road" over a thousand times in the course of my most recent game.  That seems like what you're doing the majority of the time that you're playing this game, ordering slave units to build roads/mines/irrigation.  Does that sound like Civ, or fun?

Military support is higher and they added a really dumb mechanic that works like this: every time you kill an enemy unit, there's a 1 in 16 chance that you get a "great leader" unit.  This unit works much like 70's-90's children's cartoons, such as Power Rangers, Captain Planet, Voltron, or Transformers.  I mockingly call it the Voltron mechanic and name each of these great leaders things like "Captain Planet," "Megazord," "Optimus Prime," and "Voltron."  The great leader literally "combines" with 3 or 4 of your other military units to form a super unit called an "army" with over a dozen hit points.  It's basically god until the AI has units that can stop it.

It can't uncombine either, those units are permanently fused together, unlike in the children's cartoons. 
 Destroying rival cities with Voltron is trivial.  Victory on the highest difficulty absolutely relies on this 1 in 16 dice roll landing in your favor early, multiple times.  You can never afford to slow down military operations.  This makes the game play much, much more like a military expansionist, paint-the-map game than Civ 1 or 2 played.  It's not as fun.  It's still a bit fun, don't get me wrong, but it really has no excuse to be such a backwards side-step from Civ 2.

Then there's the "strategic resources" mechanic that they also added.  Researching the required techs for the next, more advanced military unit is no longer enough to build that unit.  You also must connect roads to squares within your borders that contain "strategic resources" required for building your units.  There are quite a few of these resources that you WILL eventually need, and until you research their respective techs, you won't even know if you have these resources in your territory or not.  On my most recent game, there was only 1 horse square on my entire continent, which was the biggest continent and 40% of the whole map.  I also had only 1 coal square on the whole continent.

This is why you can never afford to slow down, militarily.  You must expand and keep those resources under your control and protected.  The more armies you have, the easier that is to accomplish, and once again, acquiring those army units relies on winning that 1 in 16 dice roll.

Due to these changes, constant expansion is the only option from the start of the game all the way to the end, unless you want to end up without the strategic resources required for the units you'll need to win the game.  In Civ 2, I tended to go military/expansionist for a while and then "cash out," go democracy, full focus on science, and build the ship parts until I got a spaceship to Alpha Centauri before any other civ could.  That's never the smartest thing to do any longer b/c taking rival cities doesn't just keep getting harder as the game goes on, it gets easier.

You could afford to start losing ground in Civ 2 to aggressive, militaristic opponents b/c all you needed was those ship parts to win the game.  In Civ 3, you could easily lose access to the very few strategic resource squares that are NEEDED to build ship parts if you aren't constantly expanding and upgrading your military.

At first and for quite some time, your new cities only have access to the squares IMMEDIATELY adjacent to them.  This reduces the number of squares in a city's radius from 21 in Civ 2 to only 8 in Civ 3, and it makes those strategic resources even less likely to be under your control b/c once again, they need to be in your borders with roads connecting to them to be taken advantage of.  If that strategic resource is on a mountain, it takes a slave 12 f***ing turns to build a road on it.

I never played a game of Civ 2 with over 200 military units to move around the map every turn, on top of dozens of enslaved workers.  I could probably play an entire game of Civ 2 in the amount of time it takes me to play 30 late game turns of Civ 3.  And it's not even as good as Civ 2.  My copy of Civ 2 is abandonware, doesn't have any of the music files or FMVs, and I still strongly prefer it.

It feels like they wanted to make it more challenging, but the way in which they changed it to make it more challenging made it impossible on the highest difficulty, so they added that stupid Voltron mechanic to make it possible, just so long as you get really lucky and spawn "great leaders" on kills.  It's probably the worst Civ game.  Civ 1 is also better than this for sure.  I'll still recommend it, b/c it's Civ.  It's a unique challenge at least, even if it relies too heavily on RNG.

I didn't mention how unfair the hardest difficulty is without Voltron.  The AI gets dozens of free units and free military support, so they can waltz around with enormous armies even under Democracy with no repercussions.  They build things at a small fraction of the real cost, so they build world wonders almost instantly.  If you even try to build a world wonder on Sid difficulty, you're an idiot.  You're wasting your time.  They'll beat you to it, 100% guaranteed.  Oh, and if you think you can just build and save up trade caravans/freight to get at least 1 world wonder built eventually, you're mistaken b/c they REMOVED TRADE CARAVANS AND FREIGHT.  All WWs need to be built in one city without help.  If you spend 30 turns building it and someone beats you to it, that valuable production time was wasted.  In other words, if you want world wonders, you must gamble AND play on a lower difficulty.  On Sid difficulty, WWs are exclusively a tool of the AI and yet another advantage of theirs that you'll need to overcome.  Which is only possible with Voltron.

TLDR:  In Civ 2 on the hardest difficulty, you get an unlucky starting position, realize it soon enough and lose, but it's no big deal.  Next game.  In Civ 3, you get an unlucky starting position and lose, next game... then when you finally get a good starting position, OOPS!  You don't have the necessary strategic resources to build those legionnaires, you lose to bad RNG 50 turns into the game!  Then when you finally get a game up to this point again, OOPS!  You lose all your dice rolls, you never get Voltron, you lose b/c 7 rivals are all outproducing you.  When you finally get a game to this point AND you roll Voltron, well... good luck.  You still need it, b/c the NEXT strategic resource must also be in your territory.  Ready to pull your hair out when that strategic resource isn't anywhere in sight?  When your Voltron is obsolete (AI gets tanks eventually), you're going to need ANOTHER good roll for ANOTHER Voltron to combine 3 tanks into an army to continue steamrolling.  GL.    Go play Civ 2.

I can't understate what a brilliant game this is.  Even in 2026, given what gaming has become, Civ III shines for its complexity of game mechanics.  

It starts easy: you explore some land, build and connect a few cities. Soon, you'll be playing a chess of a thousand factors -- as you risk a deficit economy to be the first at some tech tree milestone, or pull five adversaries into a complex web of well-timed alliances, allowing you to successfully invade neighbouring territory with your reputation intact.  

Behind the flat (almost board game) interface, it's a masterpiece mostly for all the cleverly balanced factors you can control, the large variety of angles you'll want to learn to manage, and the way those seamlessly escalate through several ages that reveal shifting priorities.  War, diplomacy, trade, economics, domestic policy, culture and technology -- they're simplified to make it fun to play, but they're woven together so each affects the other. I promise you'll be on the edge of your seat watching your careful plans come to fruition. Or, have to regroup because you misjudged.  That risk is what makes the reward. 

And btw you'll probably learn something.  Genuine effort was put into giving the user insight into the history and context of government types, military units, etc, via a "Civilopedia" that you'll want to refer to often to succeed.  (An artifact, probably, of the "educational game" era that gave rise to the Sid Meier's Civilization series.)  This is an old game, so expect some archaic UI choices, but it's a timeless classic and worth thousands of hours of your enjoyment.  I can see why so many are still playing it today.

Speaking of hours: my one caveat is how long it can take to play, especially if you decide to play carefully.  It's likely you'll have many unfinished saves, but you can always just start fresh.

Metro Exodus is one of those games that, on paper, should have been perfect for me.

I love the Fallout series. I enjoy post-apocalyptic settings, survival mechanics, scavenging, exploration, and atmospheric storytelling. Looking at Metro Exodus, it seemed like exactly the sort of game I'd lose myself in.

But for whatever reason, I never did.

The game itself is undeniably impressive. The world is beautifully crafted, the atmosphere is fantastic, and the environments do an excellent job of feeling both dangerous and believable. The move away from the tighter corridors of previous Metro games into larger, more open areas was an interesting change and gave players more freedom to explore.

The problem is that I never really connected with the Metro series as a whole.

I'd played some of the earlier games and never became particularly invested in the world, the characters, or the story. As a result, when I started Exodus, it felt less like the continuation of a journey and more like I was joining a series that I'd never fully committed to in the first place.

That's not the game's fault.

In fact, everything I played was solid. The gunplay felt good, the atmosphere was excellent, and the survival elements added just enough tension without becoming frustrating. You can tell a huge amount of care went into building the world.

The issue was simply investment.

These days, I've realised that if a game doesn't grab me within a certain amount of time, it's very easy for it to slip into the backlog and quietly stay there. Metro Exodus ended up in that category. Not because I disliked it, but because other games pulled me away before I'd become fully attached to what it was doing.

Oddly, that's probably the most frustrating type of game.

A bad game gets uninstalled and forgotten.

A game like Metro Exodus sits there in your library, constantly reminding you that one day you really should give it another chance.

And maybe I will.

Score: 8/10

Metro Exodus is clearly a well-made game with excellent atmosphere, strong world-building, and a unique take on the post-apocalyptic genre.

I should have loved it.

Instead, it became another victim of the ever-growing backlog and my inability to fully invest in a series I never completely connected with. That's less a criticism of Metro Exodus and more an admission that sometimes a good game arrives at the wrong time.

It's currently sitting in my collection alongside several others under the category:

"I'll come back to this one eventually."

[h2]TLDR:[/h2] An intriguing evolution of the Metro formula with excellent gameplay and a well-paced story, undermined by discouraging technical issues.

[h2]GAMEPLAY OVERVIEW:[/h2] Metro Exodus is a survival horror game with heavy FPS elements. The player once again takes on the role of Artyom, one of several thousand survivors in the Moscow metro after a nuclear war.

Exodus plays in first person. As in previous games, Artyom is a silent protagonist, save narrating between chapters. The game proceeds in a (mostly) linear fashion, following Artyom's journey out of Moscow and across a ruined Russian landscape by train. The player can carry up to three weapons (two in the highest difficulty), ammo, healing kits, grenades, and so on. Armor and guns can be upgraded with various enhancements found during the adventure.

This game adds a crafting element to the series. The player will find two resources: materials and chemicals. Together, these allow the player to build certain items—such as healing kits and gas mask canisters—through their backpack interface. Ammo and grenades can also be crafted at workbenches. Weapon maintenance is a factor. The player's guns collect grime and dirt through use and eventually can seize if not cleaned at the workbench using chemical resources. Amounts of crafting supplies found vary by difficulty. On the easiest mode, the player will be swimming in resources, while on the harder difficulties, players will have to make difficult decisions about what items are really needed. Difficulty also affects how much ammo is found, meaning players must account for every round fired.

Players can tackle enemy encounters by going in with guns blazing or sneaking through. Combat can be fast and intense, but is satisfying. Weapon handling generally feels pretty good and as new weapons are found, copies are stored on the train, so the player can usually tailor their loadout before setting out.

In my opinion, combat is a bit less forgiving than in previous Metro games. For one, in many areas, it is possible to alert upward of a dozen foes, which is almost certain death. A few late-game brutes are relatively easy to avoid but do nightmarish damage, all but one-shotting the player on higher difficulties. The game also features a handful of difficult fights—either with bosses or against large numbers of opponents—that cannot be skipped or avoided. Outside those encounters, stealth is a viable option in most situations; in fact, stealth is almost a mandatory part of play on Normal or higher, to avoid as many of the dangerous brawls as possible, with resource scarcity being an issue.

Much is made of Exodus moving the franchise to a more "open-world" environment but of the six major zones, only two are truly open, with the rest being relatively linear. Traversal over the zones includes a lot of vehicle travel on boats and in one chapter, a van. Vehicle handling is a little clunky but I felt the awkward movement of dilapidated boats and vans accurately reflects the decayed condition of everything.

Artyom has a whole pack of companions on his journey. Player actions have a lasting impact on the fate of several of them, and possibly the player's own ending. Exodus employs the same "morality" system of previous games, where the screen gives a light white flash on a good moral action. Good actions are what one might expect, such as sparing enemies, freeing prisoners from bandits, etc. A player pretty much has to avoid killing anyone who doesn't deserve it to make it to the good ending. If seeking that good ending, I recommend listening to your companions and NPCs as to whom to spare.

All in all, the mechanics of the game blend together into something entertaining and stressful at the same time. I spent a lot of playtime on the edge of my seat, waiting for something to go horribly wrong. I started worrying about the fate of my companions, which is a good measure of a game's ability to draw in and captivate a player. On that count, Exodus is an unqualified success.

[h2]STORY / WORLDBUILDING:[/h2] The tale opens with Artyom obsessed with finding survivors on the surface. Now married to Anna (the sniper from the last game), he is reprimanded for wasting time and resources on dangerous missions, before he and Anna witness a working train shooting across the wasteland. Investigating said train goes wrong, revealing to Artyom that much of what they'd been told was a lie. Eventually his whole squad is involved and they escape, taking the train on a crosscountry journey. Along the way, they face feudal warlords, cultists, and some other surprises. Several characters find their expectations and hopes undercut, face their disillusionment, and move on to focus on their future. The whole narrative is pretty captivating.

The grim setting builds on that of the first two games, though it mostly exchanges the filthy, claustrophobic tunnels of the subway system for a ruined and irradiated surface. Years of neglect following the war have left buildings in a state of disrepair and cars nothing but rusted hulks. Aqueducts and industrial pumps have failed, leaving basements and low-lying areas flooded. The overall sense of decay is well-represented, adding to the game's despair and depression. I enjoyed the story and world but it was enough of a downer that I also had to take breaks from it.

[h2]DLC:[/h2] This version of Exodus includes two DLCs, Two Colonels and Sam's Story. The former tells a backstory for a character Artyom meets along the way, while the latter is an adventure for one of Artyom's companions set after the main game ends. Each DLC features an interesting scenario, though both are pretty linear and involve challenging mandatory fights. Together, the two add 8-10 hours of gameplay.

[h2]TECHNICAL ASPECTS:[/h2] Exodus looks and feels great. Visuals are dark and grimy, befitting the ruined world. Character models are detailed and animations are excellent. I enjoyed the sound design, and the varied (by region) ambient sound generally adds to an area's uneasy feeling. Voice acting is decent too.

This excellent presentation is badly marred by pervasive instability. I had numerous crashes that not only froze the game but hardlocked my entire system. Disabling overlays, updating drivers, and other suggested fixes were unsuccessful. Using GPU software to lock myself to 60 FPS cut down the number of crashes but didn't eliminate them altogether. I expect most people would find this an unreasonable solution. Corrupted files and lost save data occurred about every other time I started the game.

Aside from those serious concerns, Exodus has many minor problems, such as mistimed dialogue lines or characters speaking over each other. In one section, I had enemies lock me in combat (meaning no saves) from across the map and I wasn't able to unlock without returning to deal with them. I had collectibles that refused to appear, even on restarting the game or replaying the chapter. A demon picked me up and dropped me clear out of the world, as shown:

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3823555274

If a player uses a map while driving the van, their field of vision sometimes reorients in the ceiling. Exiting the vehicle and reentering seems to be the only way to fix it. All of these issues were frequent and persistent enough to detract from my overall enjoyment.

Steam achievements will require several full runs through the game to get alternate endings, including on high difficulty and "iron man" mode (saves only allowed between chapters), and finding all collectibles.

[h2]FINAL WORD:[/h2] I enjoyed Metro enough to play through it twice and get each ending. I'd consider revisiting it, if I thought I could stomach the constant instability.

[b] Metro Exodus represents a radical break from the franchise's paradigm: the transition from the suffocating claustrophobia of the tunnels to a liberating, yet terrifying, agoraphobia. If previous titles dealt with surviving in the tomb of humanity, Exodus is about the exhaustive search for a place where it's worthwhile to start life anew under the sunlight.

The great tragedy that drives the narrative is the shattering of a monumental lie. The revelation that the world outside wasn't completely dead and that leaders kept the survivors of Moscow in the dark through radio jammers is a devastating blow. Humanity was not only trapped by radiation, but imprisoned by its own commanders. The journey aboard the Aurora locomotive then becomes an odyssey to traverse the ruins of Russia in search of a horizon free from the Cold War paranoia that the Metro leaders refused to abandon.

Mechanically, the game translates this new reality by abandoning linear corridors for vast open maps divided by seasons. This freedom of exploration brings a kind of immersive and hostile tension that echoes the unforgiving design of games like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Ammunition economy is replaced by a visceral crafting and organic maintenance system. Cleaning mud and sand from your rifle in the middle of the Caspian Desert or a swamp on the Volga ceases to be just a game mechanic and becomes a survival ritual. You are no longer just managing filters, but fighting against the physical wear and tear that the world imposes on your equipment.

However, the true core of Exodus is the Aurora crew itself. Artyom's nihilistic and solitary existentialism gives way to the dynamics of a chosen family. The journey culminates in the deadly and radioactive depths of Novosibirsk, returning to classic claustrophobic terror, but this time the sacrifice is not for a blind ideology, but for those we love. The game concludes Artyom's saga by replacing the absolute darkness of the Metro with a painful, yet genuine, glimpse of hope. [/b]

10/10 — A raw, emotional journey that stays with you long after the train stops.

Metro Exodus takes the claustrophobic terror of the Moscow tunnels and expands it across a desolate, breath-taking Russian wasteland—not just to make the world bigger, but to raise the stakes of what you are fighting for: family, hope, and a future.

Leaving the Metro behind aboard the Aurora completely shifts the dynamic of the series. The pacing between brutal, desperate survival out in the wild and the quiet, intimate moments aboard the train is what makes this game unforgettable. Sitting with Anna, sharing a smoke with the crew, listening to a guitar melody while the tracks click beneath you—it grounds the apocalypse in real, fragile humanity. When the emotional beats land in the final chapter, they hit with devastating weight. Very few games have brought me to tears, but this journey earned every single tear.

Why this game is an extraordinary experience:
- Earned emotional weight: The bond between Artyom, Anna, and Miller carries genuine heart; the ending isn't just cinematic flair, it’s a culmination of every sacrifice made along the way.
- Immersive survival mechanics: Wiping condensation from your gas mask, patching cracked filters, and cleaning jammed guns in the field make every firefight feel grounded and tense.
- Bespoke sandbox design: Rather than generic open-world filler, each season brings a distinct, self-contained region full of unique factions, wildlife, and environmental storytelling.
- Atmosphere second to none: From eerie silent swamps to the bone-chilling dread of Novosibirsk, the tension and sound design are masterclass.

It’s a rare shooter that prioritizes soul over spectacle, delivering a gripping, heart-breaking journey about fighting for the people you love when the entire world has given up. A true post-apocalyptic masterpiece.

Five minutes on the surface, and suddenly the subway doesn't seem so bad.

Metro Exodus takes the series into a beautiful, terrifying post-apocalyptic Russia. The atmosphere is phenomenal, the survival mechanics feel meaningful, and the journey aboard the Aurora gives the story a surprisingly emotional heart.

The larger environments reward exploration without turning everything into another Ubisoft-style checklist. Ammunition is precious, weapons need maintenance, and every encounter feels dangerous.

Unfortunately, stealth AI can be inconsistent, movement occasionally feels clunky, and some slower sections drag on longer than necessary. Artyom remaining completely silent during emotional conversations is also unintentionally hilarious.

Has it aged well? Absolutely. The visuals, environmental detail, sound design, and immersion still rival many newer games.

Long-time fan here, and this feels like a slap in the face.
I've been playing Metro since 2033. I've finished these games several times, and I've always loved the atmosphere of the Moscow Metro. So you can imagine how I felt when I found out that Metro 2039, a game set in the ruins of Moscow, will not have Russian at all. No voice acting, and not even text.
Some people say the lack of Russian dubbing is down to sanctions. Fine, let's accept that for a moment. But sanctions don't explain why there are no Russian subtitles or menus. Translating text doesn't require hiring Russian voice actors. If the studio can't work with Russian talent, it can hire a third-party localization company outside Russia, which is a completely normal and cheap thing to do. Plenty of studios do it for far smaller games.
So I can't shake the feeling that this is a choice, not a limitation. And I really don't understand why. The fans of this series, many of them Russian speakers who grew up with Glukhovsky's books, are being told their language isn't worth even a subtitle file. That's not a political statement, it's just disrespectful to a big part of the community that made Metro what it is.
I'd love to be wrong about this. If Russian text is added before release, I'll happily say so. Until then, I'm very disappointed.

This game is the rare sequel that understands exactly what made its predecessors special and still manages to grow without losing the soul of the series.

I came into this one the same way I played Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light: aiming for 100% achievements. Having now completed all three games that way, I can say Exodus earns its place alongside them. My total time landed at 63.6 hours, largely because Iron Mode alone took nearly 30 of those. That mode is brutally unoptimized for what it asks of you. Unskippable cutscenes become genuinely painful when you’re replaying chapters after a single death, and the lack of mid-level saves turns exploration into a constant risk calculation. I’m glad I finished it, but I wouldn’t call the experience elegant.

The main story is excellently orchestrated. Characters feel memorable rather than functional, and the decisions you make actually matter in ways that linger. I played both endings. The bad ending felt more satisfying to me, perhaps because Artyom’s fate had been hanging over the series since the first game. He barely scraped through 2033 and Last Light. Seeing that weight finally settle carried a grim sense of completion that the good ending, for all its hope, didn’t quite match.

What impressed me most is how the open levels still feel like Metro. They give you space to breathe and explore, yet the atmosphere stays claustrophobic and oppressive. The series’ signature tension never fully lifts. Enemy AI remains excellent. Stealth is still properly challenging rather than a checklist of vision cones. Mutants are more agile, versatile, and grotesque than before, which keeps encounters unpredictable. The constant mechanical pressure (cleaning weapons, repairing your gas mask, managing scarce ammo, and farming resources) forces you to min-max almost constantly. It can be exhausting, but it also makes every successful stretch feel earned.

The two story DLCs are outstanding. Both are heartfelt and funny at the same time, often in the same scene. This series has always been humble and deeply humane if you take the time to listen to the quieter dialogues that are easy to walk past. I tried both endings in Sam’s Story and found them equally satisfying in different ways. Neither DLC feels like filler.

There are a few rough edges. The new humanoid mutants are annoying and not particularly interesting to fight, though I accept they belong here if they’re drawn from the books. The short breath and low stamina also grate at times, but it makes sense once you realize you’re hauling three weapons plus a full kit through irradiated ruins. Iron Mode, as mentioned, is more painful than it needs to be.

None of that outweighs what the game gets right. Exodus respects the tone and themes of the earlier games while giving them room to expand. It’s tense, atmospheric, and emotionally grounded in a way few shooters manage.

P.S. Once I'll have ray tracing PC, I'll try enhanced version once more(which I got for free).

Only a few games left me bored- only a handful; this is one of them. The game shines in the linear section but falls flat in the open world. The graphics do look pretty, but everywhere I went, I saw the same dilapidated grey colored building near another grey colored building, near a grey-colored fence wall. The realistic approach killed anything attractive about the game. There is no music that plays in the background to make it a bit atmospheric, no EXP or any skill point system to incentivize triggering combat encounters, and an excessive amount of dialogue that could’ve been an email. I recorded a video of a woman talking to her daughter; not even side characters, the dialogue exchange went on for 4 minutes. The sad part was, all the story in the dialogue was more interesting than her 2-minute side quest. 

One major gripe I had about combat is: why does it even exist? In an open world with no XP or skill points or any sort of challenge reward for killing enemies, why should I engage in combat? Metal Gear Phantom Pain didn’t have XP or skill points, but it had a robust open world that rewarded players for exploration and crafting materials to build the base, and so on and so forth. I don’t see why I should engage in combat. Why should I waste bullets on enemies if I can skip past them to the objective? Enemies don’t drop anything on death, and I am down to fewer bullets for nothing. Once I started skipping past enemies, I just realized I’m playing the game for the stupid story. The open world is dead; all I could predict, if I play this game any longer, I will have to sit through more of the same. More of the same: people talking for hours, meaningless combat encounters, hour-long cutscenes, a bible-worth of dialogue in between, and less gameplay.

I should’ve known where the game was heading from the first hour. The first hour was nothing but the game shoving more cutscenes in my face to say the same thing over and over again. There was a stealth section, but it was mostly linear- the actual good part of my time in this game- and minutes after the real gameplay, the game decided to put me literally on a train to talk more about the story. It should’ve been a linear game; say what you will about Ubisoft games- they might not have a great story or ambience in their open-world games- but at the end of the day, they are games. They incentivize everything to make the player return to the game every day.

MY FIRST REVIEW EVER ON STEAM, AND IT COULDN'T BE ABOUT ANY OTHER GAME OTHER THAN METRO:

Where to start...

I will start with the main protagonist of this game, of course: the post-nuclear-apocalyptic world. The ones who are long gone, the notes left behind, the empty cities... every place tells you the story of the nuclear war from a different perspective. The only things moving are the sheets fluttering in the wind and the power lines swaying overhead. Death is the only thing you can see around you, especially outside the Metro. Yet, there is a certain beauty in seeing the world slowly healing from humankind, little by little, as nature takes back what had been stolen from it.

The immersion in this masterpiece is also one of the main aspects worth mentioning. The fact that the game has almost no HUD (especially on Hardcore mode and with some tweaks) helps greatly with immersion in this world, whether you're exploring or fighting the mutated creatures that are also victims of the post-war world. One example is when you encounter humanoid monsters. I felt pity for them, invading their space and killing them just so I could survive and pass through the different regions on the map. They remind me of the ones in the movie I Am Legend. If you need to check the radiation levels, you need to look at your Geiger counter. If you want to know what time it is, you look at the physical watch on your wrist, and so on... The player literally becomes the character, whose name is Artyom, who also doesn't speak throughout the game.

This is not a game, this is a piece of art, a faithful depiction of what a post-nuclear-apocalyptic world would look like. Metro doesn't give you what you wanted a post-apocalyptic world to be; it gives you what it would really be like (or very close): almost no hope, and the war continues. Humans never learn.

Metro feels like a necessary, sad goodbye.

The moving tower defense mechanic which are your heroes in this game is genuinely a good feature. it is fresh and adds a great layer of strategy to each mission. The different heroes are also well-designed — each one deals significantly more damage to certain types of enemies, and the way their attack patterns interact with those enemies is really well implemented. For example, when a hero focuses on area-of-effect damage, the game smartly spawns enemy groups that come in larger numbers but with lower health, which makes fights feel dynamic and satisfying.

That said, the grinding for upgrades feels unnecessary and only serves to slow down the pacing. It would’ve been much better if the upgrade grind was introduced after finishing the main story, so it could serve as a way to extend the gameplay rather than pad it out.

After a certain point, heroes become so powerful that strategy barely matters — it doesn’t really make a difference who’s attacking what anymore. The early part of the game is also quite slow; it takes a few missions before you even get access to most of your towers (heroes), which can make the opening feel like a slog.

Finally, the in-game economy is tedious and frustrating to deal with. It feels like unnecessary busywork that gets in the way of the fun parts of the game.

Overall, it’s a solid experience, great core mechanic — but it’s held back by grindy progression and a slow start. it’s good in concept but lacks in execution.
