Hero Defense, developed by Happy Tuesday and published by Headup, is an ambitious hybrid of tower defense, RPG, and light strategy elements, offering a unique spin on a genre that often relies heavily on static mechanics. Instead of placing traditional towers, players control a group of five heroes—each with distinct skills and attack types—who must be strategically positioned and dynamically moved across winding paths to hold back waves of undead enemies. This twist immediately sets the game apart from conventional tower defense titles, demanding not just planning but real-time tactical awareness as enemy types, strengths, and weaknesses vary significantly from wave to wave.

The game’s world is styled with a gothic, cartoon-like aesthetic that lands somewhere between Tim Burton and a haunted fairground. It establishes an atmosphere that feels quirky but sinister, without veering too far into horror or comedy. The heroes themselves are equally stylized: Jack the vampire hunter leads the group, flanked by characters like Barrows the necromancer, Sam Hain the pyromancer, Jane Doe the assassin, and Wylde the feral lycan. Each hero specializes in dealing with certain enemy types or exploiting specific vulnerabilities, and much of the game’s strategy revolves around placing the right hero in the right spot at the right time. This real-time repositioning is the game’s central mechanic, forcing players to stay alert rather than rely on passive tower upgrades or static defenses.

Beyond combat, Hero Defense introduces several layers of progression that add a long-term sense of investment. Each hero can be leveled up and customized through individual skill trees, and weapons can be enhanced using rune systems that offer stat boosts or special effects. Additionally, the town hub serves as a base of operations where players can unlock new upgrades, rebuild structures, and open up access to deeper mechanics. These systems aim to provide the player with a sense of continual growth, though some may find them a bit superficial or grind-heavy in execution. Progression is tied not just to skill but also to replaying earlier maps to gather more resources or unlock harder difficulty tiers.

The campaign spans multiple stages with a variety of map designs, but over time, the differences between missions can start to blur. Enemy paths are often predictable, and while some maps introduce environmental mechanics or more complex pathing, the core gameplay loop remains relatively unchanged throughout the campaign. Enemy variety is decent, with resistances, immunities, and special abilities adding an extra layer of tactical depth. However, the mid-game can suffer from noticeable difficulty spikes that seem designed to slow player progress unless time is spent grinding or optimizing hero builds in a specific way. For some, this adds longevity and challenge; for others, it may feel like artificial padding.

Visually and aurally, the game holds up reasonably well for an indie title. The environments are colorfully morbid, and character animations are distinct enough to keep the action clear even in the midst of chaotic enemy waves. The soundtrack supports the spooky, carnival-esque atmosphere without becoming intrusive, although the voice acting and narrative components leave something to be desired. The story is serviceable, giving context to the hero’s quest to rid the world of the undead plague, but it lacks emotional weight or deep character development. Most interactions are brief and functional, prioritizing gameplay momentum over storytelling depth.

In terms of performance, Hero Defense generally runs smoothly, though some minor bugs and visual issues can occasionally impact the experience. One recurring criticism involves visual occlusion—environmental features or awkward camera angles sometimes make it hard to place heroes accurately or see the full battlefield. This can lead to frustrating moments, especially during intense waves where placement timing is critical. Moreover, certain interface elements feel clunky or unpolished, and the targeting system for skills or items sometimes lacks the precision needed for high-level play.

For its asking price, Hero Defense delivers a fair amount of content, including a full campaign, multiple difficulty levels, and an Endless Mode that extends replayability. However, its value proposition depends largely on how much the player enjoys its core loop of hero movement and enemy wave management. Those looking for a deep RPG experience or a polished, highly replayable strategy game may find the game somewhat limited in scope. On the other hand, players who appreciate hybrid mechanics and are open to a tower defense experience that emphasizes active engagement over passive design will likely find it refreshing and satisfying, despite its rough edges.

Ultimately, Hero Defense succeeds in offering something different. It's not the most polished or narratively rich title, but its inventive blend of genres and demand for moment-to-moment decision-making help it stand out. It’s a game that rewards strategic thinking and adaptability, though it occasionally undermines its strengths with uneven pacing and progression systems that lean a little too heavily on repetition. Still, for players intrigued by the idea of a tower defense game that keeps you on your toes and asks more of you than just where to place a turret, Hero Defense is worth a closer look.

HERO DEFENSE is an unusual twist on the tower defense genre, a console ported TD game where instead of towers, you have heroes who can move between each node.  So while the TD gameplay is all there, gameplay itself is less about choosing which towers and more about deciding which hero is best at which node at any given time... so it's more like a juggling act than a strategy game.  You only get 5 heroes and they have different strengths vs different enemies, so you have to do a bunch of platespinning to make sure you can kill the creeps as they travel on their preset paths. 

This isn't fun, this kind of takes one of the core, most fun elements of the TD genre and throws it out the window. 

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

The game features low-polygon "retro" assets with cartoony, mobile app style shader effects, making this look like a barely functional mobile app from 15 years ago.  This visual style is a method that lazy devs often use when they have a lack of interest/capabilty to create highly detailed, high poly models and instead use shader effects to disguise that shortcoming under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It's far below the state of the art visuals gamers expect as a result of their decisions.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff as you tap a hero then tap the node you want them to go to.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

Because this is designed for consoles, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.

Worse than just being a console port, this is indistinguishable from a mobile app, but they put this on Steam and consoles instead of the app stores by mistake.  Was it rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all)?.

Regardless, for all intents and purposes HERO DEFENSE might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Reviewing SteamDB to check how popular this game was with players reveals a surprise... there's a modest spike in player counts for the game.  But this only happened once, around the same time that trading cards were applied to the game... so this is just card idlers getting their cards and moving on.  A closer look at the numbers shows the game just has a couple of players every week running up the game and idling it for cards, then deleting it.  We must ask how it benefits gamers for there to be so many games like this, with no merit as a serious game, that only generate sales from people idling and selling the trading cards.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

This is the kind of game I might have given a "maybe" to, but the developers ridiculous pricing has ruined all goodwill, to the point I must try to warn gamers away. 

HERO DEFENSE has the farcical price of $30 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

For comparison, the $30 asking price for this game could get you games like "Disco Elysium", "Stellaris" or "Final Fantasy XIV Online".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.  This pricing is just ridiculous.

It's a really mixed bag, but in the end I an enjoying it.
It looks very polished, and has a very professional feel. 
The graphics are cartoony, but in a good way but don't expect a game full of monsters to feel spooky, it is way too cute. For example, although the first character is a buff hero type (whose father is the main villain), and the second an old holy man(whose wife is either dead or missing), the third is oddly a sassy little girl.(With no story apparently.)
 (Probably a coincidence, but she looks like a young version of the zombies she specializes in.)
The animation is also well done, though usually pretty small. 
The sound is okay, the music is nice. The voice acting is... meh. Sometimes the emphasis is off, and I really can't tell if the mayor character is supposed to be a good guy or not. The game also has the odd habit of giving the characters cute or interesting things to say, but they get repetitive very fast, and very annoying. 
The game play is rather deceptive, they claim tower-defense, but it doesn't really quite feel like one. You have a few characters that would normally be the towers, but there are only a handful, and you constantly have to move them about. 
If I were to make a suggestion for a follow up, it would be to allow each hero type to build apprentice-towers, that stay in place and get leveled up, it would feel less busy.
The UI is already a bit of a mess, and character upgrades require you take your eye off the action for a few often critical seconds as you check your currency total, then decide which person to level up if you have enough. 
Between levels there is a town with upgrades that all you to bolsters your heroes. I only have two so far, an academy, where you buy upgrades from a rather small upgrade tree, the other is an armory where you can upgrade your weapons, and use magical icons to design what skill-bumps you get when you level. 
All in all a pretty neat system. 
Also the maps can be replayed on a higher level to get extra stars, so there seems to be a reasonable amount of game here. 
I would say the map is one of the weak points for me. Moving your point of view around is awkward, and the mouse is used both move the map, and move my characters, not a good choice. Not sure why the map isn't WASD, it would be much better. 
Oh, that reminds me, there are tactical options, and QWER picks them for you, but they could have easily used 1234.
I do feel like there is something not quite right however. I am a veteran of TD games, which this is adjacent too, but the levels come within estimate of how difficult a map should be for you, and it's wacky. Sometimes it says 'no problem' and it is easy, other times it says 'no problem' and I get defeated. Very confusing, and it makes me feel that perhaps the levels aren't as well balanced as the designers might think they are. 
Lastly I want to mention that the game did have multi-player and co-op, but apparently the developers have shut the servers down, so that isn't happening. 
Also, according to the comments, one of the achievements is no longer possible, Endless Mode. I know some people are serious abut want to complete them all, so that might be a deal breaker for some. 
All in all though, it seems a good package. Got it on a good sale, and it was easily worth the buck and a half I paid.

I started this review with a thumbs up recommendation because it is an extremely polished game that does what it set out to two. But as I tried to put words to the review I realized that the negatives really overshadow the experience.

On the bright side, it looks really good, it's fully voice acted, and the moment to moment gameplay is  smooth. It takes the core play of a tower defense and then add mobility to the towers. Throw in some skills trees and a gacha-styled rune customization system and you get Hero Defense.

While the features are in place and well-implemented, they just don't feel satisfying to actually play.

Tower Defense tend to get most of their depth from choosing which towers to deploy, but this game limits you to 5 towers, with one instance each. The intention is that you can customize these heroes to your own play style, but all of the upgrades are passive changes. They don't make the towers feel any more varied or powerful, just like you need to grind for more levels.

This feeling is compounded by the level design and game flow. Each wave of monsters is weak to a single hero (Dictating which towers to use), levels are locked by stars which require you to replay early missions, and enemies/bosses can often feel tanky unless you take time to level up your heroes. 

The rune's definitely are more successful, as they actually impact a units play-style. But it's locked behind a gacha-style purchases and merging systems. It's not micro-transactions, but still gives off the feeling of a mobile game. 

The worst part is that the game is well-made and deserves good words. It just feels like it falls short as a Tower Defense, and it falls short as an RPG... ultimately failing to create an engaging experience.

[b]Hero Defense: Haunted Island is a half-tower defense, half-RPG that pits a five-man team of monster slayers against the endless hordes of Count Necrosis. It attempts to marry the strategic elements of a tower defense with the character progression of an RPG. While it does have clean presentation and a novel premise, it's marred by poor design decisions that result in inconsistent difficulty, unwieldy mechanics, and overly grindy progression. I would recommend picking this up only if it's on sale, you're a tower defense aficionado, and you've run out of better options.[/b]


As a tower defense, it follows mostly in line with others in the genre. It revolving around the strategic placement of towers and numerous groups of enemies approaching your defensive line. However, instead of having an infinite number of towers to spend currency on, you have five towers that can be placed, repositioned, and upgraded throughout the lifetime of the level.


Towers, or heroes in this case, can only be placed once you have enough souls. Each hero deals a particular kind of damage with their chosen weapon. For example, The vampire hunter deals piercing damage with his crossbow, the gravedigger deals holy damage with his holy water, etc. These damage types pair with the enemies you encounter. Vampires are weak to piercing, skeletons are weak to holy, etc.

You gain experience by defeating enemies and completing levels, which unlocks skill points for you to invest in your heroes. Some heroes gain the ability to ricochet their shots, deal large areas of effect damage, or buff nearby party members. All of these abilities are passively chance-based, meaning you have no agency as to when they will trigger.

You can also socket your heroes with runes, which augment your heroes' abilities in some way during play. At the beginning of each level, all runes that are socketed are inactive until you invest souls into your hero. Simply attaching runes is not enough, you have to farm out the souls in the field and hit the upgrade button to unlock a runes' given bonuses.


As the game progresses, you unlock higher difficulties and more challenging versions of the same five monster types. Certain levels will feature enemies with special modifiers, mini-boss variants, or unique bosses with powerful abilities. At about the midway point, you'll have seen all of the enemies and modifiers, and the rest of the game will be spent dealing with tricky combinations of the aforementioned types.


While Hero Defense: Haunted Island is aesthetically pleasing and conceptually intriguing, it has several glaring problems. Probably the most prominent issue is that they decided to design their game using the worst aspects of the both genres.


A core element of a good tower defense is consistency. Your towers are many or infinite in number, their abilities are largely predictable, and their placement final. Each level plays out in a similar fashion, and you use your currency and intuition to carve out a strong defensive line based on the demands of the oncoming horde. Each time you replay the level, you alter your strategy in small ways to improve your chances of success. Games deviate or subvert these elements at times, but the core backbone generally remains the same.


As a tower defense, your towers are severely limited, somewhat inconsistent, and you face enemies that range from laughably easy to frustratingly hard.


You only have five towers, meaning placement is not only key, but also timing. It's not enough to build a strong defensive line, you have to decide when and where you need to shuffle it around. This means that some heroes might end up playing double, triple, or even quadruple duty across many lanes at once. You have to constantly pause and move to compensate for changing enemy positions.

Your towers also need to be upgraded outside of the level, meaning you can never truly be sure you're adequately equipped to deal with the level's threats. This can be as huge as a level gap or missing ability, all the way down to something tiny like the order or type of runes you've equipped.

Your towers also have vital abilities that are chance-based, meaning you may need an ability to trigger to stop a boss, and it never triggers. Later levels and difficulties absolutely hinge on those random abilities, meaning your hero might not perform at their potential when the time requires.

Then you have your enemies, with their random modifiers that make them frustrating to fight. Certain enemies will leap forward large swaths of the field when hit. Others will heal off almost all the damage they receive. Some will revive themselves when killed. Some rounds you'll fight enemies that you can stomp into the pavement, and other times you'll encounter foes that are nigh unkillable.

Individually these mechanics would be fine, but together they create a game state where you cannot play with much confidence in your towers or strategy. You'll start up a level only to die on the first wave because the enemy has a modifier you can't beat, or your towers lack the necessary runes, or you have the wrong upgrades equipped, etc. This inconsistency makes it difficult to gauge level difficulty or personal skill.


Then you have the RPG aspect, where you are improving your characters between levels using skill points and gold. I don't really need to say much about this. It's every bit as grindy and soul-sucking as the grindiest RPGs. Except to spend a lot of time sitting on the same level, on the same difficulty, fighting the same wave after wave squeezing out as much experience and money as you can.

You need to upgrade your town for bonuses, your heroes' skills for extra abilities, your weapons for rune slots, gamble on a rune slot machine for a chance at a powerful runes, buy in-level bonuses using special currency. Exchange gold at a loss for special currency to spend on further upgrades, etc.

Eventually, you just go into full-on farm mode to get enough resources so you can attempt the next level at a slightly higher difficulty.


For the record, I made it to the final boss in 4 hours. I was too weak to fight him for some reason(despite beating all the levels up to him). I sat on the second to last level and farmed experience points for a few hours. I then beat the final boss on easy, only to discover the game ends when you beat him on insane.

I then proceeded to grind for another 34 hours to get all the skills and runes needed to fight him on insane. I ended up using things like keyboard macros and such to make it much more palatable. I'd even start up rounds and minimize so I could go do something else.

Between the base game and the DLC levels, minus all the grinding, there is probably 6-7 hours of content here.


It's a shame the game features such a boilerplate story with boring, frustrating, and grindy mechanics, as the aesthetic could have been made into something worthwhile. Perhaps if this had been a Diablo-style RPG, or a MOBA, or a traditional RPG, this might have turned into something special. However, in its current state, it is subpar. It falls just below the halfway mark.


Sometimes mixing two genres together can create something great, or at least intriguing. Sadly, Hero Defense seems to sample from the worst aspects of the genres its mixing. It's limited in player agency, overly chance-based, inconsistent in difficulty, requires excessive grinding and currency gating, and features very little of substance in the end. At the current price, it's too expensive. Given the level of quality, I can only recommend it if you are a veteran of the genre, or you have exhausted the better alternatives.

HERO DEFENSE Review

Are you looking for an adventure? Step right up. You are in for one wild ride!

Some key points that this game offers:

1.	Strong RPG Mechanics
2.	Brilliant Campaign mode
3.	Online PvP
4.	Indie Gem 5/5

Gameplay & Controls:

The game is playable with your keyboard and mouse; it can be played with your mouse only, however the shortcuts that the keyboard offers make the game much more comfortable and easier to manage.

What we have here is a Tower Defense game mixed with some other elements and mechanics, blended together beautifully to deliver us a fresh new variant of Tower Defense game.

As you play levels your Heroes gain XP and level up; Every time they level up, they receive skill points which you can use to unlock and upgrade their abilities. You have a home base that consists of a few Town buildings, all of which can be upgraded to grant powerful bonuses to your Heroes along with several other added effects to make your journey easier.

Each Hero can be quipped with special runes granting them additional powers and effects. Their weapons can be upgraded as well to increase the damage they do. 

This little gem has all this and so much more, however to avoid spoiling all that it has to offer I’m leaving it at that!

Graphics:

Absolutely gorgeous; for an Indie game of this scale it has been created pretty stunningly. Level design was done very neatly with a lot of creativity invested into each level. The game has a Halloween theme about it and the developers did a fantastic job to represent and maintain it throughout the game.

Hero design was done just as spectacularly; each of our Heroes are unique in their appearances and behaviours.

Under the hood we have some settings to customize our game as well.

Sounds:

The background music has been implemented quite well, adding to the theme of the game and enhancing it quite beautifully. Character voice acting has been done just as well, giving each of our characters a realistic appearance.

Background sounds for the entire game have been created and implemented into the game as well, giving it a life of its own, and adding to the nature and theme that the game creates so beautifully. 

Replayability:

Each level can be replayed on a higher difficulty for extra rewards. Each level can give you a total of four stars. Replaying a level also has the option of activating extra challenges which further increases the difficulty of the level but also grants the player extra rewards which can be used to upgrade the town and their Heroes weapons.

Once you’ve had your fill of the campaign you can take things online and test out your skills there.

MGR Gaming’s Conclusions:
Spoilers ahead:

Hero defense is something new and quite different, but in all the right ways. They went and gambled quite a bit, mixing these mechanics together and it paid off. The final product is a marvel that can be very addictive and replayed over and over.

The story line is easy to follow yet quite memorable and fun to experience. The levelling system for your Heroes is another very unique add on giving you a very new take on strategic planning for a Tower defense game.

The game has a bit of grind behind it but as long as you play it at your own leisure and pace it should not get too ‘grindy’… 

All in all, a very decent game that any Tower Defense fan should give a try.

Hero Defense is a tower defence game but you control movable units (and you will be moving them a lot) rather than stationary buildings. This is not necessarily a good or bad thing compared to a normal TD game, just different.

Gameplay is fun and can be frantic and fast paced depending on the map. You control 5 heroes (a mixture of ranged and melee) who fight off waves of monsters and bosses. Because your "towers" are mobile it's a lot more interactive during waves than your typical tower defence game, as you reposition your units to be in their most optimal locations or chasing down those few mobs that got away.

Each hero has their own talent tree, and you can upgrade their weapons and runes that boost their stats and powers. On each level the more monsters you kill the more you can "charge up" your hero, which basically means leveling up, boosting their power for that map.

Art style has a nice cartoony-gothic feel to it, but the animations are jerky and almost look like they're fixed at 20fps while the game is sat at 60+.

The default controls are rubbish because the developers seem to think I have three hands. Moving heroes is done with the mouse, the camera is moved with the arrow keys, and you switch between heroes with 1-5 and use consumables with QWER. Once I rebound the camera to WASD playing became much more enjoyable. But changing the camera keys isn't even possible from within the UI, I had to edit an .ini file to do it. Bizarre decision.

In single player you have a campaign mode with 14 levels. Each level has 4 different difficulties offering some replayability. Once you complete the game an endless mode unlocks, as well as 12 brand new levels. Multiplayer is dead, and I don't mean there's nobody playing it, I mean the severs are offline and have been for a long time. It has a co-op mode but I couldn't get it to do anything so I suspect that's broken too.

My main criticism is it's impossible to beat the game on the base difficulty setting without grinding earlier levels over and over to get coins and XP and upgrades for your heroes. This is not fun. Replaying levels on an increased difficulty for a challenge? ok cool, that's fun! but forcing you to do it for hours just to try and artificially lengthen the game really sucks.

It's not perfect, but the single player campaign is enjoyable and I think the positives outweigh the negatives.

Hello, reader. Different folks read different reviews based on which ones have the most thumbs up, thumbs down, or even only the positives, or only the negatives...and some folks try to read as many as they can, regardless of rating or positive/negative opinion of the game, hoping to figure out if it's right for them before purchasing. For Hero Defense, I would specifically encourage you to look at what almost everyone agrees on, whether positive or negative: [b]the grinding[/b].

This is a competent tower defense with a nice visual aesthetic, some alright gameplay, and a corny plot (those can be fun in games). However, upgrading your weapons and your heroes requires a very large amount of runes, gold, and experience, which requires playing the same levels many, many times. The positive reviews and negative reviews will both quite frequently point out that there is a grind, and I will say that it is a very prominent part of the game.

The grind in the game both looks and feels to me like a mobile free-to-play game at times, which I found very disconcerting, personally. There are no purchases in this game using real money as of right now, but it has a grind reminiscent of a "freemium" game, with little stars filling in next to each level as you complete different difficulties, and a second currency (runestones) which you can buy with the less-useful and more plentiful currency (gold). Character progress stagnates without these resources to increase XP gains, weapon damage bonuses, unlock more equippable bonuses, etc.

If even the slightest sensation of a game feeling like a freemium game turns you off on a game, then Hero Defense is not for you, as was the case for me. If you love the feeling of a freemium game without spending real money and dealing with the grind that entails, then Hero Defense might be something you would enjoy if you like the other aspects of the game.

Devs took TD idea and replaced towers with heroes. If there are usually a lot of towers in other TD games, there you can find only 5. Only 5, really? Yeah, it's the main game idea. You need to use heroes to defeat enemies. Every hero is strong against special type of monsters; the guy with arbalet kills vampires in a couple of shots, the old mage with holy water wipes out a pack of skeletons.

There is a city, where you can power up your heroes. You can learn skill for each of them. Tree skill is small, but anyway it's interesting to choose which skill you will learn right now. 
Also, there is rune system. You can put different runes into hero's weapon and when you charge him (upgrade) in the battle, he will receive this bonus. For example, there are damage runes, range runes and more interesting tunes, like "75% change to attack with extra projectile".

So, you pass a mission, go to the town, unlock new heroes/buildings, upgrade your heroes and start new mission. Easy to understand.

What I like

- Fresh gameplay idea
- Easy to undestand
- Good voice acting

What I didn't like
- There are only 5 towers/units. It's a really small amount. Also, you summon them all in every battle, so every mission you play with the same towers.. It's quite boring.
- The TD game is supposed to be strategy game. You need to think about tactic, find the best spots for towers and etc. The main part of gameplay of this game is relocating these 5 towers. When a wave starts you move them to a start point, some of them pass through, you move heroes to the end point. When new wave starts, enemies go on another road, you need to move heroes there. Repeat these actions X times (x - number of waves in the mission) to complete the level.
- The gameplay is the same in all missions. Yeah, there are different roads, some bosses come, and there are shrines for heroes. But, you play the same mission exactly is previous. I would like to see more diversity in enemies, more special skills, something new, which could let me give a desire to continue the game.
- Story is boring. Characters are usual. Dialogues bring nothing interesting to the game.
- Game requires playing previous stages to unlock new ones. I got stuck 3 times because of it. I couldn't finish the game, because i was forced to replay 6 stages to unlock the final mission. But I didn't want to do that.
- I would like to see active heroes’ skills. It's really boring when you can only move them around the map and upgrading them. For example, KR series has 2 active spells, meteor shower and reinforcements. It's really enjoyable to use them. There are no such spells.
- Rune system reminds me free-to-play mobile games. Grind gold, buy runes, combine runes to get stronger one. Repeat. I think, it wasn't a good idea to put this mechanic in PC game. So, it's better to summon heroes instead of upgrading them.
- There are no numbers. You can't see amount of health of monsters, you can't find how much extra damage hero does. It's a bad for mw. I would like to see more information. It's an important part of a strategy game, which helps players to find the best tactic.

This is a fun game, nice presentation. It reminds me a lot of Defender's Quest, which is a pretty big complement. Basically, if you took Defender's Quest, bumped up the graphics (by a lot), and gave it a Halloween vibe, you'd just about have this game. The "towers" you get are heroes, and you only get the ones that come with the game. Instead of placing towers you move your heroes around, which gives you lots to do during each map. You also get upgrades in the form of skill unlocks, runes to add to your weapon, the weapons themselves, and various buildings in your town that, when upgraded, give you bonuses.

The game isn't easy. I'm not the best gamer in the world but not the worst, and if you just play straight through each map on easy, you'll eventually hit a wall. To get over it, you have to go back and play previous maps on higher difficulties, or in challenge mode, to earn gold, runes, and XP.

The game has personality, the different characters have dialog they speak during missions, and there's a bit of a story there.

There are a few things I think they could have done a bit better. Choosing maps requires you to scroll through a horizontal list, which is a little clunky compared to just clicking on a map. Also, the camera is zoomed in a bit on maps, requiring you to scroll around to move your heroes where you want them. This wouldn't be so bad except scrolling is either done with mousing to the edge of the screen or using the arrow keys. WASD is reserved for consumables you deploy during fights.

I haven't tried the multiplayer, but supposedly it offers both co-op and PVP. I can't speak on it since I don't know how it works, but it's there.

All in all though, this is a pretty cool twist on the tower defense genre. The Halloween vibe is awesome if you're into that sort of thing, and I am.

[h1]And here's the many things I didn't like: (Cons)[/h1]

_______________________________

Unfortunately while I wanted to give this game a chance, for the $15.00 price tag it genuinely wasn't worth it to me. I've played plenty of other games around the same price and received significantly more content, that is much more polished. Perhaps it's unethical to compare other games with this, but I feel like it's reasonable to do that; [b]when you pay $15.00 and get a really good game that you like, you come to expect something of the same or really similar quality for that price.[/b] Here's WHY I don't recommend you buy this game.

[b]-The Tutorial[/b]
I know I said the tutorial above was simple, which it was, I have a complaint. While the tutorial was explaining what to do, the monsters in the game continued to move, this really annoyed me because I ended up losing that round because I was trying to read and understand what I was doing, I don't know why but it really rubbed me the wrong way. The other thing that really bothered me was the dialogue popups for the tutorial. They literally come up right in the middle of the screen and they overlap buttons, creatures, everything. I feel like the placement is really invasive, and even after I thought I completed the tutorial, the game was still 'barking orders' and holding my hand through a couple missions. It really bothered me, I just wanted to play at that point but I had to deal with random popups

[b]-Talents[/b]
While the talents that were available were kinda cool, there was like 8 of them per character. I was really concerned with this because I knew that once I max out those talents there's not really much more progression beyond that aside from augmenting and improving my weapons, which might be enough for some people, but I really look for more of that end game content early on because for me it's something to set goals for, and I didn't feel like I could keep myself hooked on talents and weapon upgrades alone

[b]-Poor Balancing[/b]
To be honest, the initial maps while being very visually appealing, are extremely short in length, I'm sure they get longer as you progress through the game; however because of the short length, the poor balancing became extremely noticeable. Even after completing the tutorial the next 1 or 2 missions right after that were relatively difficult (Was forced to use 'freeze' powerups) and I almost lost some lives because of some enemies being too powerful. I understand how the game works with some heroes being stronger to certain enemy types, and I assure you with the utmost confidence that I do/did understand how the mechanics worked and that it wasn't a personal struggle causing me to have difficulty killing creatures. The poor balancing was obvious

[b]-The deal breaker, Microtransactions[/b]
This was what did it for me, I really wanted to give this game a chance, I thought maybe, you know for $15.00 I could live with minimal talents, having some weapons upgrades, etc. everything else wasn't a huge concern. But upon entering into the game in the top right corner I noticed the little Gem icon, and a little 'uh oh' went off in my head.[b] I thought to myself "Joe, don't freak out just yet, it's all gonne be okay, maybe they allow people to buy gems just for cosmetics.", unfortunately that was a lie.[/b] Upon entering the weapons shop, I discovered, to my dismay, that they allowed people to purchase what appeared to be 'legendary' (Orange) weapons augments for 500 Gems/Diamonds, and also in order to upgrade your weapon with diamonds. Being that this game offers Co-Op, PVP, and Ranked matches, I figure this will give players an unreasonably fair advantage over other players that do not intend to purchase Gems/Diamonds.

[b]If you can really support a developer that makes you purchase a game for $15.00 and then hits you with a 'paywall' (Essentially forcing you to purchase gems to enhance your character to a point where you can further progress in the game), by all means purchase this game[/b]; everything but the microtransactions wasn't too awful, and I could see why some people may like this game. However I do feel that the game was poorly balanced to give players more incentive to purchase diamonds to augment and enhance their character. 

Personally, I cannot support a developer that charges $15.00 for a game that allows you to purchase and upgrade/enhance your equipment with gems. I totally wouldn't care or even make a big deal about it if it were cosmetics, but we are talking about the potential for giving one player an advantage over another. If I spent $100.00 in gems, it wouldn't be fair to Billy Joe Bob from Arkansas who didn't buy any gems at all. I've come to expect gear enhancing microtransactions from free games, or even cosmetic microtransactions from purchased games; however when a game that you purchased supports gear enhancing microtransactions. I cannot, and will not stand behind it or it's developers.

I'm not some guy who doesn't support developers at all, I understand there are costs for server maintenance, etc. But there are BETTER types of microtransactions to add to your game to generate revenue, but to allow players to gain an advantage over one another based upon who has the bigger pocketbook, in my eyes, extremely unethical; to be honest I'm a tad shocked that nobody else who has reviewed the product has taken issue with this.

[h1][u][b]What to expect of Hero Defense - Haunted Island:[/b][/u][/h1]
Hero Defense - Haunted Island is a tower defense with a different twist on it: you don't use actual towers, you control them in the form of heroes, while far from being the first in the genre, it is the first time I've played a game where you can have control up to five different characters at the same time and are free to move them as you like.

[h1][u][b]SINGLE-PLAYER EXPERIENCE REVIEW[/b][/u][/h1]
If you're here looking for an opinion on the co-op or PvP mode then move along. You won't find it here since I still didn't have the chance to play them (and I'm not keen on the idea of playing PvP anyway).

[h1][u][b]Tower Defense or Hero Defense?[/b][/u][/h1]
Call it whatever you want, but having control over your towers/heroes is nice and refreshing, I know people that never got into tower defense genre as - in their own words - "you just click and watch" (although personally that is one of the reasons I like it). 

Hero Defense has only five heroes, but they are unique on their own way and each one has defining traits and weak points which you'll have to work with in order to win.

[h1][u][b]Hero Management:[/b][/u][/h1]
The controls are simple enough: 1 to 5 selects the hero, left-click moves them and Space will level them up if you have enough orbs. The game keeps it clean and simple as it should be.

Of course if these controls are not to your liking you can reassign them.

[h1][u][b]Town to rebuild, bonuses to get[/b][/u][/h1]
Everything starts simple enough: pay gold (gems for one building) and get a permanent bonus. 

But as you may already be thinking: Grinding? Yes. Read below.

[h1][u][b]Grinding[/b][/u][/h1]
This is what could be the ugly part for me. Grinding is a VERY delicate balance that either makes a game good and tolerable or downright insufferable. And I personally can be very much fickle about this as well.

Hero Defense does it… Mildly right. While the beginning will certainly be bumpy and hard, the game has a nice, and may I add cathartic, surprise later on that will tell the difficulty of grinding to go suck a big one. But it's there merely to help you as town and weapon upgrades will get ridiculously expensive.

[h1][u][b]Skill trees[/b][/u][/h1]
Every hero has its skill tree which will define their own style. Most of them are clear cut on what the hero does: focus on a single target, deals with crowds and so on.

For those who played games which give you tons of skills and makes you pull your hair just thinking what to do, what skills to leave behind, Hero Defense allows you to have all skills at once. 

However you'll have to grind and level up your heroes accordingly. Some will love this, others will not. This left a mixed taste in my mouth; as in initially sweet but sour aftertaste. Why? While I do love having everything, it takes away some potential unique builds that would give characters even more distinction.

[h1][u][b]Heroes and runes[/b][/u][/h1]
There's the usual tower defense: you get resources to start, put a hero, kill enemies, get money, level up your heroes, put another hero... Nothing out of the usual.

What makes it unique then? 
Runes does.

Runes are how you make each hero unique on their own even with their skill tress. You can give runes to turn a mild damaging hero into something powerful, or give an attack speed rune to that slow attacking hero and watch them fill the screen with attacks.

Runes are scaled as this: Common - Uncommon - Rare - Epic. As you can imagine Epic runes will take the longest to get as they are fairly expensive, but at least you are granted to get one, but you'll still need to luck out to get the one you want (power up, speed up, extra projectile chance…).

The game has a simple craft system defined as "Merge" which allows you swap lower rarity runes into better quality ones. Use all of the same type and it'll ensure you a better rarity rune of that type. If you don't, you'll need luck as the result will be random.

[h1][u][b]Complaints and suggestions[/b][/u][/h1]
Hero Defense may not receive a ton of awards, but it sure does try hard and the efforts of the team behind it clearly show. But the game, like 100% of everything out there, has its share of problems.

1) The loading time to use the Town is unacceptable. It is far too long and wears down on the player really fast.

2) Hero AI can be random or downright stupid at times. They tend to focus on enemies in the middle instead of the last in the group. While manual targeting DOES help, options of automatic targeting (most health, etc.) would be greatly appreciated.

3) Shrines costs gem. No problem. Shrines are permanent until you build something on them. No problem. Shrine cost increases with each one you build. No problem. The game doesn't keep track where you built shrines. [b][i][u]THAT'S a problem.[/u][/i][/b]

4) This is a very little something but bugs me to no end: whenever you finish a map with a victory there's no Restart button. Sounds like nitpicking, but this is a game about farming to a certain degree and having to go back to the World Map to choose the map you want again gets tiresome.

5.1) The game has only five types of enemies and while they try to be distinct from each other they always feel "samey" when you reach higher levels. Since every enemy can have about every ability (with some exceptions), the only thing you'll end worrying about in most cases is which hero should fight which enemy.

5.2) Enemy abilities feel uninspired as they only affect themselves, enemies will never actively hamper your heroes' progress. Enemies could have other things like swapping heroes' position, swapping one hero for another, blocking one hero, reducing their range or attack speed, punishing players for clustering heroes too much or leaving them too far from each other…

6.1) Another complaint is the lack of runes that can give unique effects like Poisoning enemies, slowing them and similar effects to somewhat emulate other characters.

6.2) Lack of variety in weapons. While rune slot upgrades are good it'd give much more character definition having equipable weapons that increases their attack rate, attack strength or range.

7) And this feels more like nitpicking from me, but the game gets [i][b]too easy once[/b][/i] you get everything; town upgrades, powerful Epic runes, and weapons maxed. While it does feel immensely good crush Insane difficulty levels that were getting under your skin, that also loses its charm fast. And no, Endless is not a solution for this, Survival Mode in tower defenses never felt accomplishing or anything since, you know, they don't have end. Maybe a fifth difficulty could solve this.

8) Camera control. You don't have free control of your camera and more often than not you can end up having an obstacle obstructing your view which may cause anything from an annoyance to costing you the entire map.

[h1][u][b]Final words[/b][/u][/h1]
Hero Defense - Haunted Island is a hidden gem that is still being polished by Happy Tuesday even after taking off its Early Access status, but it's far from being bad, broken or unplayable. As I've just noted, this game has its issues, feels like it still has a lot of potential, but it's very well worth playing.

In the end its lack of diversity of enemies, runes and weapons can make the game feel repetitive for some people, but Hero Defense - Haunted Island was charming enough to keep me captive for good 55 hours (as of this writing). And that's not counting the co-op mode which I haven't tested yet.

Knowing Happy Tuesday is still working and releasing patches on *drums rolls* Tuesdays to address known issues and seeing that they at least care enough to ask and answer people in their Community Hub is another good thing I want to point. If you have the chance, give Hero Defense a try.

Hero defence is a tower defence game which I was hoping to really enjoy but left me feeling somewhat disappointed.

It's got some good ideas with using up to five heroes which can move around instead of towers in fixed locations.
You can level up the heroes weapons and attach runes to sockets which effects their attack in the game when you 'charge' them up - the equivalent of upgrading a tower in other TD Games.
The heroes gain experience when you complete a level and gain permanent levels which reward you with skill points, these allow you to upgrade each heroes skills in their own tech tree.

Unfortunately there are too many problems with the game which really lets it down.

Firstly, there's very few enemy units. There are 5 monsters which are each weak to a different hero and then several similar bosses. At some points you need to decide which hero to bring into the field and where's best to place them but when you have all five out and there's only one.. and on some occasions two.. kinds of monster wave it really doesn't matter because you just put all five heroes together where the monsters are coming from and destroy them without any tactic needed.

Next, there are very few maps available, The game is padded out by having to repeat maps on a higher difficulty which gives you a star for each difficulty you complete each map on,  however, you only need 17 stars to unlock the last level required for the final boss making the campaign really short. There's an additional map but that's only a requirement of 24 stars, given that you can get over 50 stars it makes half of the level difficulties pointless besides getting a higher reward. This leads onto another problem I have with the game..

Grinding.. in order to advance in the game you need gold coins and gems.. at first it's a reasonable amount but after a few levelling up the amount drastically increases. To upgrade weapons, it costs 5, 10, 20, 40, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600 gems.. This needs to be done for all 5 weapons for a total of nearly 11k gems.
There's 2 ways of getting the gems, first is by completing challenges on the maps, Each map has one challenge which will reward you with a number of gems, completing them on easy gives you 5, normal gives 10, hard gives 15 and insane gives 20. These increments are so small and doesn't match up with the difficulty and time it takes to complete them making Level 1 on Easy being the quickest way to farm them.. meaning to get the required gems for levelling up your weapons you will need to repeat the exact same thing 2,175 times. Even if you did the farming on insane it's still 544 times you will need to complete them but these are a lot harder and can be less reliable to complete as well as take longer than doing Easy 4 times. This leaves you with more loading time than game time.
Gems can also be used to upgrade the forge which give a small improvement to your heroes and this can cost more than upgrading weapons. There's two rune packs you can purchase using gems, one is 100 gems and the other is 300 gems.
All of this adds up to an absolute ridiculous amount of farming maps over and over and over again and not giving you anything new to do.
The second method of obtaining gems is buy converting gold coins into gems at the bank, To get the most efficiency out of this you need to upgrade the bank allowing you to trade in higher amounts of gold for a better ratio of gems and a higher discount on the cost but to upgrade the bank it costs a lot of gold coins in the first place so it will take a while to farm the gold before you can get a nice amount of gems coming in from the bank as well. You will also need the gold to upgrade the academy which allows you to level up the heroes skills and gain more XP.

Having this second currency and the stupidly high amount required suggests it was intended to be a premium currency for a Facebook/mobile game where you can buy your way through and not having to do this grinding. While it's nice that there aren't micro-transactions they seem to have forgotten to make the game a little more friendly to get by playing the game.

The interface (dragging the heroes onto the level) and the fixed camera angles also suggest that it was aimed for mobile gaming. While I can just about tolerate them both they're not exactly great.

Once you've completed the campaign there's an endless mode, this has 500 waves so it's not endless as such but it's extremely difficult to achieve given that even with a highly decked out team of heroes you are massively out numbered and they seem to take a lot of damage so getting through the first few waves can be a challenge.. Unfortunately unless you win all 500 waves the reward you get is absolutely horrible and not worth the time and effort it takes leaving endless mode pointless unless you want to just burn some time for the sake of it.

My final problem with this game is the multiplayer, I find the whole system for it terrible.
There's two modes.. PvP and Co-op.
PvP can be done in ranked or a friendly match, There's only a couple of maps available for this and works by picking one of the three monsters displayed to be sent to your opponents side of the map. Personally this doesn't appeal to me and find it really dull. You're given a decent collection of runes to set up your heroes so you don't need to worry about other people being able to get a greater setup than you which is nice.

Co-op, which is what I got the game for, is abysmal. There's one map and that's it.
On top of that you need to unlock your heroes in the campaign so co-op isn't fully available to you until both players have progressed enough through the campaign meaning you can't jump right into this mode - like I did which was a shot in the leg for me. After we both unlocked characters and got some better set up we still found ourselves out numbered and unable to deal with the first few waves.
The devs have said they plan on changing this very soon to allow people to be able to jump in quicker without having to progress through the story first, I'm not sure if that will change the difficulty and setup or not. So this may still mean you will need to grind for gems/money to get better runes and levelling up your heroes plus their skills.


Currently at the time of writing this, there's an event going on which rewards players with gems and money a few people can also win rune bags which contain runes I believe and tickets which can get you Razor products as a prize these can also gain you "additional rewards" which i assume will be gold/gems, Steam keys for the game can also be won. These are rare to get but what makes this annoying is that each time a person wins any of these a message is displayed across the screen and are incredibly irritating and distracting. (there's also a bug that prevents certain features working while these messages are displayed which can take several minutes to finish displaying)


Overall, the game has some nice ideas, an interesting concept for a Tower Defence game but there's such a lack of content that makes the game feel underwhelming unfinished. The grinding in the game is not in the slightest bit fun.
You can get some hours of entertainment and might be worth it when it's on sale (I bought at 70% off and is a reasonable price) but at full price and in its current state it's not worth it in my opinion.
A lot of work needs to be done to this game to make it  friendlier to play and more content is needed before I can recommend this at full price or as a finished game. I hope that changes are made to fix these problems because it has a really good chance of being a great game and different from all the other TD games available.

Sorry that it's such a long review but I feel that a lot of these needed to be addressed and things I wish will get tweaked to be a more enjoyable game as I really wanted to like this.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Tower Defense is by far my favorite genre. Therefore I've played already a couple of games, knowing different concepts and ideas. 

Hero Defense - Haunted Island is (somewhat) unique to a regular tower defense. Instead of building different towers you gain the control of up to 5 heroes. Defending several lines, you have to move appropriate heroes across the map to fight incoming enemies.

The heroes itself can be leveled-up on the map, activating runes (boosts), once you've earned enough orbs by killing enemies. Beating a map you will be rewarded with gold and gems, which will be used to unlock more powerful boosts and to upgrade different buildings and weaponry. Unlike a few negative reviews mentioned, it isn't an endless grind, for my taste way too short (15-18 hours playtime).

No worries if it sounds weird to you, the tutorial is a prime example of how a tutorial has to be. Many developers can take a leaf out of this book. Very detailed and on point while you are playing the story mode - A+.


[h1]A short summary[/h1]

[b]Pros[/b]
[list][*]unique concept / idea
[*]nice graphics, perfectly fits into the game
[*]A+ tutorial, detailed and on point
[*]RPG elements, build your hero to your liking
[*]different lines to defend
[*]fast forward feature[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]
[list][*]overall too short (for me as TD fan... 14 maps, 4 difficulties)
[*]bonus map (after defeating 'count') rewards way too much gold, decreases replay value of other maps and massively decreases time needed to level-up buildings and heroes.
[*]too small playerbase for pvp/coop, played just 2 matches yet (for whose who like to pvp/coop)[/list]

Finally have managed to finish Skyrim and get all achievements so it is finally review time. I'm gonna say my opinion for all DLCs and the main storyline, aswell as throw in what my all time favourite questline was  so [b] spoiler warning [/b] :)

[h3] Main Storyline [/h3]

It definitely didn't WOW me but I did enjoy it, especially because im a sucker for dragons. It just was a little underwhelming at times, especially when compared to some of the side quests. With that said though it still was a great story, just slowly becoming an absolute powerhouse and uncovering the mystery behind Alduin and lets not forget the places you have to go to, honestly just the whole world in general is beautiful (I took sooo many screenshots). The end part I enjoyed the most but the start will always be iconic. 

[h3] Dawnguard DLC [/h3]

I did the dawnguard dlc pretty early on in my playthrough and I loved it. The storyline adds some interesting characters and a bunch of new followers which I chose Serana of course. When it came to choosing to fight against the vampires or become one of them I chose to fight against them, however, I've heard the pro-vampire side is more interesting so make sure you take that into count ig. I personally wanted to fuck them up even if it was the less interesting side but you do you. Overall, I think its an awesome expansion to the base game and gives you so much stuff to try out such as a whole new form, vampire lord, with its own skill tree and busted abilities. 

[h3] Hearthfire DLC [/h3]

I wasn't gonna review this dlc because it's just mainly roleplaying and customisation but why nottt. It's a nice little addition for anyone who enjoys the more relaxing side of Skyrim. I was a big fan of the whole building your own home part and being able to decide where you want your home to be out of 3 locations (or just build 3 houses to use all the locations lmao). I will say the houses don't change and just are the same layout and structure with all 3 which I felt kinda disappointed with. You can choose different add-ons to your house to kinda change it up a bit but the structure is the same. So overall its a cool addition to the base game and worth giving it a try if you are into customising, just don't expect insane customisation options. 

[h3] Dragonborn DLC [/h3]

Probably my favourite DLC overall. Travelling to Solstheim, exploring the island and learning more about Miraak and the history of the Dragonborn adds so much to the base game. It honestly feels like a whole other adventure rather than just extra content for the base game. Miraak is just an insane character to be introduced too and following his story just from the start you want to know more. Reading a black book than getting teleported to Apocrypha was so cool and the enemies you encounter were pre hard and horrifying to look at such as the squid looking seekers. This addition also brings the "flying dragon" mechanic which I thought was sick, though you don't actually get to control the dragon which is kinda disappointing but I still thought it was sick (I'm a HUGE fan of dragons in general). I could say more but this review is already so long so ill stop it here for this DLC but overall I LOVED this DLC. 

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]

To end this review I will say my favourite questline in the whole game was the Thieves Guild questline. The Nightingales are fucking awesome and the betrayal actually had me surprised. The outfit you get aswell has to be the best fit look-wise. So yeah thats my Skyrim review, pre long but it honestly deserves a long review but if you skipped most of it fair enough lol. A true classic RPG, one of the MUSTS I think any RPG fan ought to experience at least once. Thanks to an extremely active modding community, even this many years on, this already replayable gem remains well worth coming back to. DON'T IGNORE THE MODDING COMMUNITY on this one. Their collective labour of love on this project over the years has only served to made this timeless classic all the more fun not just to play, but to replay, time and again.

At a minimum, in 2026, even for a first playthrough (there are still some of you out there, I know!) I would recommend considering using mods and/or time-tested curated collections (modsets) that preserve the vanilla story experience while bringing the graphic quality in line with much more modern titles, as well as peppering in some quality of life enhancements most of us would consider must-haves in 2026. The bit of extra time spent will be well worth the effort. 

Beyond that, some of the other mods/modsets out there basically offer entire new looks, new gameplay, even entire new storylines. For me, this is a title that just keeps on delivering more value every time I revisit it.

As a final note on the Anniversary Edition and/or Upgrade: that's a mixed bag. I wouldn't really recommend it on its own, especially for new players. If you can get it at a good price on offer, the real attraction there is that modders have developed some stunning and massively comprehensive (and FREE*) experiences that require some of the Anniversary Upgrade content assets.  I'd personally recommend waiting until at least a 2nd playthrough (or later) before checking any of those out, though. 

*That said, please do consider throwing some support the mod developers' way, if you end up using any of the many collections that can easily deliver scores, if not hundreds of additional hours of engaging gameplay.

Set in the rugged, dragon-haunted northern realm of Skyrim amid a bitter civil war, the narrative centers on your destiny as the Dragonborn—the only hero capable of stopping Alduin, the World-Eater. While the main storyline is straightforward, the real magic lies in the world itself and its countless faction questlines, Daedric quests, and hidden lore. The Anniversary Edition enriches this further with dozens of new quests, artifacts, and dungeons from the Creation Club, though the way many of these additions are introduced through generic courier notes can feel slightly disconnected from the core narrative.

[h2]Gameplay Mechanics and Combat[/h2]
Freedom of progression is still Skyrim’s greatest strength. Whether you want to play as a stealth archer, a heavy-armored warrior, a dual-casting mage, or an alchemist-merchant, the classless skill system lets you shape your character organically. Additions like Survival Mode, fishing, camping, and new spells and gear add welcome depth and fresh ways to play. That said, melee combat still feels somewhat weightless and dated compared to modern action-RPGs, and companion AI can occasionally get in the way.

[h2]Graphics and Atmosphere[/h2]
Atmospherically, Skyrim remains iconic. Wandering across misty pine forests, ancient Nordic ruins, and glowing aurora-lit tundras while Jeremy Soule’s legendary soundtrack plays in the background creates an unforgettable mood. Even with upgraded lighting, textures, and smoother performance, the engine inevitably shows its age in stiff character animations and occasional Bethesda quirks, yet the sheer beauty and scale of the world easily compensate.

[h2]Overall Impressions[/h2]
The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Anniversary Edition is the ultimate, content-packed version of one of the most influential open-world RPGs ever made. Despite dated melee mechanics, aging animations, and minor technical rough edges, its boundless freedom, rich atmosphere, and sheer volume of adventure make it a timeless classic well worth diving into.

[h1] My beloved. Our sanctuary. Skyrim. [/h1] 

It is true what you have almost certainly heard: [i] The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim [/i] is a generational piece of playable narrative. An entire world, filled to its brim with untold stories, mysteries, and places to explore.

For a game that is now over 15 years old, I have never played a title so enriched with true love in every corner. From the very first time I played Skyrim on my Xbox 360, I was enthralled in its ever-expansive playable world. The options of classes, unique weapons, multitudes of NPCs, and magnificent structures scatter the conflicted rocky peaks of Skyrim from bottom to top. Underground, to the highest mountains, there is something to find. 

[h3] Classes and Perk Options [/h3] 
Skyrim boasts an astounding amount of build choices. Want to be an ancient dreadnaught with heavy plated armor, a giant sword, and a voice powerful enough to make your opponents flee? You can. Want to be a slim and sleek thief, prioritizing stealth, bows, and paralyzing your foes before they even have a chance to fight back? You can. Even if you wish to spew fire and lightning from your palms, igniting your enemies, scorching them to crisps? You absolutely can.

Each of the aforementioned classes can also benefit from sub-classes which you can spec into if you so choose. [b] Alchemy [/b], for example, can be used to create any potion you can think of. These potions can benefit you so tremendously that even the biggest, scaliest dragons stand no chance. Don't care for potions? Consider [b] Enchanting [/b] your armor and weapons. These enchants can be used to steal the life essence from your enemies, or provide fire immunity to yourself. Whatever choice of class you choose, your sub-class will improve whichever aspect you wish.

[h3] Unique Weapons [/h3]
The weapons of this unforgiving land reflect its grueling nature. Of course there are your traditional weapons. Think iron and steel swords, axes, maces. Fantastical metals like dwarven alloys, enchanted ice, and malachite, a glass-like material. Most impressive are the late game metals and materials. Take ebony for example. Ebony is sort of volcanic glass made of the literal blood of a god ("badass" would be an immense understatement). There is also armor made of the bones of resurrected dragons. Which one you clad yourself with is entirely up to you.

[h3] Story, Lore, and the NPCs [/h3]
Now lets get into the real meat and potatoes of this game. You will get to experience a beautiful story as you chase the once dead god of time, a literal World-Eater, through numerous trials that will test you and your choice of class in many different ways. Find ancient ruins, piece together your journey learning bits of information to form a plan, and work with countless NPCs to progress towards your goal. Did the main story not provide enough explanation as to the time before or during your tour of Skyrim? Luckily for you, there are literal HUNDREDS of books with you can read through to expand your understanding. Some of which are written by scholars in a professional manner, some written by explorers and curious minds explaining their findings. All of which giving you deep insight to almost anything in the game. I'm serious, read the books. They give a lot of color to some of the rough sketches of lore given to the player throughout the game.

The DLCs also provide wonderful story arcs of their own, without breaking any base game lore, but rather accentuating it, providing both broad and minor details, which help to paint the full picture. I personally am a massive fan of the Dragonborn DLC, however my friend much prefers the Dawnguard DLC. They all are worth atleast one playthrough.

The NPCs of Skyrim make the world feel lived in. Fully furnished houses, people working their crops, running businesses, or walking the many paths of Skyrim, hunting game or travelling from one hold to another. No matter where you are, there is probably someone else there, too. Sometimes these strangers will be hostile. Sometimes friendly. Most impressively though, is sometimes they will tell you to back away, if you listen to them you might make it out alive- if you don't, prepare for a fight to the death.

[h3] Summary [/h3]
if you find yourself on the fence, consider this. Skyrim is like the Halo: Reach of Bethesda games. Arguably its greatest effort before [i] the great drought [/i] of nothing for 15 years. Probably in excess of 200,000 mods, and enough content to actually get thousands of hours of unique gameplay. As stated earlier, I have played this game since it was on Xbox 360, and I still find new and interesting things all the time.

The Review

Total War: WARHAMMER II is an incredible strategy game that combines large-scale real-time battles with deep turn-based empire management. It takes everything that makes the Total War series great and mixes it with the fantastic fantasy world of Warhammer.

The variety of factions is one of the biggest strengths. Each race feels completely different, with unique units, buildings, technologies, and playstyles. Whether you're commanding massive armies of High Elves, hordes of Skaven, terrifying Lizardmen, or the deadly Dark Elves, there is always something new to learn.

The battles are absolutely spectacular. Watching hundreds of units clash at the same time never gets old, and positioning your troops correctly can completely change the outcome of a fight. Managing your economy, territories, diplomacy, and armies on the campaign map adds another layer of strategy that keeps things interesting.

The biggest downside is the learning curve. There are a huge number of systems to understand, and new players can easily feel overwhelmed. Campaigns can also take a very long time to complete, and some battles can become repetitive once you've played for dozens of hours.

Despite that, Total War: WARHAMMER II is one of the best fantasy strategy games ever made. The incredible faction variety, massive battles, deep campaign mechanics, and enormous amount of replayability make it a game you can easily spend hundreds of hours playing.

I really wanted to enjoy this game because I've been a long-time fan of the historical Total War titles. The battles are visually impressive, and there's clearly a lot of content, but Warhammer just wasn't for me.

My biggest issue is how much the game revolves around magic, abilities, monsters, and faction-specific mechanics. Compared to games like Napoleon or Empire, where good tactics and positioning could carry you through most battles, Warhammer feels much more dependent on bringing the exact right units to counter the enemy. It often felt like I was fighting the game's mechanics rather than enjoying large-scale strategy.

The Vortex campaign also felt overly complicated for a first playthrough, with rituals and race-specific objectives adding pressure when I was just trying to learn the game.

My other major complaint is multiplayer. Like other Total War titles, there is still a noticeable input/synchronisation delay when playing campaign battles with friends. Every command feels slightly delayed compared to single player, and after experiencing it across multiple Total War games, it's something that really takes away from the enjoyment.

I can see why many people love Warhammer, especially if they're fans of the fantasy setting. Unfortunately, I much prefer the historical Total War games where battles feel more grounded and success depends more on battlefield tactics than on spells, monsters, and unique faction mechanics. For me, this entry just wasn't as enjoyable as the classic Total War experience.

I have mixed feelings about this game. I love it and have spent countless hours with it, yet I can't shake the feeling that it falls just short of its full potential. At its best, it delivers some of the most exciting fantasy strategy gameplay available. Few games can match the thrill of commanding dragons, hydras, giant monsters, and other fantastical creatures on a massive battlefield.
The fantasy setting is both a strength and a weakness. The sheer variety of units makes battles spectacular, but it also creates a steep learning curve. In historical strategy games, most players intuitively understand the roles of spearmen, cavalry, and archers. Here, understanding whether an axe-swinging dwarf, a flamethrower-wielding rat, a giant wheel of death or a flying monster is effective in a given situation often requires experience and experimentation. This can make evaluating army strength and deciding when to engage an enemy surprisingly difficult, especially for newer players.
The campaign layer offers tremendous strategic depth. Every faction plays differently, encouraging exploration and experimentation with new mechanics, economies, and army compositions. The game constantly presents meaningful decisions, and managing a large empire can become an incredibly complex puzzle. Sometimes that complexity borders on overwhelming, but it also creates a rewarding experience for players who enjoy mastering intricate systems.
My biggest criticism is the pacing on higher difficulties. Because automatic battle results are often unfavorable, many engagements must be played manually. Since campaigns involve a huge number of battles, this can significantly slow progress on the strategic map. Over time, fighting similar armies repeatedly can become repetitive, especially when the outcome is already fairly obvious.
Despite its flaws, the game strikes an impressive balance between grand strategy and tactical combat. The combination of empire management, faction diversity, and large-scale fantasy warfare creates an experience that few strategy games can rival. While it may not fully realize all of its ambitions, it remains one of the most engaging and ambitious fantasy strategy games out there.

As of this date, I haven't yet switched to Warhammer III. "Why?" You may ask, given its better siege mechanics, diplomacy, and so on and so forth... One, my laptop would likely burst into flames after prolonged gameplay, but two - and more importantly - I can't simply leave this one behind, not yet. I have played it for 500+ hours and have not yet managed to play all of the factions I wanted to explore. Their individual “quests”, to be exact - the Vortex campaigns. 

Discounting the basic ones - fighting for the Vortex itself - which you can enjoy only once or twice, the campaigns tied with the stories of individual lords have so much to offer. I cannot recommend them enough - Huntsmarshal's expedition into the jungle, Snikch's quest for the power source, Bretonnia's crusade, amber hunt of the Twilight sisters, Tombkings' hunt for the Pyramid, Elvish Batman seeking revenge… - all engaging you from the very start and so, so rewarding due to the included cut-scenes.

If you are new to TW series, like fantasy, can appreciate some absurd flavours here and there and are willing to tolerate some mechanical imbalance, TW Warhammer 2 is for you. It is simpler than other titles (less intense than W3), easier to master, and therefore makes for a good entry into the series. Not to mention, the campaigns to which I sing praises here, serve as perfect introductions to each of the included factions, teaching you the ins and outs of their respective gameplay styles. Plus, once you get down to it, it may feel like many different games merged in one.

I am just in awe of the plethora of unique gameplay styles associated with each faction, including the more subtle differences connected with individual lords. The uniqueness of each faction that was achieved in TW Warhammer series is unsurpassed. It does not make for an exactly well-balanced game, but the different gameplay styles are so interesting you'll be willing to let it slide. Adding to the havoc, but very appreciated still, is the presence of magic. If you've ever wanted to throw a fireball (or something larger) into a deftly assembled blob of enemy units, you can definitely do so here (and be duly annoyed when your own army gets hit by a warp lightning for a 5th time in a single battle).

As hinted above, I also love Warhammer titles for their special combination of grim-dark and parodic vibes - it is completely unhinged. I still keep discovering new things to be amused by – yes, yesss.

All in all, W2 may not offer much compared to W3 with regard to general gameplay (except perhaps more peace without the incessant demon invasions), but its value lies in its Vortex campaigns, which, in my humble opinion, make it worth of your attention even today.
