THE SHORT REVIEW:
Button bashing supernatural beat em up, with a good plot that is poorly told. Looks alright, but plays like a mediocre piece of shit.

THE LONG REVIEW:
I think it was Einstein who said this, or maybe Confucius, or perhaps I just read it in a fortune cookie somewhere: "a man might have the ambition to shoot for the stars, but what does that matter if he just ends up shooting himself in the foot" 

Which sums up this game really nicely. The devs have looked at the likes of God Of War and Devil May Cry, and thought to themselves "hey! we can do that, an indie studio making a AAA blockbuster action button basher". And, well...the end result is perhaps only surprising to them, but they were wrong to think they could achieve this. 

For an indie title this is quite lavish narratively, in that it is trying to conjure up this deep story of a war between heaven and hell, and spends a lot of time somewhat ham-fistedly laying out this "epic" plot. Unfortunately as a game it's rather mediocre. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2206835394

You play as a guy called Desmond, which, if Assassins Creed has taught us nothing else, is synonymous with being a boring bastard. Desmond is seemingly both an executive for a company and also a bare knuckle fistfighter in the underground bare knuckle fistfighting scene (it's not that much of a stretch, as I've heard Elon Musk likes to fight with wild rabid bears in his spare time) 

Yet despite these massively contradictory talents in business and bashing peoples faces in, Desmond is still a dull boy (apparently this fate was determined the moment his parents named him Desmond. It's a "Desmond" type thang) and the story is...well, lets be frank here...a bit stoopid.

You start off in hell and have demonic abilities. Beat up some kind of horned demon, seriously Hulk out and skull fook it to death with it's own ripped off horn, and then it cuts back to earlier. We see Desmond mucking up a business deal, where his boss (who also happens to be his father) says something ridiculously obvious and on the nose, like "I would sell your soul to Lucifer himself if it made this deal go through". He also says Desmond is a massive loser, with a big fat stinky poo face to boot.

Then we see Desmond losing a bare knuckle fistfight (in case you forgot he's a bare knuckle fistfighter) to someone who appears to be demonically possessed. His dear Pappy was at the fight and gives him a chewing for not only losing the business deal, but the fight too, and lays a massively shitty guilt trip on him about how he's glad Desmonds mum didn't live to see how crap he is. Because she surely would kill herself seeing what a loser she gave birth to.

Desmond ends up in a funk, and what he needs is to spend some time with his girlfriend, who he just proposed to. The only problem there is that he comes home to find her in bed with his best friend. Enraged Desmond sets out to murder him, but decides to kill himself instead because he's such a massive loser.

As a suicide he goes to hell, finds out he's the prophesied one who will save Hell, and then he strikes a deal with Lucifer to be a vessel for the power of the devil.

Two hours into the "game" and I'm thinking "WTF? You know what this beat em up needs? more beating up of things, and less goddamn cutscenes for the shit story" It was 25 / 75 between the wonky mildly entertaining mauling of monsters, and sitting out an earnestly produced narrative that is unfortunately a bit crap. 

To me these games have three elements: combat, setpieces, and plot. So far Devils Hunt has been mediocre in all three departments. 

The fighting is ish. Responsive, relatively capable in terms of animation / hit detection / feedback, but never as polished or enjoyable as the top dogs in the genre.  Desmond also starts off with a painfully dull amount of moves, so repetition sets in pretty quickly, and the enemies are rather bland punch-sponges on hard.

The spectacle is slightly shonky: there's hordes of demons running through a city...witness the terrifying sight of this humongous mob that can sometimes be as high as THREE or FOUR in number as they run amok.

Watch a building get smashed down by a giant monster, and see the framerate tank just enough to lessen the impact of the otherwise cool destruction. 

See what would be otherwise impressive graphics, lighting and particle effects...if only they weren't a bit washed out. Marvel at the super smooth animation...if only it were super smooth and not actually a smidge whiffy.

As for the plot...not impressed so far. Trying way too hard to set up serious melodrama and tension, only to puncture it  with bad dialogue and a hero who has all the charisma of a particularly uncharismatic plank of wood (he also looks like Frank West from Capcoms 'Dead Rising' made an ugly baby with Henry Rollins)

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2208240369

Ninja Theory managed to meld a sense of reality to the unreal with DMC, and on the other side Capcom can always be relied upon to churn out stylish stupidity, but clearly these devs don't have Ninja Theory' talent for writing or Capcoms brazen balls to not give a shit about how ridiculously bad a plot is. 

THIS IS SERIOUS DRAMA!! And they're going to drown you in cutscenes like they were Hideo Kojima until YOU UNDERSTAND JUST HOW SERIOUS IT IS! And that would be fine if only they weren't, well, a bit shit at it. And, you know, if the actual gameplay  backed up this effort by not being shit.

But they are shit at telling an otherwise passable story, and the gameplay is shit. After 2 hours I'm bored with this "game" now. It's janky, overblown and yet underwhelming.

This is a VERY soft recommendation because personally I loved the hilarious dumb jank this game had, absolute euro jank that's trying it's very hardest and it's hard not to bless it. The combat was quite fun as well once you knew how to properly use your skills and the story was actually pretty good if incredibly silly. But it has some MASSIVE technical flaws, soft crashes, hard crashes, bugs, glitches, the whole shabang - it was released in a messy state and still is a mess sadly. As usual I break things down:

Pros:
- Fun and challenging combat
- Lots of variety and tactical play with a great skills system
- Adorably janky and hilarious
- Amazing art direction
- Great soundtrack
- Interesting story, got me curious about the Equilibrium series of books the game is based on

Cons:
- The angel enemies are absolutely the worst thing ever
- Committing attacks and being unable to dodge out of combos makes standard attacks quite frustrating at times
- Exploration gameplay is dull, no platforming or anything to keep you engaged as it's mostly straight lines with some upgrade pickups off the beaten path
- Lots of bugs and glitches
- Poor optimization despite the lower budget graphics
- Can hard crash your entire PC in fullscreen mode

It's a game I really adore because of how hiilariously jank it is but it's definitely a game with real heart and soul put into it, a small team trying to make the best game possible and that's very obvious throughout the entire run time. I can really appreciate it for what it's going for and while the combat isn't amazing, it's still a lot of fun and its skill system was actually pretty great and I can see it being a lot more fun in an action MMO rather than a spectacle fighter beat 'em up. The story was interesting if hilariously dumb at points and the soundtrack really helped the game out a lot - Devil's Hunt has everything going for it to be a beloved euro jank cult classic.

Sadly those technical problems, especially the hard crashes (play in borderless windowed with your task manager set to always be on top, saves you from having to reset your PC) are huge black marks against the game and may hurt your enjoyment of the game. And also those angels can seriously go screw themselves with a big pitchfork.

If you see it on sale, I'd say it's well worth buying - it's not a long game and thankfully the angels only appear in two sections so it doesn't outstay its welcome and is very fun and charming the vast majority of its runtime. Just do NOT go in expecting Devil May Cry, Bayonetta or anything of that caliber, it's fun but not on the level of masterpieces such as those.

It's not hard, whatsoever; but it's pretty damn cool to be so OP.

Right, so back in 2016 when this came out as an actual physical thing you could touch with your hands - remember those?  - I was absolutely mad for Mystic Vale. Proper obsessed. Now, several years later, I've found it on Steam, and I'm delighted to report it's still brilliant.

Mystic Vale is a deck-building game, except, and here's the clever bit, you don't actually build a deck. Stay with me. Instead of hoarding cards like a dragon with commitment issues, you upgrade the ones you've already got by slapping see-through improvements on them. It's called "card crafting," which sounds like something your nan does on a rainy Tuesday, but it's genuinely innovative. You're essentially Pimp My Ride-ing your cards, yeah? Xzibit would be proud.

The Gameplay? Here's where it gets interesting. Every card in your starting deck has these "blight" symbols on them, which are basically little warnings that say "draw too many of us and your turn's ruined, mate." So every turn you're playing this game of chicken with yourself - do I draw another card and risk it all, or do I play it safe like a coward? It's push your luck mechanic and it's brilliant. It's like that feeling when you're waiting for toast to pop and you're not sure if it's going to be perfect or on fire.

You spend mana - magic points, keep up - to buy advancements that permanently stick onto your cards. So that rubbish starting card gradually becomes less rubbish. You're building synergies, creating combos, basically becoming a tactical genius or at least feeling like one, which is almost as good.

They've thrown in expansions like Vale of Magic, Vale of the Wild, and Mana Storm, which is great because the base game, while solid, would get a bit samey otherwise. These expansions chuck in new mechanics and cards, keeping things fresh without making you feel like you need a degree to understand what's happening. It's that sweet spot of "oh, that's new and interesting" without "oh god, I need to read a manual."

Once you've played it enough, you start seeing the optimal strategies, and suddenly you're doing the same thing every game. The AI's decent - it'll give you a game - but it's not going to replace actual human opponents who can properly wind you up with their annoying perfect plays.

Mystic Vale is one of those rare digital adaptations that actually works. Nomad Games have done a proper job here - it's faithful to the physical version but takes advantage of all the digital conveniences like not having to manually shuffle transparent cards, which I imagine would be an absolute nightmare in real life.

If you like strategic card games and you're bored of the same old deck-building formula, this is worth your time. Like finding an old favorite game on Steam and realizing it still absolutely slaps. Just don't expect it to change your life or anything. It's a card game, not therapy.

Mystic Vale, developed and published by Nomad Games, is a thoughtfully crafted digital adaptation of the innovative card game originally designed by John D. Clair and published by Alderac Entertainment Group. At its heart, Mystic Vale introduces a unique spin on the deck-building genre through a mechanic known as “card crafting,” where instead of adding new cards to your deck, you upgrade existing ones by layering transparent advancements. This mechanic, faithfully translated to digital format, offers a refreshing strategic challenge while maintaining a smooth and intuitive interface that supports both single-player and multiplayer gameplay.

The premise of the game is rooted in a magical, nature-themed setting where players take on the role of druidic clans attempting to cleanse a cursed valley and restore its natural beauty. This theme is well-supported by the game’s visual presentation, with richly illustrated card art, ambient sound design, and clean animations that enhance the atmosphere without overwhelming the core mechanics. The lush visuals and immersive sound effects help maintain a relaxing yet competitive tone throughout gameplay, and each advancement you apply to your cards feels visually and functionally satisfying. The interface is clean and responsive, making it easy to track your deck’s development and manage your resources.

The gameplay loop revolves around balancing risk and reward. At the start of each match, all players have an identical set of basic cards, many of which contain "blight" symbols that can cause a turn to be forfeited if you draw too many at once. This push-your-luck mechanic adds a layer of tension to each turn, forcing players to consider whether to draw more cards and risk spoiling their turn, or play it safe and make fewer moves. As the game progresses, players spend mana to purchase advancements, which are placed directly onto the cards in their deck, effectively customizing and evolving them with each turn. This crafting element provides long-term strategic depth, as players can pursue specific synergies and build toward powerful combinations that maximize their scoring potential.

Mystic Vale includes several expansion packs, such as Vale of Magic, Vale of the Wild, and Mana Storm, which introduce new advancements, vale cards, and mechanics that significantly increase variety and replayability. These expansions layer new tactical possibilities onto the core gameplay without disrupting its elegant structure. Each one introduces novel strategies and subtle rules that veteran players will appreciate, while still being accessible enough for newer players to pick up with a bit of guidance. The game’s AI opponents offer different difficulty levels in solo mode, and the online multiplayer functionality allows for smooth matchmaking, whether with friends or random players.

Despite its many strengths, Mystic Vale does have limitations, especially in terms of long-term engagement. While the card crafting system is undoubtedly innovative, some players may find that optimal strategies emerge over time, leading to repetitive play patterns across multiple sessions. The game leans heavily on the strength of its core mechanic, and although expansions help diversify gameplay, the overall loop can become predictable once you've experienced most of the card combinations. Additionally, while the AI offers a decent challenge, it may not consistently simulate the nuanced tactics of a skilled human opponent, particularly for experienced players looking for deeper competition.

Another consideration is that Mystic Vale doesn’t offer a strong narrative component or campaign structure. It is firmly a systems-driven game, focusing on mechanics over story. While the thematic elements and art direction are cohesive and attractive, they serve more as a backdrop than a driving force. Players looking for a rich, evolving narrative or a branching single-player campaign may find the experience somewhat static. However, for those who value strategic planning, efficient engine-building, and a unique approach to deck construction, the game delivers a satisfying and replayable experience.

In its current form, Mystic Vale stands as a shining example of how a well-designed physical card game can be successfully adapted into the digital space. It remains faithful to its source material while offering the conveniences and enhancements of modern digital play. Whether you're a fan of board games looking for a solo experience or a competitive player seeking a strategic card game with a twist, Mystic Vale offers a compelling package. With beautiful visuals, clever mechanics, and a refreshing take on deck-building, it earns its place as one of the more original and engaging digital card games available on Steam.

Mystic Vale on Steam is a PC port of a board game designed by [url=https://www.alderac.com/mystic-vale/]Alderac Entertainment Group[/url].  Players take the role of druids competing to restore life to the vale.  It is essentially a deck-builder but instead of adding cards to your deck, you add effects to your cards.  It can be played solo against computer opponents or online with friends.  

The graphics are good - the UI looks nice and the card art approaches par with Magic the Gathering.  The sound effects are adequate and the UI is pretty good once you understand how the game works.  It does have a number of unconventional rules, though, so be prepared to be puzzled for a while before it starts to make sense.  Rather than explain it here, I'll simply link you to [url=https://www.alderac.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/mystic-vale-rulebook.pdf]the official rulebook[/url] - it's not long and it's a good idea to read it before you get started.  

The core conceit of the game is the idea of building your cards rather than (or in addition to) building your deck.  Instead of choosing or buying a card, you choose a top, bottom or middle section to add to a card.  Your deck of twenty cards will be mostly blank to start with but you'll add effects that generate resources or do other things and, ideally, add sections that coordinate with other sections to produce more powerful effects.  

The problem is that there's no strategy around which section (top, middle or bottom) to pick and this makes choosing a feel-bad mechanic.  If you have played Gloomhaven, you'll know that normally attack actions are found on the top half of a card and move actions are on the bottom.  This means that when you choose a card that has a bottom attack or top move, you unlock new tactical possibilities in combat.  In Mystic Vale, you can be trying to build a strong card but be blocked by a previous choice that you had to make at random because you had no idea what choices you'd have in the future.  You can finally afford to buy the combo section you want?  Too bad you already filled that section on the card where it would matter!

Part of the problem is that a Mystic Vale match is set up by taking a selection of the card sections from the available pool.  Unlike Dominion where you have a known selection from the possible card pool, Mystic Vale's selection is random.  In Dominion you can strategise from your knowledge of the cards that are available but in Mystic Vale you won't know whether a given section is available until it shows up.  This means that players will sometimes invest in potential combinations that turn out to be ineffective, wasteful or even impossible.  

Unfortunately, since scoring points directly leads to the end of the match, players will often find the match is decided by the time they've found their footing in terms of what sections are available and how they should be playing.  You can increase the number of points it takes to end the match but having good or bad luck in the early rounds still seems to have more impact than game plans requiring longevity.  

As far as mechanics are concerned, the creators have done their best to explore the available design space.  While there are a lot of different discard effects that boil down to the same thing, there are other kinds of effects that make different game plans possible.  While the base game doesn't take a lot of decision-making power to play, the expansions greatly increase the number of potential options and interactions.  

Unfortunately, even the breadth of new mechanics in the expansions don't help Mystic Vale overcome its basic limitations as a game and this brings me to the worst problem of all:  Mystic Vale is not a game.  

You see, while individual players can approach a match with a variety of game plans, there's essentially no interplay or counterplay between players.  You all buy from the same selection of sections and you all take from the same pool of victory points but nothing in your deck will ever interact with anything in another deck.  While you can see what sections other players choose and you can hope to snag something before an opponent does, you can't actually do anything to interrupt or alter another player's game plan or decision-making process.  Instead of being a game, Mystic Vale is a race against ghosts and by the time you know you're losing, it will almost certainly be too late to catch up.  

It turned out, after I looked into it, that Mystic Vale was developed as another use of the card-building technology originally developed for one of AEG's other games; [url=https://www.alderac.com/edge-of-darkness/]Edge of Darkness[/url] which is, apparently, a lot more involved.  Mystic Vale only exists because the manufacturer didn't want to be printing out these parts for only a single game.  

All that being said, Mystic Vale is still an interesting experiment.  It tries a lot of things that other deck-builders haven't tried and it explores a lot of options within those constraints.  Mystic Vale is not itself a good game but I think there are lessons to be taken from it that could inform future games in the genre.  Overall, I'm glad that it exists but most people just plain don't need to play it.  Maybe go and try that other game or just wait for someone to build something good on this foundation.

Mystic Vale has been a favorite tabletop game of our gaming group for years.  We currently own all the expansions.  The digital version contains many of the positive aspects of the game, such as attractive graphics, interesting game play, and a variety of expansions to add.  It also makes the logistical aspects, such as sleeving the cards, set up, and tear down, painless compared to the tabletop version.   Adding card animation was a nice touch.

That said, there are downsides to digital.  First, you cannot choose to leave out cards you don't care for that will clog up the offerings on display during a game.  This results in some games where there is nothing anyone wants to buy, but to clear space, you must.  It also does not provide for leaving out certain options contained in an expansion, which we often do on tabletop.  Because of this, we rarely play with the Mana Storm expansion.  It would be helpful if excluding cards were possible, as in some other digital versions of games.   Also, we are all disappointed that more of the expansions are not available here on Steam.  They just stopped after Mana Storm and never released any more.  Perhaps because Mana Storm was not as popular?

I would really welcome the addition of more of the expansions, and options for card inclusion.  Overall, Mystic Vale is a great game and we still really enjoy playing it online when we can't get together.  For those who have never tried it, it's quite an interesting set of mechanics not often found elsewhere in Euros.  Despite the downsides, I would recommend the game.

As the board is replenished after every players turn, that means these options will simply pop up and be bought instantly in most cases. Either you are lucky and get some - or you basically lost. It's not a rare occurance to have 3 players around the same point range and the winner being at more than double. There is no way to stop a running engine and overtaking one requires even more luck.
You can, however, push your luck. You will automatically draw cards until you reach the maximum amount of red symbols. Then it's up to you to risk another draw (or multiple). And that's what the game basically boils down to - calculated risk and lots of luck. If that's your thing, the game will keep you entertained for a few hours. If you are looking for more of a strategic deckbuilder like Dominion, Mystic Vale is not quite it.

TLDR: If you like the board game, then you'll most likely like the video game. I'd recommend it.

The translation from board game to video game is pretty good, but there is nothing to compare to "house rules." 

[h1]Level 1 Advancement Limitation Madness[/h1]
We like to play with a lot more level one advancements, for example. It's pretty dumb that several of the level two advancements specifically have abilities that refer to level one advancements, but they usually come out after all the level one advancements are gone anyway. That's annoying.

[h1]Duplicate Annoyance[/h1]
Another house rule we use that improves the game a lot is for a player to discard one card from those available to purchase if it is a duplicate and immediately get a replacement option. This is great for getting some card-turnover when there are not-so-great cards out. Playing with a not-very-bright AI in the game can help as the AI is likely to buy some of the less desirable duplicates, but this isn't really a "fix." 

[h1]Leader Options[/h1]
Yet a third house rule we enjoy is being able to pick from a larger selection of leaders. Having only two options for leaders can feel really cramped. What if you really hate both options?

[h1]Timer[/h1]
You may put a timer on turns, but thus far I've found this to be a bad idea. Early in the game it is easy to work with a time limit, but as your field and options become more complex, a time limit becomes unreasonable.

[h1]Amulets[/h1]
For some reason I have experienced being unable to evoke my amulet after making one purchase and wanting to evoke it before making a second. I can't imagine any good reason for this limitation. Also, I've had times when the "undo" option wasn't there and it was very unclear why that would/could be the case when I had [i]not[/i] bought something with an immediate effect.

[h1]Extended VP Pool[/h1]
I really love that there is an option to play with an above-normal amount of VP chits in the pool. We often play to 30 VPs with two players instead of 23 when playing the board game. However, the extended pool in the video game is an obnoxious amount. It's fun to do that on rare occasion, but some middle-ground would be nice. I'm not sure why we can't just manually type in the amount of victory point tokens we'd like to play to.

[h1]Custom Decks[/h1]
One last very special sort of "house rule" thing that is possible with the board game but not with the video game is this: we created a "play in parallel" way to enjoy Mystic Vale where each player has their own area to buy from that is not shared with other players, and each grouping of advancements and vales are *meant* to combine nicely with each other, meaning each player gets to enjoy more strong combinations – which are what I find most satisfying anyhow. There is, obviously, no way to do anything remotely like this in the digital version. You can select and unselect expansions, but that's it. You can't even remove a card you find annoying from play.

First off, let me say that I have a physical copy of [i]Mystic Vale[/i] with the [i]Vale of the Wild[/i] expansion. I've been on the fence about getting [i]Nemesis[/i] for the solo-play variant, mostly because I'm not 100% on board with the other mechanics that expansion includes.

That aside, this digital version provides [b]a lot[/b] of the bookeeping for the player. The game filling out the field for you, as well as all the in-game counters are all incredibly welcome. I just kinda wish I had more control over what to include with the various DLC. I have the season pass, so, for example, I think it might be interesting to use base + [i]Vale of Magic[/i] for the commons and vale cards, but use only the leaders from [i]Vale of the Wild[/i] and amulets from [i]Mana Storm[/i]. Though, I can understand if this is only a pipe dream on my part.

A card crafting game, based on a table top game. You don’t build decks by adding cards, but you add enhancements to your starting deck. A starting deck consists of some empty cards and cards with some enhancements. But enhancements might come with negatives. The game is played over several rounds until the common win-points are used up. Besides enhancements there are as well special cards. 

What is special?
The craft/ enhance your cards is a really nice mechanic, as the ones you build up you want to keep and there are no cards which you don’t want to use, as you can enhance any of the cards. And a round does not take longer than 30 minutes, normally.

How does it feel to play?
It has a nice fantasy romantic art style, solid/ fitting animations and unobtrusive music. The game feels relaxing, as it is not about fighting but about building (the theme is about making waste land fertile again).

Little interaction.
All players want to build up and don’t fight each other. This is nice, but as well a bit boring, as it would be nice to have more direct interactions. The only interactions are about taking enhancements/ special cards from the common deck.

Summary.
If you like card games and want a different mechanic I can really recommend it. If you hate non-intense games, don’t play it. It feels good to relax for a round in between of an intense fighting card deck game. I think the price is fair! The season pass is worth it.

Mystic Vale (MV) is a card game with a unique mechanic that merges up to three cards into one, with gorgeous fantasy art (which even animates when you hover your mouse over a card), and with fairly relaxed gameplay - while players do compete for victory points, they cannot really act against each other.

It is marketed as a deck-buiding game, which I consider as a bit of a stretch, since players start every game with the same set of basic cards. The "deck-building" takes place by adding up to two cards from a public pool to your deck each turn. I would prefer the term "in-game deck-building" to be used for such games, otherwise there will always be customers who buy them under the expectation that they include an out-of-game deck-building mechanic that may not actually be present.

MV does make use of an innovative mechanic that lets you merge different cards into one. Each card in your deck consists of three slots, and when you start the game, almost all slots in your deck are empty. The cards from the public pool that you add to your deck over time, are actually just "sleeves", and each sleeve will take up one slot on the card of your choice. This means that you can construct very powerful cards by combining sleeves with good synergies on the same card. The mechanics aren't very complex, but diverse enough to allow for very different strategies.

For example, you could combine a sleeve that has powerful positive _and_ negative effect, with another sleeve that cancels the negatives. Or you could combine a sleeve that gives you a bonus for each "X" element on the same card, with sleeves that provide lots of those "X" elements.

Games are usually pretty quick, as players compete for a limited supply of victory points. This can be considered a boon for a fairly casual card game like this one, but it also makes the game very dependent on luck. In order to execute a strategy, a) a card that fits it needs to be in the public pool on your turn, b) you need to have the resources to acquire it, and c) you then need to draw that card often enough from your deck to make use of it. If the cards that you need don't show up in the pool, or if they were drawn and purchased in an opponent's turn, or if they do show up in a turn where you drew a bad hand with not enough resources to buy them, or if you assembled an extremely powerful endgame card that gets shuffled at the bottom of your deck and you don't even draw it before another player wins the game, then plain bad luck may have thwarted your entire strategy. That's not necessarily a bad thing because it ensures that even the worst player will occasionally feel the thrill of winning, but if you prefer skill to have a much higher effect than luck, then other games may suit you better.

It's also noteworthy that the game provides almost no interaction between players. Every player builds up their own "valley" but they have no means of impacting an opponent's progress. (In theory you could specifically take cards that another player needs out of the pool, but if those cards don't actually help your own strategy, then you won't catch up, and if there are more players, then you'd just be the kingmaker for somebody else.) Once again this can be seen as a boon: The age-old "You worked against me, but I thought you like me!" problem won't occur with this game. On the other hand, players who prefer more competitive gameplay will miss opportunities to throw wrenches into the frontrunner's strategies. In fact, in my experience, 4-player games are are often decided by someone's luck to get just the cards they need, and then running away with no way for the others to stop them or catch up.

MV's UI reflects the game's focus on each player's own build-up. You can see what each other player is doing, but peeking at their "valley" and "field" requires three different clicks per player, there is no way to see all players' cards on the entire "table" at once. So if you want to adjust your strategy depending on what your opponents are doing, you'd need to click through them every time, which is rather unwieldy and makes me think that you're probably just not supposed to do that regularly.

Some cards are much better than others (they help almost every strategy), while others require specific synergies to be useful at all. If a player gets some of those particularly good cards in their first few turns, while another player can't get anything special, then that affects their chance to win right form the start. You need to get lucky to have one of those good cards added to the pool in your own turn, so that you can buy it immediately, because otherwise one of your opponents certainly will. The number of players has a pretty huge effect here - in a 2-player game, you may still have a chance to get that card in your next turn. In a 4-player game, probably not unless every other player has an unlucky turn.

In the end, MV is a beautiful, positive, conflict-free, family-friendly, casual card game with an interesting and innovative "card assembly" mechanic. The things that it wants to do, it does well. If you prefer competitive and/or skill-based gameplay though, then it probably won't satisfy you. Personally, even though I _usually_ prefer something a bit more skill-based, I still like to play MV if I'm in the mood for something quick and casual.

Mystic Vale has grown to be one of my favorite Deckbuilders and I've played quite the amount of deckbuilders on Steam and on my iPad. You have a bunch of cards, some with fertile soil, most with cursed lands and a few blanks. Each card has 3 slots where you can place advancements, which you can buy from the middle row to enhance your cards. Your hand can vary in size, as you play cards till there are 3 Decay symbols, that's the field you use for the turn. Then there are also the Vale cards, which can be purchased through symbols on the cards in your field. You can play a gamble and add extra cards to the field with the risk of spoiling (1 decay too much), which means you skip the turn (and you get an extra point in the next turn to buy advancements).

Due to the way the game plays and you build your deck, combined with decisions like deliberately spoiling and what your opponents do, there are various choices to be made. Do you continue on your current strategy or are you going to counter what an opponent does? Will you risk spoiling to get that on-deck card that would greatly enhance the choices for your turn at the risk of losing the whole field? Do you gather Vale cards to enhance flexibility or do you keep them for the points?

The art too is lovely as the cards "live" when you hover over them or click them. The music too is good, it fits the feeling of being a druid trying to heal the land. I also have all the DLC and the added cards, leaders and amulets greatly enhance the way you play. They provide extra options and choices and like the rest of the game, the art is lovely.

Games are quick, they usually run somewhere between 10 and 20 minutes for me, I usually play against 3. In that it fits the rest of the Deckbuilders that the games aren't that long.

Fun and faithful adaptation of the physical board game. Very fun game to play for a round or two when short on time. I really hope to see additional expansions released on steam.

This is a deck builder with the unique twist of keeping the same number of cards and customizing them one third at a time. Of course in computer form, you don't have to deal with putting these cards in sleeves, or damaging the sleeves. The game itself has great art, and in this form you can enjoy some nice animation.
Fun.

Fun "deck builder" with a twist - deck size stays the same, but you're building the cards - each card has a top, middle, and bottom section, and you buy sections during your turn and add them to one of the cards played that turn. Lots of variety and fun to make combos both on a card and between cards.
Pretty okay. lacks interactivity like most deck builders. I still enjoy it from time to time.
